7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|ASGI frame.what_it_is: ASGI (Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface) is the successor to WSGI — a standard interface between Python web servers and applications/frameworks that supports asynchronous request handling, WebSockets, and long-lived connections. FastAPI is built on top of Starlette, an ASGI framework, which is why every FastAPI app is 'async by default' — route handlers can be declared with `async def` and run on an event loop instead of one-thread-per-request.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|ASGI frame.why_it_exists: WSGI (used by Flask/Django classic) is fundamentally synchronous: one worker thread/process blocks for the entire duration of a request, including any I/O wait (DB query, HTTP call to another service, LLM API call). For ML serving workloads — where a request often spends most of its time waiting on a model inference call, a vector DB lookup, or a downstream LLM API — that blocking model wastes resources. ASGI lets a single worker handle thousands of concurrent connections by suspending a coroutine while it waits on I/O and running another one in the meantime, which is exactly the profile of an LLM-backed API (slow network calls, not CPU-bound work) needs.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|ASGI frame.how_it_works: An ASGI server (Uvicorn, Hypercorn) implements the event loop and speaks the ASGI protocol — a callable `async def app(scope, receive, send)` — to the framework. Starlette/FastAPI implements that callable, routing each incoming connection's `scope` (HTTP request, WebSocket, lifespan event) to the matching path handler. When a handler is `async def`, FastAPI awaits it directly on the event loop; when it's a plain `def`, FastAPI runs it in a thread pool (via `run_in_threadpool`) so a blocking call doesn't stall the whole event loop. This dual model is why FastAPI supports both async and sync handlers without breaking concurrency.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|ASGI frame.use_when: Use FastAPI/ASGI for any ML serving API where requests involve waiting on external I/O — calling an LLM provider, querying a vector store, hitting a feature store, streaming tokens back to a client, or fanning out to multiple microservices. It's also the right choice when you need WebSockets or Server-Sent Events for streaming responses.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|ASGI frame.avoid_when: If your endpoint does pure CPU-bound work (e.g., a heavy NumPy computation or a synchronous model `.predict()` call that holds the GIL), async doesn't help and can hurt — that work still blocks the event loop unless offloaded to a thread/process pool or a separate worker process (e.g., via `run_in_executor` or a task queue). In those cases the bottleneck is CPU, not concurrency, and you scale with more worker processes (Gunicorn workers) rather than more async concurrency.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|ASGI frame.what_goes_wrong: The most common mistake is calling a blocking/synchronous library (e.g., `requests`, a sync DB driver, or `time.sleep`) inside an `async def` route handler. This blocks the entire event loop, so every other concurrent request on that worker stalls — under load, latency spikes for ALL users, not just the one making the blocking call. The fix is to use async-native clients (`httpx.AsyncClient`, `asyncpg`, async ORM sessions) or, if a sync library is unavoidable, declare the handler as plain `def` so FastAPI offloads it to a thread pool.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|ASGI frame.real_example: An inference API has an `async def predict(...)` endpoint that internally calls `requests.post()` to an LLM provider synchronously. Under 50 concurrent users, p99 latency jumps from 200ms to 8 seconds because each blocking call freezes the shared event loop for its full duration. Switching to `httpx.AsyncClient` with `await client.post(...)` (or making the function a plain `def` so it runs in FastAPI's thread pool) restores concurrent throughput.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Type hints.what_it_is: FastAPI uses standard Python type hints on function parameters and Pydantic models to automatically validate, parse, and serialize request/response data. Declaring a parameter as `item: Item` (where `Item` is a Pydantic `BaseModel`) tells FastAPI to parse the incoming JSON body into that model, validate every field's type and constraints, and return a 422 error with a detailed diagnostic if validation fails — all without writing any manual `if`/`try` validation code.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Type hints.why_it_exists: Before FastAPI, validating incoming JSON in Python web frameworks meant writing manual checks (`if not isinstance(data['age'], int): raise ...`) or bolting on a separate schema library (marshmallow, voluptuous) that duplicated the type information already implied by your function signature. FastAPI's design goal was 'the type hints you'd write anyway for editor autocomplete and mypy should ALSO be the runtime validation and the API documentation' — eliminating duplication between code, validation, and docs.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Type hints.how_it_works: At startup, FastAPI inspects each route function's signature via Python's `typing` and `inspect` modules. For parameters typed as Pydantic models, it builds a JSON Schema from the model's fields (including `Field(..., gt=0)`-style constraints) and registers it for OpenAPI docs. On each request, it instantiates the Pydantic model from the parsed request body — Pydantic's validators run (type coercion, enum checks, regex/length constraints, custom `@validator`/`@field_validator` methods) — and either passes the validated object into your function or raises a `RequestValidationError`, which FastAPI's exception handler converts into a 422 response listing every failing field and why.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Type hints.use_when: Use Pydantic models for any non-trivial request body, response body, or settings object — anywhere you'd otherwise hand-write validation. Use nested models, `Field()` constraints (min/max length, regex, ranges), and `Enum` types to push validation rules into the schema so they're enforced consistently and documented automatically.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Type hints.avoid_when: For extremely simple endpoints with one or two scalar query parameters, plain typed function arguments (e.g., `q: str | None = None`) are simpler than wrapping them in a model — FastAPI validates these directly too. Also avoid over-nesting models so deeply that error messages become hard to map back to user input; flatten where the API contract allows.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Type hints.what_goes_wrong: A frequent gotcha is using a mutable default (e.g., `items: list = []`) in a Pydantic model or function signature — in plain Python this shares state across instances, though Pydantic models handle this correctly by default (unlike dataclasses) as long as you don't manually override `__init__`. Another common issue: silent type coercion surprises — Pydantic v1 by default coerces `"123"` (string) to `123` (int) for an `int` field, which can mask bad client data; Pydantic v2's strict mode or `Field(strict=True)` avoids this when exact types matter.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Type hints.real_example: A `/predict` endpoint accepts `class PredictRequest(BaseModel): text: str; max_tokens: int = Field(256, gt=0, le=4096); temperature: float = Field(0.7, ge=0.0, le=2.0)`. A client sending `{"text": "hello", "max_tokens": 10000}` gets an automatic 422 response: `{"detail": [{"loc": ["body", "max_tokens"], "msg": "Input should be less than or equal to 4096", ...}]}` — without the handler code ever running, and the same constraint shows up in `/docs` as the field's allowed range.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Path param.what_it_is: FastAPI infers where each piece of request data comes from based on how a function parameter is declared: variables in the URL path template (`/items/{item_id}`) become path parameters, simple scalar parameters not in the path become query parameters (`?skip=0&limit=10`), and parameters typed as Pydantic models become the JSON request body. This gives a single, consistent way to define an endpoint's entire input contract directly in its signature.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Path param.why_it_exists: REST APIs conventionally split request data across the URL path (identifying a resource), the query string (filtering/pagination options), and the body (the payload being created/updated). Without a framework convention, developers manually parse `request.path_params`, `request.query_params`, and `request.json()` and then validate each — repetitive and error-prone. FastAPI's signature-based inference removes that boilerplate while keeping each parameter's source explicit and documented.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Path param.how_it_works: FastAPI parses the path template (e.g., `/users/{user_id}/items/{item_id}`) and matches parameter names against it — any function parameter whose name appears in `{}` is a path parameter and is required. Remaining parameters that are simple types (`str`, `int`, `bool`, `float`, or `Optional`/`= default`) become query parameters. A parameter typed as a Pydantic `BaseModel` (or explicitly wrapped in `Body(...)`) is parsed from the JSON request body. You can mix all three in one function signature, and FastAPI assembles them correctly per request, validating each against its declared type/constraints.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Path param.use_when: Use path parameters for identifying a specific resource (`/models/{model_id}`), query parameters for optional filters, pagination, or feature flags (`?status=active&page=2`), and the request body for the structured payload of POST/PUT/PATCH operations (e.g., the input features for a prediction, or a new resource's fields).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Path param.avoid_when: Don't put large or sensitive payloads (e.g., full feature vectors, file contents, secrets) into query parameters — URLs are logged by proxies, browsers, and servers, and have practical length limits. Don't use path parameters for optional or filter-like data; reserve them for resource identity so routes stay RESTful and cacheable.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Path param.what_goes_wrong: A common bug is parameter name collisions or ordering issues that aren't actually bugs but look confusing: FastAPI determines a parameter's source purely by name-matching against the path template and by type, not by the order you declare them, so a query parameter that happens to share a name with a Pydantic model field can shadow it unexpectedly. Another issue: forgetting that path parameters are always required and always strings unless typed otherwise — `/items/{item_id}` with `item_id: int` will 422 on `/items/abc` automatically, which is correct but can surprise developers expecting a 404 instead.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Path param.real_example:
`@app.put("/models/{model_id}/predict")
async def predict(model_id: str, version: int = 1, request: PredictRequest = ...):` — `model_id` comes from the URL path, `version` is an optional query parameter defaulting to 1 (`/models/gpt/predict?version=2`), and `request` is parsed from the JSON body. All three are validated and documented automatically in `/docs` with no manual parsing code.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|HTTPBearer.what_it_is: `HTTPBearer` is a FastAPI/Starlette security utility that extracts a Bearer token from the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` HTTP header and makes it available to route handlers via dependency injection. It's the standard building block for JWT-based authentication: the security scheme handles extracting and validating the *presence* of a token, while your application code decodes and verifies the JWT itself.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|HTTPBearer.why_it_exists: Most production APIs need to authenticate callers via a token issued at login (often a JWT signed by an auth server or identity provider). Manually reading the `Authorization` header, checking the `Bearer ` prefix, and returning a proper 401/403 with the right `WWW-Authenticate` header on every protected route is repetitive. `HTTPBearer` standardizes this extraction as a reusable dependency and also registers the security requirement in the OpenAPI schema, so `/docs` shows a padlock icon and an 'Authorize' button for protected endpoints.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|HTTPBearer.how_it_works: `HTTPBearer()` is instantiated once and used as a FastAPI dependency: `credentials: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials = Depends(security)`. On each request, FastAPI calls this dependency, which inspects the `Authorization` header; if it's missing or malformed, it raises an `HTTPException(403)` automatically. If present, it returns an `HTTPAuthorizationCredentials` object with `.scheme` ('Bearer') and `.credentials` (the raw token string). Your handler (or another dependency layered on top) then passes `.credentials` to a JWT library (e.g., `python-jose` or `PyJWT`) to verify the signature, expiry, and claims, and to look up/construct the current user.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|HTTPBearer.use_when: Use `HTTPBearer` (often combined with a `get_current_user` dependency) for stateless authentication of API clients — mobile apps, SPAs, service-to-service calls — where the token is a signed JWT containing claims like user ID, roles, and expiry, issued by your own auth endpoint or an external identity provider (Auth0, Cognito, Keycloak).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|HTTPBearer.avoid_when: For browser-based session login flows where you control both frontend and backend on the same domain, signed cookies with `SameSite`/`HttpOnly` flags may be simpler and more secure against XSS token theft than storing JWTs in `localStorage`. Also avoid rolling your own JWT verification logic from scratch — use a maintained library and verify signature, algorithm, expiry (`exp`), and issuer/audience claims explicitly to avoid classic JWT vulnerabilities (e.g., accepting `alg: none`).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|HTTPBearer.what_goes_wrong: A serious and common vulnerability is trusting the JWT's claimed algorithm header (`alg`) without pinning the expected algorithm — libraries that allow `alg: none` or let an attacker switch from RS256 (asymmetric) to HS256 (symmetric, using the public key as the HMAC secret) can be tricked into accepting forged tokens. Always specify `algorithms=["RS256"]` (or whatever you use) explicitly when calling `jwt.decode()`. Another common issue: forgetting to check token expiry (`exp`) or not handling clock skew, leading to tokens that are accepted long after they should have expired (or rejected just before they should).

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Dependency.what_it_is: FastAPI's dependency injection (DI) system lets route handlers declare what they need (a DB session, the current authenticated user, a config object, a loaded ML model) as function parameters wrapped in `Depends(...)`, and FastAPI resolves, calls, and injects those dependencies automatically before running the handler. Dependencies can themselves depend on other dependencies, forming a resolution graph.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Dependency.why_it_exists: Without DI, every handler that needs a database connection or the current user has to manually open/close connections or re-implement auth-checking logic, leading to duplication and inconsistent resource management (e.g., forgetting to close a DB session). DI centralizes this: define `get_db()` once, and every handler that needs a session just adds `db: Session = Depends(get_db)` — FastAPI handles calling it, running any setup/teardown (via `yield`), and caching the result per-request if the same dependency is needed multiple times.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Dependency.how_it_works: A dependency is just a callable (function or class). FastAPI inspects the handler's signature for `Depends(callable)` parameters, recursively resolves the callable's own parameters (which may themselves be `Depends(...)`), and calls each one — async dependencies are awaited, sync ones run in a thread pool if needed. Dependencies defined with `yield` (e.g., `def get_db(): db = SessionLocal(); try: yield db; finally: db.close()`) act as context managers: code after `yield` runs as cleanup after the response is sent, even if an exception occurred. Within a single request, FastAPI caches a dependency's result so it's computed once even if multiple handlers/sub-dependencies request it.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Dependency.use_when: Use DI for anything that needs setup/teardown per request (DB sessions, transaction-scoped connections), anything shared across many endpoints (auth/current-user checks, rate limiters, feature flags), or anything you want to swap out in tests (override `app.dependency_overrides[get_db]` with a test DB fixture without touching handler code).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Dependency.avoid_when: Don't use DI for things that are truly global and stateless (e.g., a constant config dict) — a module-level singleton is simpler. Avoid deeply nested dependency chains that make it hard to trace what's actually being constructed for a request; if a dependency graph becomes a maze, consider consolidating into a single composed dependency.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Dependency.what_goes_wrong: A common mistake is loading an expensive resource (e.g., an ML model checkpoint) inside a per-request dependency without caching — this reloads the model on every single request, killing latency and memory. Expensive, request-independent resources (loaded models, DB connection pools) should be created once at app startup (via the `lifespan` context manager or `@app.on_event("startup")`) and stored on `app.state`, then a lightweight dependency just retrieves the already-loaded object from `app.state`. Another pitfall: forgetting `try/finally` in a `yield`-based dependency, so a DB session isn't closed if the handler raises — leaking connections under error conditions.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Dependency.real_example:
```python\[email protected](lifespan=lambda app: load_model_on_startup(app))

def get_model(request: Request):
    return request.app.state.model  # loaded once at startup

def get_db():
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db
    finally:
        db.close()

@app.post("/predict")
async def predict(payload: PredictRequest, model=Depends(get_model), db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    result = model.predict(payload.features)
    db.add(PredictionLog(input=payload.dict(), output=result))
    db.commit()
    return {"prediction": result}
```
The model is loaded once and reused across all requests; the DB session is opened per request and always closed, even on error.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Background.what_it_is: `BackgroundTasks` is a FastAPI feature that lets a route handler schedule a function to run *after* the response has been sent to the client, within the same process. You declare a `background_tasks: BackgroundTasks` parameter, call `background_tasks.add_task(func, *args, **kwargs)`, and FastAPI runs `func` once the response is on its way out — without making the client wait for it.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Background.why_it_exists: Many operations triggered by a request don't need to block the response: logging a prediction to a database, sending a notification email, updating an analytics counter, or writing an audit log. Making the client wait for these adds latency for no user-facing benefit. `BackgroundTasks` provides a lightweight, in-process way to defer such work without standing up a separate task queue for simple cases.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Background.how_it_works: FastAPI collects all tasks added via `add_task` during the handling of a request into a list. After the response body has been fully sent to the client (the ASGI server has finished writing the response), FastAPI executes each queued task in order — async functions are awaited on the same event loop, sync functions run via the thread pool. Because they run on the same worker process, they share the worker's resources (memory, connections) but also compete with it for CPU/event-loop time.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Background.use_when: Use `BackgroundTasks` for quick, best-effort, fire-and-forget work tied to a single request — writing a log line, incrementing a metric, sending a single notification — where occasional loss (e.g., if the worker crashes right after responding) is acceptable and where the work is light enough not to noticeably delay the next request on that worker.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Background.avoid_when: Avoid `BackgroundTasks` for anything that's slow, resource-intensive, must survive a process restart, needs retries, or needs to be distributed across workers/machines — e.g., sending bulk emails, retraining a model, processing a large file, or any task where failure must be observable and retried. For those, use a real task queue (Celery, RQ, Arq) or a stream/queue (Kafka, SQS) consumed by separate workers.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Background.what_goes_wrong: A background task that raises an exception does so silently from the client's perspective — the response was already sent successfully, so the client sees a 200 even though the background work failed. Without explicit logging/monitoring inside the task, these failures go unnoticed. Another pitfall: a long-running background task on a worker with a single event loop delays that worker from picking up its next request, effectively reducing throughput — under load this creates a 'task queue in disguise' with no visibility, retries, or backpressure.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Background.real_example:
```python
def log_prediction(payload: dict, result: dict):
    db = SessionLocal()
    db.add(PredictionLog(input=payload, output=result))
    db.commit()
    db.close()

@app.post("/predict")
async def predict(req: PredictRequest, background_tasks: BackgroundTasks):
    result = model.predict(req.features)
    background_tasks.add_task(log_prediction, req.dict(), result)
    return {"prediction": result}  # client gets this immediately; logging happens after
```
If `log_prediction` raises (e.g., DB connection error), the client still sees a successful prediction — the failure must be caught and logged inside the task itself to be noticed.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Streaming.what_it_is: `StreamingResponse` (and `EventSourceResponse` for Server-Sent Events) lets a FastAPI endpoint send the response body incrementally as chunks become available, rather than buffering the entire response in memory and sending it all at once. This is the standard mechanism for streaming LLM output token-by-token to a client, mirroring how OpenAI/Anthropic APIs stream completions.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Streaming.why_it_exists: LLM generation produces tokens incrementally over potentially many seconds. Waiting for the full response before sending anything means the user stares at a blank screen for the entire generation time — bad UX for chat interfaces. Streaming lets the client start rendering tokens as soon as the model produces them, dramatically improving perceived latency (time-to-first-token) even if total generation time is unchanged.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Streaming.how_it_works: `StreamingResponse` takes an (async) generator/iterator that yields chunks of bytes or strings. FastAPI/Starlette reads from this generator and writes each chunk to the HTTP response as it's produced, using chunked transfer encoding (or SSE framing with `text/event-stream` content type for `EventSourceResponse`). For LLM serving, the generator typically wraps the model's streaming API (e.g., `model.generate(stream=True)` or an async iterator over an LLM provider's streaming response) — each `yield` corresponds to one or more new tokens, often formatted as an SSE `data: {...}\n\n` event so the client (e.g., using `EventSource` or `fetch` with a `ReadableStream`) can parse incremental updates.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Streaming.use_when: Use streaming for any chat/completion endpoint where total generation time is more than ~1 second and the client can render incremental output (chat UIs, CLIs printing tokens as they arrive). Also useful for streaming large file downloads or exports without loading everything into memory.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Streaming.avoid_when: Don't stream for endpoints where the client needs the complete, validated response before doing anything (e.g., a classification endpoint returning a single label/score) — streaming adds complexity (client-side parsing, reconnection handling) with no UX benefit there. Also be cautious with streaming behind proxies/load balancers that buffer responses (some default Nginx configs buffer by default) — streaming benefits disappear unless buffering is disabled for that route.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Streaming.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is that intermediate infrastructure (reverse proxies, API gateways, certain `gunicorn` worker classes) buffers the entire response before forwarding it, defeating streaming and reintroducing the full latency — `proxy_buffering off` (Nginx) or using an ASGI-aware worker (Uvicorn) is required end-to-end. Another pitfall: if the generator raises partway through, the client has already received a 200 status and partial headers — there's no clean way to signal an error via HTTP status anymore, so errors must be encoded *within* the stream (e.g., an SSE `event: error` message) and handled by the client.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Streaming.real_example:
```python
async def token_stream(prompt: str):
    async for token in llm.astream(prompt):
        yield f"data: {json.dumps({'token': token})}\n\n"
    yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"

@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(req: ChatRequest):
    return StreamingResponse(token_stream(req.prompt), media_type="text/event-stream")
```
The client opens an `EventSource`/`fetch` stream and renders each token as it arrives, giving a typewriter effect instead of waiting for the full response.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|CORS middl.what_it_is: `CORSMiddleware` (from `fastapi.middleware.cors`) configures Cross-Origin Resource Sharing headers, telling browsers which origins (domains), HTTP methods, and headers are allowed to make requests to your API from JavaScript running on a different domain. Without it, a browser blocks frontend JavaScript on `app.example.com` from calling an API on `api.example.com` due to the same-origin policy.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|CORS middl.why_it_exists: Browsers enforce the same-origin policy as a security default: a script loaded from one origin cannot make requests to a different origin unless that origin explicitly opts in via CORS response headers. Modern web apps almost always have a separate frontend (React/Vue app on one domain or port) and backend API (FastAPI on another) — without CORS configuration, every `fetch`/`axios` call from the frontend to the API would be blocked by the browser, even though the request itself would succeed at the network level (CORS is enforced client-side by browsers, not by servers refusing connections).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|CORS middl.how_it_works: `app.add_middleware(CORSMiddleware, allow_origins=[...], allow_methods=[...], allow_headers=[...], allow_credentials=True/False)` registers middleware that inspects the `Origin` header on incoming requests. For 'simple' requests, it adds `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` (and related headers) to the response if the origin is permitted. For 'non-simple' requests (custom headers, methods like PUT/DELETE, or `Content-Type: application/json` with credentials), browsers first send a preflight `OPTIONS` request — the middleware responds to this preflight with the allowed methods/headers/origins, and only if the preflight succeeds does the browser send the actual request.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|CORS middl.use_when: Use CORS middleware whenever your API is called directly from browser JavaScript hosted on a different origin (different domain, subdomain, or port) than the API itself — which is the default for any SPA + API architecture, including local development (`localhost:3000` frontend, `localhost:8000` API are different origins).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|CORS middl.avoid_when: If your API is only ever called server-to-server (no browser JS involved) or always served from the exact same origin as the frontend (e.g., FastAPI serves both the API and the built frontend assets), CORS middleware isn't needed — CORS is purely a browser-enforced mechanism and irrelevant to non-browser clients (curl, mobile apps, server-to-server calls), which ignore it entirely.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|CORS middl.what_goes_wrong: The most dangerous mistake is `allow_origins=["*"]` combined with `allow_credentials=True` — browsers actually forbid this combination (a wildcard origin cannot be used with credentialed requests) because it would let any website make authenticated requests to your API using the user's cookies/session. Beyond that, even without credentials, a wildcard origin in production effectively means any website can call your API from a logged-in user's browser, which can enable CSRF-like abuse if the API relies on cookies for auth. The fix is to enumerate exact allowed origins (`["https://app.example.com"]`) rather than wildcarding in production.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|CORS middl.real_example:
```python
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["https://myapp.com", "http://localhost:3000"],
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["GET", "POST"],
    allow_headers=["Authorization", "Content-Type"],
)
```
Without this, a React app on `localhost:3000` calling `fetch("http://localhost:8000/predict")` would fail in the browser console with a CORS error, even though `curl http://localhost:8000/predict` from the terminal works fine.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Auto-gener.what_it_is: FastAPI automatically generates an OpenAPI (formerly Swagger) schema describing every route, its parameters, request/response models, and status codes — derived entirely from your type hints and Pydantic models — and serves an interactive Swagger UI at `/docs` (and a ReDoc UI at `/redoc`) where you can browse endpoints and execute live requests directly from the browser.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Auto-gener.why_it_exists: API documentation traditionally drifts out of sync with the actual code because it's maintained separately (a wiki page, a Postman collection) and nobody remembers to update it when an endpoint changes. By generating the schema directly from the code's type hints, the docs are *guaranteed* to match the implementation — if a field is required in the Pydantic model, it's required in the docs; if you add a query parameter, it appears in `/docs` automatically. This also enables auto-generating client SDKs from the OpenAPI spec.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Auto-gener.how_it_works: FastAPI builds a JSON Schema for every Pydantic model used in request bodies and response models (via `response_model=...`), and an OpenAPI 3.x document describing all routes, parameters, and schemas, exposed at `/openapi.json`. The `/docs` route serves a static Swagger UI page that fetches this JSON and renders it interactively (including a 'Try it out' button that issues real HTTP requests). `/redoc` renders the same schema with ReDoc's static three-panel layout. Both can be disabled (`docs_url=None`, `redoc_url=None`) or customized (title, description, tags via `app = FastAPI(title=..., description=..., openapi_tags=[...])`).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Auto-gener.use_when: Keep `/docs` enabled during development and for internal/partner APIs — it's the fastest way for any consumer (including yourself, six months later) to understand what an endpoint expects and returns, and to manually test it without writing a client. Use `Field(description=...)`, docstrings, and `tags=[...]` on routes to enrich the generated docs.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Auto-gener.avoid_when: For public production APIs, consider disabling or gating `/docs`/`/redoc`/`/openapi.json` behind auth — exposing your full API surface (including internal/admin routes) to anyone is an information-disclosure risk, especially if error responses or internal model field names leak implementation details.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Auto-gener.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is response models that don't match what's actually returned — if you don't set `response_model=...` (or it's too loose, e.g., `dict`), the docs show an inaccurate or empty schema for responses, misleading API consumers. Another pitfall: leaving `/docs` and `/openapi.json` publicly accessible on a production API reveals every endpoint, including ones not meant for external use (admin/debug routes), giving attackers a complete map of the API surface.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Auto-gener.real_example: Visiting `http://localhost:8000/docs` on a running FastAPI app shows every route grouped by tags, with expandable sections showing the exact request body schema (field names, types, whether required, example values) and possible response schemas/status codes — and a 'Try it out' button to send a real request with the 'Authorize' button pre-filling the `Authorization` header for `HTTPBearer`-protected routes.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Uvicorn +.what_it_is: Uvicorn is a lightweight, high-performance ASGI server (built on `uvloop`/`httptools`) that runs FastAPI applications; Gunicorn is a battle-tested process manager traditionally used for WSGI apps that, via the `uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker` class, can manage multiple Uvicorn worker processes. The common production pattern is 'Gunicorn manages N Uvicorn worker processes,' combining Gunicorn's process management (restarts, graceful reloads, worker recycling) with Uvicorn's ASGI/async serving.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Uvicorn +.why_it_exists: A single Uvicorn process runs on one CPU core (Python's GIL means one process = effectively one core for CPU-bound work, though async I/O concurrency within that process is still high). To use multiple CPU cores and to get production-grade process management (auto-restart on crash, graceful worker reloads during deploys, pre-fork worker model), you run multiple Uvicorn processes behind a manager. Gunicorn provides that manager with mature, well-understood operational tooling; alternatively, Uvicorn itself now supports `--workers N` directly for simpler setups, or Kubernetes can run N single-worker pods instead.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Uvicorn +.how_it_works: Gunicorn's master process forks N worker processes, each running its own Uvicorn event loop and its own copy of the FastAPI app (each with its own loaded model/memory if applicable — so N workers means N× the model memory footprint). Gunicorn handles binding the socket, distributing incoming connections across workers (the OS does this via shared socket accept), restarting workers that die or exceed memory limits, and graceful rolling restarts (`--graceful-timeout`) during deploys so in-flight requests finish before a worker is replaced.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Uvicorn +.use_when: Use this pattern (or `uvicorn --workers N`) for production deployments on a single host/VM/container where you want to use multiple CPU cores. The number of workers is typically `(2 × CPU cores) + 1` as a starting heuristic for I/O-bound workloads, tuned down for memory-heavy workloads (e.g., each worker loading a large model) where you might run 1 worker per GPU/large-model instance instead and scale horizontally via Kubernetes replicas.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Uvicorn +.avoid_when: In Kubernetes, it's often simpler to run a single Uvicorn worker per pod and scale horizontally via replica count + HPA — this gives more granular scaling and avoids the complexity of two layers of process management (Gunicorn workers + K8s pod replicas) both trying to handle restarts/scaling. Also avoid multiple workers when each worker loads a large GPU model — you'll multiply GPU memory usage and likely OOM; one worker per GPU is standard for large-model serving.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Uvicorn +.what_goes_wrong: Loading a large model (e.g., a multi-GB transformer) at app startup with `workers=4` loads 4 separate copies into memory (or onto the GPU), which can OOM a host that was sized assuming one copy. Another common issue: long-lived in-memory state (caches, in-progress request tracking) isn't shared across workers since each is a separate process — if your app relies on shared in-memory state, you need a shared external store (Redis) instead, or must pin to a single worker (which then can't use multiple cores).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Uvicorn +.real_example: `gunicorn main:app --workers 4 --worker-class uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --timeout 120 --graceful-timeout 30` runs 4 Uvicorn workers under Gunicorn; during a deploy, `--graceful-timeout 30` gives in-flight requests 30 seconds to complete before a worker being replaced is forcibly killed, avoiding dropped requests during rolling updates.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Your Skubi.what_it_is: This is a 'connect the dots' topic: taking the individual FastAPI building blocks (ASGI/async, Pydantic validation, path/query/body params, JWT auth, dependency injection, background tasks, streaming, CORS, OpenAPI docs, Uvicorn/Gunicorn) and recognizing how they compose into the actual production APIs you've built — e.g., a chatbot backend (Skubiq) and an inventory-management bot (InventoryBot). In interviews, this is the topic where you describe *your own system's* architecture concretely rather than abstract FastAPI features.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Your Skubi.why_it_exists: Interviewers ask 'walk me through a system you built' specifically to test whether you understand *why* you made each architectural choice, not just that you can name the technology. A chatbot API and an inventory-bot API share the same framework but have different request/response shapes (streaming chat tokens vs. structured CRUD operations on inventory records), different auth needs (per-user chat sessions vs. service accounts for warehouse systems), and different latency/throughput profiles (LLM round-trips vs. fast DB-backed lookups) — articulating these differences demonstrates real engineering judgment.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Your Skubi.how_it_works: A typical chatbot API (Skubiq-style) exposes a `/chat` endpoint that accepts a conversation history + new message (Pydantic model), authenticates the user (JWT via `HTTPBearer`), retrieves conversation state (dependency-injected DB/session store), calls an LLM (often streamed back via `StreamingResponse`/SSE for token-by-token rendering), and logs the interaction (background task) for analytics/fine-tuning. An inventory-bot API exposes CRUD-style endpoints (`/items/{item_id}`, `/items?category=...`) backed by a relational DB, with stricter Pydantic validation on quantities/SKUs, role-based auth (warehouse staff vs. admin), and synchronous (non-streamed) JSON responses since there's no incremental generation involved.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Your Skubi.use_when: Use this framing when asked to describe a project end-to-end: start with the request lifecycle (auth → validation → business logic → response), name the FastAPI feature responsible for each step, and explain a design decision you made (e.g., 'I used streaming for the chatbot because users were waiting 5-10 seconds for full responses, but the inventory API doesn't need it because lookups are sub-100ms').
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Your Skubi.avoid_when: Don't describe these projects purely in terms of 'I used FastAPI, Pydantic, and JWT' as a list of nouns — that doesn't differentiate you from someone who's only read the docs. Avoid overclaiming scale/complexity that doesn't match the project's actual size; interviewers often probe with 'what would break if traffic 10×'d?' and a mismatch between your claimed architecture and your answer to that question is a red flag.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Your Skubi.what_goes_wrong: A common interview misstep is not being able to explain trade-offs you didn't personally choose (e.g., 'why JWT and not session cookies?') — even if a teammate or template made that choice, you should be able to reason about it. Another pitfall: forgetting operational details (how is the model loaded — at startup or per-request? how many Uvicorn workers? how is auth shared between the chatbot and inventory APIs if they're separate services?) — these are exactly the follow-up questions that distinguish 'used the tutorial' from 'operated this in production.'
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|FastAPI|Your Skubi.real_example: A strong answer: 'Skubiq's chatbot API is a FastAPI service with a `/chat` POST endpoint — request body is a Pydantic model with `session_id` and `message`; `HTTPBearer` + a `get_current_user` dependency authenticates the user; we fetch conversation history from Redis (DI'd connection), call the LLM with streaming enabled and return a `StreamingResponse` over SSE so the frontend renders tokens incrementally, and a background task logs the full exchange to Postgres for analytics. InventoryBot is a separate FastAPI service with synchronous CRUD endpoints over a Postgres-backed SQLAlchemy model, role-based auth via JWT claims (warehouse vs. admin scopes), and no streaming since responses are sub-100ms DB lookups — deployed as its own Uvicorn+Gunicorn service so a chatbot traffic spike doesn't affect inventory operations.'

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Flas.what_it_is: Flask is a lightweight, synchronous (WSGI-based) Python web framework, often used as a quick way to wrap an ML model in an HTTP endpoint for prototyping or low-traffic internal tools. 'Blueprints' are Flask's mechanism for organizing routes into reusable modules (e.g., a `predictions` blueprint, an `admin` blueprint) that get registered onto the main app.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Flas.why_it_exists: Before FastAPI's rise, Flask was the default 'put a model behind an HTTP endpoint' choice because of its minimal boilerplate (`@app.route("/predict")`) and huge ecosystem of extensions. Blueprints exist because as a Flask app grows beyond a handful of routes in one file, you need a way to split routes, templates, and static files into logical modules without each module needing its own full `Flask` app instance.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Flas.how_it_works: A Flask app is a single WSGI callable. Each `@app.route` decorator registers a URL pattern → view function mapping. A Blueprint is created with `Blueprint("name", __name__)`, decorated routes are added to it the same way, and then `app.register_blueprint(bp, url_prefix="/api/v1")` mounts all of its routes under a prefix. Because Flask is WSGI (synchronous), each request occupies a worker (thread or process) for its entire duration — concurrency comes from running multiple workers (via Gunicorn/uWSGI), not from async I/O.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Flas.use_when: Use Flask for simple internal tools, admin dashboards, low-QPS model endpoints, or when integrating into an existing Flask codebase where rewriting in FastAPI isn't justified. Blueprints are useful once an app has more than ~3-4 logical groups of routes (e.g., separating `/auth`, `/predict`, `/admin`).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Flas.avoid_when: Avoid Flask for new ML serving APIs with meaningful traffic, especially anything involving LLM calls, streaming, or high concurrency with I/O-bound work — its synchronous model means a slow downstream call (e.g., to an LLM API) blocks an entire worker, requiring far more workers/memory than an async framework to handle the same load. Also avoid it when you want automatic request validation and OpenAPI docs out of the box — Flask requires extensions (Flask-RESTX, Marshmallow) to approximate what FastAPI provides natively.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Flas.what_goes_wrong: Running a Flask app with the built-in development server (`app.run()`) in production is a classic mistake — it's single-threaded, not designed for concurrent load, and lacks production hardening; it must be fronted by Gunicorn/uWSGI. Another common issue: a Flask endpoint that calls a slow model synchronously ties up a worker for the full inference time — under load, all workers can become busy waiting on inference, and new requests queue or time out, even though the actual CPU/GPU work is the same as an async setup.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Flas.real_example: A legacy fraud-detection service exposes `POST /v1/score` via a Flask blueprint registered at `/v1`, running under Gunicorn with 8 sync workers. Each request blocks its worker for the ~50ms model inference time; at 200 requests/sec, all 8 workers are saturated and p99 latency balloons — the team either adds many more workers (more memory) or migrates the endpoint to FastAPI with async I/O for any downstream calls, keeping Flask only for the admin UI blueprint.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Bent.what_it_is: BentoML is an open-source framework for packaging trained ML models (from any framework — scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow, XGBoost, Hugging Face, etc.) into a standardized, deployable unit called a 'Bento,' which bundles the model artifact, a Python serving API, dependencies, and a Dockerfile. It aims to be the 'build tool' that turns 'I have a trained model' into 'I have a production-ready container.'
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Bent.why_it_exists: Every ML framework saves models differently (pickle, `.pt`, `SavedModel`, ONNX), and every team historically wrote bespoke Flask/FastAPI wrappers plus Dockerfiles for serving — duplicating effort and creating inconsistent serving code across models/teams. BentoML standardizes this: define a `bentofile.yaml` and a `service.py` once, and `bentoml build` + `bentoml containerize` produce a consistent, versioned, deployable artifact regardless of the underlying ML framework.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Bent.how_it_works: You save a trained model into BentoML's local model store (`bentoml.sklearn.save_model(...)`, `bentoml.pytorch.save_model(...)`, etc.), which versions and tracks it with metadata. A `service.py` defines a `bentoml.Service` with API endpoints (decorated functions specifying input/output schemas via `bentoml.io`). `bentoml build` packages the service code, model(s), and a `bentofile.yaml` (dependencies, Python version) into a Bento — a self-contained directory/archive. `bentoml containerize` then turns that Bento into a Docker image with an HTTP (or gRPC) server, ready to deploy to Kubernetes, BentoCloud, or any container platform.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Bent.use_when: Use BentoML when you need a consistent packaging/serving pattern across multiple models and frameworks, when you want adaptive batching and multi-model composition (a 'Bento' can host several models with a pipeline between them) without writing that infrastructure yourself, or when targeting BentoCloud/Yatai for managed deployment.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Bent.avoid_when: For a single simple model with one well-known serving target (e.g., a PyTorch model going straight to TorchServe, or a TF model to TF Serving), the framework-native server may be simpler and have more mature framework-specific optimizations. Also, if your team already has a standardized FastAPI-based serving template, introducing BentoML adds another abstraction layer to learn.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Bent.what_goes_wrong: A common pitfall is treating the local 'model store' as if it were a remote model registry — BentoML's model store is local to the machine/container unless explicitly pushed to BentoCloud or a shared store, so a `bentoml build` on one machine may fail on another if the referenced model isn't present there. Another issue: adaptive batching (BentoML's automatic request batching for throughput) has tunable parameters (max batch size, max latency) that, if misconfigured, either under-batch (no throughput gain) or over-batch (added latency for early-arriving requests waiting for a batch to fill).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Bent.real_example: A team with three models (a scikit-learn fraud classifier, a PyTorch embedding model, and an XGBoost ranker) each previously had separate hand-rolled Flask wrappers with inconsistent health-check and metrics endpoints. Migrating to BentoML, each model is saved via its framework-specific `save_model`, wrapped in a `bentoml.Service` with consistent `/healthz`, `/metrics`, and `/predict` endpoints, and containerized with `bentoml containerize` — giving the platform team one Helm chart template that works for all three.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Torc.what_it_is: TorchServe is PyTorch's official model-serving framework, providing a production HTTP/gRPC server for PyTorch models (including TorchScript and eager-mode models) with built-in support for multi-model serving, versioning, A/B testing of model versions, metrics, and dynamic batching.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Torc.why_it_exists: Before TorchServe, deploying a PyTorch model meant writing a custom Flask/FastAPI server that loaded the `.pt` checkpoint and called `model(input)` — every team reinvented request batching, model versioning, logging, and metrics. TorchServe, built by AWS and Meta, provides these as configuration rather than code, specifically tuned for PyTorch's serialization formats and execution modes.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Torc.how_it_works: A model is packaged into a `.mar` (Model Archive) file via `torch-model-archiver`, bundling the model weights, a 'handler' (Python class defining `preprocess`/`inference`/`postprocess` — default handlers exist for common tasks like image classification, or you write a custom one), and any extra files. `torchserve --start --model-store ... --models model.mar` launches the server, which exposes an inference API (port 8080) and a management API (port 8081) for registering/scaling/versioning models at runtime without restarting the server. It supports dynamic batching (grouping concurrent requests into a single forward pass) configured via `batch_size`/`max_batch_delay`.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Torc.use_when: Use TorchServe when serving PyTorch models (especially multiple models or multiple versions of the same model needing A/B comparison) and you want production features (metrics, logging, dynamic batching, model management API) without building them yourself, particularly within AWS-centric stacks (SageMaker's PyTorch serving containers use TorchServe under the hood).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Torc.avoid_when: If you need the absolute lowest latency / highest throughput on NVIDIA GPUs across multiple frameworks (not just PyTorch), Triton Inference Server's CUDA-graph and concurrent-model-execution optimizations typically outperform TorchServe. If your model is a small scikit-learn/XGBoost model, TorchServe's PyTorch-centric tooling is overkill.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Torc.what_goes_wrong: Writing a custom handler incorrectly (e.g., not handling batched input shapes when dynamic batching is enabled — the handler receives a *list* of requests and must return a list of equal length) silently produces wrong outputs or crashes under load that didn't appear in single-request testing. Another common issue: the `.mar` archive bundles a snapshot of the model code/handler at build time — forgetting to rebuild the archive after changing the handler means the running server still uses old logic.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Torc.real_example: A PyTorch image classifier is archived with `torch-model-archiver --model-name resnet --version 1.0 --serialized-file model.pt --handler image_classifier --extra-files index_to_name.json`, then served with `torchserve --start --models resnet=resnet.mar`. Dynamic batching is configured with `batch_size=8, max_batch_delay=50` (ms) — requests arriving within a 50ms window are batched into a single GPU forward pass, improving throughput at a small added-latency cost for the first request in each batch.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|TF S.what_it_is: TensorFlow Serving is TensorFlow's official high-performance serving system for `SavedModel`-format models, exposing both REST (JSON over HTTP) and gRPC (Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2) APIs, with built-in model versioning and hot-swapping (loading a new model version without downtime).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|TF S.why_it_exists: TensorFlow models trained and exported as `SavedModel` have a defined computation graph and signature (input/output tensor names and shapes) — TF Serving exploits this fixed structure to provide a generic, highly optimized C++ server that can load and serve *any* `SavedModel` without per-model Python code, unlike a hand-written Flask wrapper that re-implements pre/post-processing and tensor handling for each model.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|TF S.how_it_works: You export a trained model via `model.save("export_path/1/")` (the `1` is a version number) in `SavedModel` format. TF Serving's `tensorflow_model_server` binary watches a model base path; when it sees a new version directory, it loads it and (by default) atomically switches serving traffic to the new version while optionally keeping the old one warm for in-flight requests. It exposes REST endpoints (`POST /v1/models/<name>:predict`) and a gRPC service using the `PredictionService` proto, both accepting tensors matching the model's input signature.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|TF S.use_when: Use TF Serving for TensorFlow/Keras models in production, especially when you need versioned hot-swapping (deploy a new model version with zero downtime, with the server managing the transition) and when gRPC's lower latency/overhead vs. REST matters for high-QPS internal services.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|TF S.avoid_when: For PyTorch models, use TorchServe or Triton instead — TF Serving only understands `SavedModel` format. For multi-framework model fleets, Triton (which supports TensorFlow, PyTorch, ONNX, and more in one server) avoids running separate serving stacks per framework.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|TF S.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is input signature mismatches — if the exported `SavedModel`'s expected input tensor name/shape/dtype doesn't match what the client sends (e.g., expecting `float32` but client sends `float64`, or a batch dimension mismatch), TF Serving returns a cryptic gRPC/REST error that doesn't clearly say 'wrong input shape.' Another pitfall: version directories must be integer-named (`1/`, `2/`, ...) and TF Serving by default serves only the *latest* — deploying a new version without a rollback plan means an immediate full cutover unless you configure specific version policies.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|TF S.real_example: A recommendation model is exported to `/models/ranker/1/` (SavedModel) and `/models/ranker/2/` (retrained version) — TF Serving, configured with `--model_base_path=/models/ranker`, automatically detects version `2`, loads it, and switches traffic to it while finishing in-flight requests on version `1`, then unloads `1` — all without restarting the server or any client-visible downtime.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Trit.what_it_is: NVIDIA Triton Inference Server is an open-source, framework-agnostic model serving platform that can host multiple models (PyTorch, TensorFlow, ONNX, TensorRT, Python custom backends, and more) simultaneously on the same GPU(s), with built-in dynamic batching, concurrent model execution, and model ensembles (pipelines of models).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Trit.why_it_exists: Large-scale inference deployments often need to serve many different models (or many versions/variants of a model) efficiently on expensive GPU hardware. Running each model in its own framework-specific server (TF Serving, TorchServe, etc.) on separate GPUs wastes utilization — GPUs are often underused by a single model's traffic. Triton was built to maximize GPU utilization by running multiple models concurrently on shared GPUs, batching requests dynamically, and supporting cross-framework model ensembles in one server.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Trit.how_it_works: Each model lives in a 'model repository' directory with a `config.pbtxt` specifying its backend (e.g., `tensorrt`, `onnxruntime`, `pytorch`, `python`), input/output tensor specs, and instance count (how many copies run concurrently, potentially on different GPUs). Triton's scheduler implements dynamic batching (queueing requests for a few milliseconds to form a batch up to `max_batch_size`) and concurrent execution (running multiple model instances in parallel CUDA streams). 'Ensembles' chain multiple models/preprocessing steps into a single pipeline defined declaratively, so a client makes one request that internally flows through several models (e.g., tokenizer → embedding model → reranker).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Trit.use_when: Use Triton when serving multiple models or model variants on shared GPU infrastructure and you need to maximize GPU utilization, when you need cross-framework support in one server (e.g., an ONNX preprocessing step feeding a TensorRT-optimized model), or when request batching/concurrency tuning has a measurable cost impact at your scale.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Trit.avoid_when: For a single model with simple, low-volume serving needs, Triton's configuration overhead (model repository layout, `config.pbtxt`, backend selection) is more complexity than needed — a framework-native server or even a simple FastAPI wrapper may be faster to stand up and maintain. Also avoid it if your team has no GPU infrastructure to optimize — Triton's main value proposition is GPU efficiency.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Trit.what_goes_wrong: Misconfigured dynamic batching parameters (`max_batch_size`, `max_queue_delay_microseconds`) can either fail to batch at all (each request processed individually, no throughput gain) or add unacceptable latency (requests wait too long for a batch to fill under low traffic). Another common issue: model instance count vs. GPU memory — setting too many concurrent instances of a large model across GPUs causes OOM, while too few underutilizes available GPUs; this requires empirical tuning per model and hardware.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Trit.real_example: A search-ranking pipeline deploys an embedding model and a reranker model as a Triton 'ensemble' — a single client request to the ensemble endpoint internally runs the embedding model, then feeds its output to the reranker, with Triton handling the data flow between the two GPU-resident models. Dynamic batching with `max_queue_delay_microseconds=5000` (5ms) groups concurrent embedding requests into batches of up to 32, roughly doubling GPU throughput compared to per-request inference at the cost of a worst-case 5ms added latency.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|KSer.what_it_is: KServe is a Kubernetes-native model serving platform (originally part of Kubeflow as 'KFServing,' now a standalone CNCF project) that provides a standardized `InferenceService` Custom Resource Definition (CRD) for deploying models with serverless autoscaling (including scale-to-zero), canary rollouts, and a unified interface over multiple serving runtimes (TorchServe, TF Serving, Triton, ONNX Runtime, scikit-learn, custom containers).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|KSer.why_it_exists: Deploying a model on Kubernetes 'by hand' means writing Deployments, Services, Ingress rules, HPA configs, and integrating whatever serving runtime the model needs — every model deployment reinvents this YAML. KServe abstracts this into a single `InferenceService` resource: declare the model's storage location and runtime, and KServe generates and manages the underlying Kubernetes resources, including request-based autoscaling via Knative (scaling pods to zero when idle and back up on traffic, which traditional HPA cannot do based on request count alone without extra components).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|KSer.how_it_works: You define an `InferenceService` YAML specifying `predictor.model.modelFormat` (e.g., `pytorch`, `sklearn`, `tensorflow`) and `storageUri` (e.g., an S3/GCS path to model artifacts). KServe's controller selects the appropriate pre-built serving runtime container (or your custom one), deploys it via Knative Serving (which handles autoscaling, including to zero replicas), and wires up a standardized prediction URL/protocol (the 'V2 inference protocol,' shared with Triton) regardless of the underlying framework. It also supports `transformer` and `explainer` components for pre/post-processing and explainability, and traffic-split canary deployments between model revisions.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|KSer.use_when: Use KServe when you're already on Kubernetes/Kubeflow and want a declarative, standardized way to deploy models from many frameworks with serverless autoscaling (especially valuable for spiky or low-traffic models where scale-to-zero saves significant GPU cost) and built-in canary rollout support.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|KSer.avoid_when: If you're not on Kubernetes, or your traffic is steady/high enough that scale-to-zero provides no benefit (cold-start latency from scaling up from zero can be significant for large models), the added abstraction layer (Knative + KServe CRDs on top of K8s) may not be worth the operational complexity compared to a plain Deployment + HPA running a serving container directly.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|KSer.what_goes_wrong: Scale-to-zero introduces cold-start latency — the first request after a scale-down can take seconds to tens of seconds while a pod starts and loads the model, which is unacceptable for latency-sensitive paths unless mitigated (minimum replica counts, pre-warming). Another pitfall: KServe's abstraction can obscure what's actually running underneath — debugging requires understanding both the `InferenceService` layer and the underlying Knative/K8s resources it generates, which adds a layer of indirection during incident response.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|KSer.real_example: A team deploys a rarely-used document-classification model as a KServe `InferenceService` with `minReplicas: 0, maxReplicas: 5` — during idle periods it scales to zero (no GPU cost), and on the first request after idling, Knative spins up a pod, KServe's serving runtime loads the model from S3, and subsequent requests are served normally; the team accepts the ~15s cold-start for this low-traffic, non-latency-critical internal tool in exchange for near-zero idle cost.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|ONNX.what_it_is: ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) is an open standard format for representing trained ML models in a framework-independent way; ONNX Runtime is a high-performance inference engine that executes models in this format, with hardware-specific 'execution providers' (CPU, CUDA, TensorRT, DirectML, CoreML, etc.) that accelerate execution on the available hardware.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|ONNX.why_it_exists: Models are typically *trained* in framework-specific formats (PyTorch `.pt`, TensorFlow `SavedModel`), but production environments may want to run inference without depending on the full training framework (smaller deployment footprint, different language runtime, or different hardware acceleration). ONNX provides a common 'export once, run anywhere' intermediate representation, and ONNX Runtime provides an optimized engine to execute it across CPUs, GPUs, and specialized accelerators without needing PyTorch/TensorFlow installed at inference time.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|ONNX.how_it_works: A trained PyTorch model is exported via `torch.onnx.export(model, dummy_input, "model.onnx")`, which traces the model's computation graph and serializes it as a `.onnx` file (a protobuf describing operators, weights, and tensor shapes). ONNX Runtime loads this file and applies graph-level optimizations (operator fusion, constant folding, redundant node elimination) before execution. At inference time, you select an execution provider (`CUDAExecutionProvider`, `TensorrtExecutionProvider`, `CPUExecutionProvider`) — ONNX Runtime dispatches each operator to the most efficient available implementation for that hardware, falling back to CPU for unsupported ops on a given provider.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|ONNX.use_when: Use ONNX/ONNX Runtime when you need to decouple inference from the training framework (e.g., deploying a PyTorch-trained model into a C++/Java/C# production service, or onto edge devices), when you want a single model artifact that can run on CPU or GPU depending on deployment target, or as an intermediate step before further optimization (e.g., ONNX → TensorRT for NVIDIA GPUs).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|ONNX.avoid_when: Some models use operators or dynamic control flow (data-dependent shapes, certain custom layers) that don't export cleanly to ONNX, or export but behave subtly differently (e.g., different handling of dropout/batchnorm in eval mode if export flags are wrong). For models that are fully supported and already optimized within their native framework's serving stack (e.g., a TF model on TF Serving with no cross-platform need), ONNX conversion adds a validation burden without a clear benefit.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|ONNX.what_goes_wrong: Export correctness is the biggest risk: a model can export 'successfully' (no errors) but produce numerically different outputs than the original due to unsupported operators being silently approximated, incorrect handling of training-vs-eval mode (e.g., `model.eval()` not called before export, so dropout/batchnorm behave as in training), or dynamic shapes not being marked as dynamic axes (baking in a fixed batch size that breaks at different batch sizes in production). Always validate exported model outputs against the original on a representative set of inputs before relying on it.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|ONNX.real_example: A PyTorch sentiment classifier is exported with `torch.onnx.export(model, dummy_input, "model.onnx", dynamic_axes={"input_ids": {0: "batch", 1: "seq"}})` to allow variable batch size and sequence length. ONNX Runtime with `CUDAExecutionProvider` then serves this model in a lightweight C++ inference service with no PyTorch dependency — but the team first runs a validation script comparing ONNX Runtime outputs to the original PyTorch model on 1000 held-out examples, catching a subtle mismatch caused by forgetting `model.eval()` before export (which left dropout active in the exported graph).

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Tens.what_it_is: TensorRT is NVIDIA's SDK for high-performance deep learning inference on NVIDIA GPUs. It takes a trained model (from ONNX, TensorFlow, or PyTorch via export) and compiles it into an optimized 'engine' specific to the target GPU architecture, applying optimizations like layer fusion, precision calibration (FP16/INT8), and kernel auto-tuning — commonly yielding 2-4× latency/throughput improvements over running the same model in PyTorch/TensorFlow directly.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Tens.why_it_exists: General-purpose deep learning frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow) prioritize flexibility for training (dynamic graphs, autograd, broad operator support) at some cost to inference efficiency. TensorRT exists purely for inference: given a fixed, trained graph, it can afford expensive ahead-of-time compilation and hardware-specific tuning that wouldn't make sense during training (where the graph might change every iteration), squeezing out latency/throughput that matters at production scale where the same forward pass runs millions of times.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Tens.how_it_works: TensorRT's builder takes a model (typically via ONNX import) and performs graph optimizations: fusing consecutive operations (e.g., Conv+BatchNorm+ReLU into one kernel) to reduce memory traffic and kernel-launch overhead, selecting the fastest available CUDA kernel implementation for each operation on the *specific* GPU (via auto-tuning/benchmarking at build time), and optionally reducing numerical precision (FP32 → FP16 or INT8) where accuracy permits. The output is a serialized 'engine' file — tied to the specific TensorRT version and GPU architecture it was built for — which the TensorRT runtime executes with minimal overhead.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Tens.use_when: Use TensorRT when serving models on NVIDIA GPUs at high volume where the 2-4× speedup translates to meaningful cost savings (fewer GPUs needed) or latency SLAs that can't otherwise be met, especially for CNN-based vision models and increasingly for transformer-based LLMs (via TensorRT-LLM).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Tens.avoid_when: Avoid TensorRT when you need rapid iteration — the build/optimization step can take minutes and engines are tied to specific GPU architectures and TensorRT versions, so every model update or hardware change requires rebuilding the engine. Also avoid it for models with operators TensorRT doesn't support well (requiring custom plugins) unless the performance gain justifies that engineering investment, or for low-volume serving where the optimization effort isn't worth the cost savings.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Tens.what_goes_wrong: INT8 quantization (the most aggressive TensorRT optimization) requires a calibration dataset representative of production inputs — using an unrepresentative calibration set can cause significant accuracy degradation on inputs that differ from it, sometimes invisibly (no errors, just worse predictions). Another common pitfall: engines built on one GPU architecture (e.g., A100) often don't run, or don't run optimally, on a different architecture (e.g., T4 or H100) — engines must be rebuilt per target GPU type, complicating multi-GPU-type fleets.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Tens.real_example: An object detection model running at 45ms/image in PyTorch on a T4 GPU is converted to ONNX, then compiled to a TensorRT FP16 engine, reducing inference to ~15ms/image (3×) — but the team discovers that this specific engine, built on a T4, must be rebuilt separately for their newer A100-based inference nodes since TensorRT engines are architecture-specific; they add an engine-build step per GPU SKU to their CI/CD pipeline.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|vLLM.what_it_is: vLLM is an open-source, high-throughput inference and serving engine specifically for large language models, built around 'PagedAttention' — a memory management technique for the KV (key-value) cache that dramatically improves GPU memory utilization and throughput compared to naive LLM serving implementations.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|vLLM.why_it_exists: Autoregressive LLM generation requires storing a growing KV cache (one entry per token per layer per attention head) for every in-flight request. Naive implementations allocate a contiguous block of GPU memory for the maximum possible sequence length per request up front, leading to massive memory fragmentation and waste — most requests don't reach the max length, but the memory is reserved anyway, severely limiting how many requests can be batched concurrently. vLLM was created to solve this memory-efficiency problem, which directly translates to serving more concurrent users on the same GPU.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|vLLM.how_it_works: PagedAttention borrows the 'virtual memory with paging' concept from operating systems: the KV cache is divided into fixed-size blocks, and a request's KV cache is stored as a non-contiguous set of blocks (like pages), with a block table mapping logical positions to physical memory blocks. This eliminates fragmentation — memory is allocated/freed in small blocks as sequences grow/finish, allowing near-100% memory utilization. Combined with continuous batching (dynamically adding new requests to a running batch as old ones complete, rather than waiting for a fixed batch to fully finish), vLLM achieves much higher throughput (often 2-24× over naive HuggingFace `transformers` serving) for the same GPU.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|vLLM.use_when: Use vLLM for self-hosting open-weight LLMs (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, etc.) where you need high request throughput and efficient GPU memory usage — e.g., serving many concurrent chat sessions. It provides an OpenAI-compatible API server out of the box, making it a drop-in replacement for OpenAI's API for self-hosted models.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|vLLM.avoid_when: For very low-traffic or single-user local inference (e.g., a developer running a model locally for testing), simpler tools (Ollama, llama.cpp, plain `transformers` with `generate()`) have less setup overhead. Also, vLLM's sweet spot is NVIDIA GPUs with sufficient memory for the model plus KV cache headroom — for CPU-only or heavily memory-constrained edge deployment, quantized `llama.cpp`-style runtimes are more appropriate.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|vLLM.what_goes_wrong: Under-provisioning `gpu_memory_utilization` (the fraction of GPU memory vLLM is allowed to use for the KV cache pool) can cause out-of-memory errors or unnecessarily limit max concurrent sequences; over-provisioning can starve other processes on the same GPU. Another issue: continuous batching means request latency becomes somewhat variable depending on what else is currently in the batch — a request might get slightly slower if many other requests join the batch concurrently, which needs to be accounted for in latency SLAs/monitoring (P50 vs P99 can diverge more than in fixed-batch serving).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|vLLM.real_example: A team self-hosting a 7B-parameter Llama model with naive HuggingFace `generate()` on an A100 (80GB) can serve roughly 8-16 concurrent requests before running out of KV-cache memory due to fragmentation. Switching to vLLM with PagedAttention and continuous batching on the same GPU serves 50+ concurrent requests at similar per-request latency, because the KV cache is packed far more efficiently — directly cutting the number of GPUs needed for a given QPS target.

7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Batc.what_it_is: Three fundamental serving paradigms for ML predictions: **batch inference** runs predictions on a large set of inputs on a schedule (e.g., nightly), writing results to storage for later use; **real-time (online) inference** responds to individual requests synchronously with low latency (milliseconds to a few seconds); **streaming inference** continuously processes a stream of incoming data (e.g., from Kafka) and produces predictions as new data arrives, often with sub-second-to-second latency per event.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Batc.why_it_exists: Different business use cases have fundamentally different latency, freshness, and cost requirements, and conflating them leads to over- or under-engineered systems. A recommendation that's precomputed nightly (batch) doesn't need a live API; a fraud-detection check on a credit card swipe (real-time) can't wait for a batch job; a real-time bidding system reacting to user clickstream events (streaming) needs continuous low-latency processing of an unbounded data flow. Choosing the right paradigm dramatically affects infrastructure cost, complexity, and what freshness guarantees you can make.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Batc.how_it_works: **Batch**: a scheduled job (Airflow, cron) loads a large dataset, runs `model.predict()` over it (often distributed via Spark/Ray for scale), and writes predictions to a database/data warehouse for downstream consumption — no serving infrastructure needed, just compute that runs periodically. **Real-time**: a model is loaded into a long-running server (FastAPI, TorchServe, Triton, etc.) behind an API; each client request triggers one (or a small batched group of) forward pass(es), with latency directly visible to the user. **Streaming**: a model is embedded in a stream-processing job (Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming) that consumes events from a topic, applies the model per-event or per-window, and emits results to another topic/sink — the model runs continuously, processing data as it arrives rather than on-demand.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Batc.use_when: Use batch when predictions can be precomputed and don't need to reflect data newer than the last batch run (e.g., monthly churn scores, daily product recommendations). Use real-time when a user-facing action needs an immediate model response (search ranking, chatbot reply, fraud check at transaction time). Use streaming when you need to react to events as they happen with intermediate freshness requirements (seconds, not milliseconds, but continuously) and/or need to maintain running aggregates/features over time windows (e.g., 'transactions in the last 5 minutes').
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Batc.avoid_when: Don't build a real-time serving API if nothing actually needs sub-second responses — it adds always-on infrastructure cost (servers running 24/7) for no benefit over a much simpler batch job. Don't build a streaming pipeline if your data naturally arrives in large periodic dumps (e.g., daily exports) — that's a batch problem dressed up as streaming, adding unnecessary operational complexity (Kafka/Flink cluster management).
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Batc.what_goes_wrong: A common mistake is building real-time infrastructure for a use case that's actually batch (e.g., standing up an always-on API for predictions that are only ever consumed once a day), wasting cost on idle capacity. The opposite mistake — using batch for something that needs freshness — causes staleness bugs: e.g., a fraud model using yesterday's batch-computed risk score misses a pattern that emerged in the last hour. Streaming systems have their own failure mode: feature computation logic (e.g., a 'transactions in last 5 minutes' sliding window) implemented differently in the streaming pipeline vs. the batch pipeline used for training creates training/serving skew, where the model sees systematically different feature distributions at serving time than it was trained on.
7|🔴 T1 Serving & APIs|Model Serving|Batc.real_example: An e-commerce platform uses batch inference (nightly Spark job) to precompute 'recommended products' for all users, stored in a key-value store the website reads from with single-digit-millisecond lookups — no model inference happens at request time. Separately, a fraud-detection model runs in real-time (FastAPI + Triton) on each transaction, returning an approve/deny decision within 100ms. A third model runs in a Flink streaming job consuming clickstream events, maintaining a rolling 'session intent score' per user updated within seconds of each click — feeding both the real-time fraud model (as a feature) and a dashboard.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_it_is: A Dockerfile is a text file of instructions for building a container image.
