The core instructions are `FROM` (base image to start from), `WORKDIR` (sets the working directory for subsequent instructions), `COPY` (copies files from the build context into the image), `RUN` (executes a command during the build, creating a new image layer), `EXPOSE` (documents which port the container listens on), and `CMD` (the default command run when a container starts from the image).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.why_it_exists: Before containers, 'works on my machine' meant deployment required replicating the exact OS, library versions, and system dependencies on every target server — a constant source of environment drift bugs (especially with ML's heavy native dependencies: CUDA versions, BLAS libraries, compiled wheels). A Dockerfile captures the *entire* environment construction as code: starting from a known base image, every dependency installation and file copy is explicit and reproducible, so the same image runs identically in dev, CI, and production.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.how_it_works: Docker builds an image by executing each instruction in order, and each instruction that changes the filesystem (`RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD`) creates a new immutable 'layer' stacked on top of the previous one — the final image is the union of all layers. `FROM python:3.11-slim` starts from a minimal Python base; `WORKDIR /app` sets `/app` as the directory for subsequent `COPY`/`RUN`/`CMD`; `COPY requirements.txt .` then `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt` installs dependencies into a layer; `COPY . .` copies the application code; `EXPOSE 8000` documents (but does not actually publish) the port the app listens on; `CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]` defines what runs when `docker run` starts a container from this image (overridable at runtime).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.use_when: Use a Dockerfile for any service you want to deploy consistently across environments — virtually mandatory for ML serving APIs given how sensitive they are to exact library/CUDA versions. Order instructions from least-to-most frequently changing (base image → system deps → Python deps → app code) to maximize layer cache reuse.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.avoid_when: For pure local exploration/notebooks with no deployment target, containerizing adds overhead without benefit — a virtualenv/conda env is faster to iterate in. Avoid putting secrets (API keys, credentials) directly in `COPY`'d files or `RUN` commands — they get baked into image layers and are extractable even if a later layer 'deletes' them.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_goes_wrong: A very common mistake is `COPY . .` *before* installing dependencies — any change to application code (which changes constantly) invalidates the cache for the `pip install` layer that follows it, forcing a full dependency reinstall on every build even though `requirements.txt` didn't change. Another frequent issue: `CMD` vs `ENTRYPOINT` confusion — `CMD` is fully overridable by `docker run` arguments, while `ENTRYPOINT` is not (arguments are appended); using the wrong one leads to either commands being silently ignored or unable to be overridden for debugging.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.real_example:
```dockerfile
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
```
Because `requirements.txt` is copied and installed *before* the rest of the code, changing `main.py` and rebuilding reuses the cached `pip install` layer — the build takes seconds instead of minutes, as long as dependencies haven't changed.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_it_is: Docker layer caching is the mechanism by which Docker reuses previously-built layers if the instruction and its inputs (files copied, command run) are unchanged since the last build, avoiding redundant work. Each Dockerfile instruction produces a layer identified by a hash of the instruction plus its inputs; if that hash matches a cached layer, Docker skips re-executing it and reuses the cached result.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.why_it_exists: ML Docker images often involve installing large dependency sets (PyTorch, CUDA libraries, transformers) that can take many minutes and download gigabytes. Rebuilding these from scratch on every code change — which happens dozens of times a day during development and in CI — would make iteration unbearably slow. Layer caching exists so that only the layers actually affected by a change need to be rebuilt, while everything 'above' an unchanged layer in the Dockerfile is reused instantly.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.how_it_works: Docker computes a cache key for each instruction based on the instruction text and (for `COPY`/`ADD`) a checksum of the copied files' contents. Starting from the top of the Dockerfile, Docker walks instructions in order; the moment one instruction's cache key doesn't match the cache (e.g., because a copied file changed), that layer is rebuilt, AND every subsequent layer is also rebuilt (cache invalidation cascades downward) — even if those later layers' own inputs didn't change, because they're built on top of a now-different layer. This is why instruction *ordering* matters enormously: put rarely-changing instructions (base image, system packages, dependency installs) first, and frequently-changing ones (application source code) last.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.use_when: Structure every Dockerfile with this ordering principle in mind: `FROM` → OS-level deps (`apt-get install`) → language-level deps (`pip install -r requirements.txt`, copied and installed *before* app code) → application code (`COPY . .`) → final config (`EXPOSE`, `CMD`). In CI, use a remote/registry cache (`--cache-from`) so cache benefits persist across ephemeral CI runners that don't share local Docker state.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.avoid_when: Don't rely on layer caching for correctness — e.g., don't assume `apt-get update` from a cached layer reflects current package indexes; if you need fresh package lists, that layer should be deliberately busted (or accept it's cached and periodically rebuild without cache). Also, `RUN` commands with side effects that depend on external state (downloading 'latest' artifacts) shouldn't be cached silently, or you'll get stale artifacts without realizing it.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_goes_wrong: The most common anti-pattern, as noted for the Dockerfile structure itself, is copying application code before installing dependencies — every code change busts the cache for the expensive dependency-install layer. A subtler issue: combining `apt-get update && apt-get install -y X` in one `RUN` (correct) vs. separate `RUN apt-get update` and `RUN apt-get install` layers (incorrect) — if cached separately, a later `apt-get install` layer can run against a stale `update` from days/weeks ago, installing outdated or unavailable package versions.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.real_example: A team's ML training image took ~12 minutes to rebuild on every CI run because `COPY . .` (including frequently-changed training scripts) was placed before `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt`. Reordering so dependencies are copied and installed first, with application code copied last, dropped rebuild time to ~30 seconds for code-only changes — the `pip install` layer (10+ minutes for PyTorch + CUDA deps) is now reused unless `requirements.txt` itself changes.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_it_is: Multi-stage builds let a single Dockerfile define multiple `FROM` stages — e.g., one stage with full build tooling (compilers, dev dependencies, source code) that produces artifacts, and a second, minimal stage that copies only the needed artifacts from the first stage, discarding everything else (build tools, intermediate files, dev dependencies) from the final image.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.why_it_exists: Building ML applications often requires heavy build-time tooling — compilers for native extensions, build-only Python packages, large intermediate files (e.g., compiled CUDA kernels, downloaded wheels) — none of which are needed at runtime but which, if left in the final image, bloat its size (slower pulls/deploys, larger attack surface, more disk usage across many replicas). Multi-stage builds let you 'have your cake and eat it' — use a fully-equipped build environment, then ship only the slim runtime result.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.how_it_works: Each `FROM ... AS <name>` starts a new stage with its own filesystem, independent of previous stages (though later stages can `COPY --from=<name>` files from earlier stages). A typical pattern: stage 1 (`FROM python:3.11 AS builder`) installs build dependencies and compiles a wheel or installs packages into a virtualenv; stage 2 (`FROM python:3.11-slim`) copies *only* the compiled virtualenv/wheel from stage 1 via `COPY --from=builder /opt/venv /opt/venv`, without including the compilers, build caches, or source artifacts that stage 1 accumulated. The final image is built from stage 2's layers only — stage 1's layers exist solely during the build and aren't part of the shipped image.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.use_when: Use multi-stage builds whenever your build process needs tools/dependencies that aren't needed at runtime — compiling native extensions (e.g., packages requiring `gcc`), building frontend assets (`npm run build` producing static files served by a different runtime image), or any case where the 'build image' and 'run image' have meaningfully different dependency sets.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.avoid_when: For simple pure-Python applications with no compiled dependencies and a small dependency tree, a single-stage build is simpler to read and debug, and the size savings from multi-stage may be marginal. Don't over-split into many stages if it makes the Dockerfile hard to follow without a proportional size/security benefit.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_goes_wrong: A common mistake is forgetting that each stage starts from a clean filesystem — environment variables, installed system packages, or files set up in an earlier stage are NOT automatically available in a later stage unless explicitly copied via `COPY --from=`. Another issue: copying an entire virtualenv across stages can fail if the two stages use different base image versions with incompatible system libraries (e.g., different glibc versions) — the copied binaries may not run in the minimal final image.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.real_example:
```dockerfile
FROM python:3.11 AS builder
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y gcc
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . /app
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0"]
```
The final image excludes `gcc` and apt caches entirely (saving hundreds of MB), shipping only the installed Python packages and application code — reducing image size from ~1.2GB to ~400MB, which speeds up deploys and reduces the attack surface.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_it_is: NVIDIA publishes official base Docker images (e.g., `nvidia/cuda:12.1.0-cudnn8-runtime-ubuntu22.04`) that include the CUDA toolkit/runtime and cuDNN libraries pre-installed, providing the GPU-accelerated foundation that ML framework images (PyTorch, TensorFlow GPU builds) are built on top of. Running GPU-enabled containers also requires the NVIDIA Container Toolkit on the host, which exposes the host's GPU drivers and devices to containers.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.why_it_exists: CUDA, cuDNN, and GPU drivers have strict version compatibility requirements with each other and with the ML framework version being used — mismatches cause cryptic errors or silent fallback to CPU. Pre-built `nvidia/cuda` base images pin known-compatible combinations of CUDA/cuDNN, so teams don't have to manually install and version-match these complex native libraries inside every image from scratch.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.how_it_works: An `nvidia/cuda` base image comes in variants: `base` (just CUDA runtime libraries), `runtime` (adds cuDNN and other libraries needed to *run* GPU code), and `devel` (adds compilers/headers needed to *build* GPU code, e.g., custom CUDA kernels). A Dockerfile for a PyTorch GPU service typically starts `FROM nvidia/cuda:12.1.0-cudnn8-runtime-ubuntu22.04`, installs Python and `pip install torch` (with the CUDA-matching wheel). At runtime, the container itself doesn't contain GPU *drivers* (those live on the host) — the NVIDIA Container Toolkit (`nvidia-docker` / `--gpus all` flag, or the `nvidia` runtime class in Kubernetes) bind-mounts the host's driver libraries and exposes `/dev/nvidia*` devices into the container, so the CUDA runtime inside the container can talk to the host's GPU driver.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.use_when: Use `nvidia/cuda` base images (or framework-specific GPU images like `pytorch/pytorch:2.x-cuda12.1-cudnn8-runtime`) for any containerized service that runs GPU-accelerated inference or training. Match the CUDA version in the base image to the version your ML framework's GPU build expects.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.avoid_when: If a service doesn't use the GPU at all (e.g., a CPU-only preprocessing microservice), don't use a CUDA base image — it's significantly larger and provides no benefit. Also avoid mixing CUDA versions across an image's layers (e.g., a `devel` build stage with one CUDA version copying artifacts into a `runtime` stage with a different CUDA version) without verifying ABI compatibility.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_goes_wrong: The single most common GPU container issue is a CUDA version mismatch between the container's CUDA runtime/toolkit and the host's NVIDIA driver — drivers are generally backward-compatible with older CUDA versions but not forward-compatible, so a container built with a newer CUDA than the host driver supports fails with errors like 'CUDA driver version is insufficient.' Another frequent issue: forgetting `--gpus all` (Docker) or the appropriate `resources.limits` / `runtimeClassName` (Kubernetes) when running the container — the container starts fine but `torch.cuda.is_available()` returns `False` because no GPU devices were passed through, and the workload silently runs on CPU (often dramatically slower, sometimes mistaken for a model bug).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.real_example: A team's training image is built `FROM nvidia/cuda:12.1.0-cudnn8-devel-ubuntu22.04` (needed to compile a custom CUDA op), but their inference image uses the much smaller `nvidia/cuda:12.1.0-cudnn8-runtime-ubuntu22.04` (no compilers needed at inference). Running the inference container with `docker run --gpus all my-image` exposes the host's GPU; running it without `--gpus all` starts successfully but `torch.cuda.is_available()` returns `False`, and the team's monitoring catches the resulting 50× latency increase before it reaches users.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_it_is: Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications using a single declarative YAML file (`docker-compose.yml`). It lets you specify multiple services (e.g., an API, a database, a Redis cache, a model server), their networking, volumes, environment variables, and startup dependencies, then bring the whole stack up or down with one command (`docker compose up`).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.why_it_exists: Real ML applications rarely consist of a single container — a typical local dev setup might need the API service, a Postgres database, Redis for caching, and maybe a vector DB or a separate model-serving container. Manually running `docker run` for each with the correct networking/volume flags every time is tedious and error-prone. Compose captures this entire local environment as code, so any developer can reproduce the full stack with `docker compose up`.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.how_it_works: `docker-compose.yml` defines a `services:` map; each service specifies an `image` (or `build:` context to build from a Dockerfile), `ports` (host:container port mappings), `environment` variables, `volumes` (for persistent data or live code mounting during development), and `depends_on` (startup ordering — though this only waits for the container to *start*, not for the service inside to be *ready*, which often requires healthchecks). Compose creates a shared Docker network where services can reach each other by service name as hostname (e.g., the API connects to `postgres:5432`, not `localhost:5432`).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.use_when: Use Docker Compose for local development and testing environments that mirror production's multi-service architecture — e.g., spinning up your FastAPI app alongside Postgres and Redis with one command, with hot-reload volumes mounting your source code into the container for live editing.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.avoid_when: Docker Compose is not a production orchestrator — it has no built-in autoscaling, rolling updates, self-healing, or multi-host scheduling. For production, use Kubernetes (or a managed container service). Also avoid Compose for CI test environments that need to be fully ephemeral and parallel-safe unless you're careful with unique project names/networks to avoid port collisions between concurrent CI runs.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_goes_wrong: A common confusion is `depends_on` only controlling container *start order*, not application *readiness* — an API container might start before the Postgres container inside it has finished initializing and is accepting connections, causing connection errors on the API's first requests. The fix is application-level retry logic on startup, or `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy` plus a `healthcheck` defined on the database service. Another pitfall: bind-mounting source code for hot-reload (`volumes: - ./app:/app`) can mask issues that only appear when code is *copied* into the image (as it would be in production), leading to 'works in Compose, fails in the built image' surprises.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.real_example:
```yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://user:pass@db:5432/appdb
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pass
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U user"]
      interval: 5s
```
`docker compose up` starts both containers; the API waits for Postgres's healthcheck to pass before starting, and connects to it via the hostname `db` (Compose's internal DNS) rather than `localhost`.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_it_is: The four foundational Kubernetes objects for running and exposing an application: a **Pod** is the smallest deployable unit (one or more containers sharing network/storage); a **Deployment** manages a set of identical Pod replicas, handling rolling updates and self-healing (restarting crashed Pods); a **Service** provides a stable network endpoint (virtual IP + DNS name) that load-balances across a Deployment's Pods even as individual Pods are replaced; an **Ingress** routes external HTTP(S) traffic into the cluster to the appropriate Service based on hostname/path rules.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.why_it_exists: Pods are ephemeral by design — they can be killed and rescheduled (due to node failure, scaling, or updates), and each gets a new IP address when recreated. Without higher-level abstractions, you couldn't reliably run 'N copies of my app' (need a Deployment) or have a stable address other services/clients can connect to (need a Service), or expose HTTP routes from outside the cluster with TLS/routing rules (need an Ingress). Each layer solves a specific problem in the gap between 'a container is running somewhere' and 'users can reliably reach my application.'
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.how_it_works: A Deployment's spec defines a Pod template (container image, resources, env vars) and a replica count; Kubernetes' controller continuously reconciles actual state toward this desired state — if a Pod dies, a new one is scheduled to maintain the replica count, and rolling updates replace old Pods with new ones gradually (controlled by `maxUnavailable`/`maxSurge`). A Service selects Pods by label (`selector: app: my-api`) and provides a stable ClusterIP + DNS name (`my-api.namespace.svc.cluster.local`); `kube-proxy` (or eBPF equivalents) load-balances traffic to that IP across all matching healthy Pods. An Ingress resource defines routing rules (host/path → Service+port); an Ingress Controller (NGINX, Traefik, cloud-provider load balancer) reads these rules and configures an actual reverse proxy/load balancer to implement them, often handling TLS termination.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.use_when: This is the baseline pattern for almost any HTTP service on Kubernetes: Deployment for the running Pods, Service for internal stable addressing/load-balancing, Ingress for external access with routing/TLS. For ML serving specifically, the Deployment's Pod template is where you specify GPU resource requests, the serving container image, and model-loading configuration.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.avoid_when: For batch/training jobs that run to completion rather than running continuously, use a `Job` or `CronJob` instead of a Deployment (Deployments assume long-running, restart-on-failure Pods, which is the wrong model for 'run once and exit successfully'). For stateful workloads needing stable network identities and persistent storage per replica (e.g., a database), use a `StatefulSet` instead of a Deployment.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_goes_wrong: A common misconfiguration is Service `selector` labels not matching the Deployment's Pod template labels exactly — the Service silently has zero healthy endpoints, and requests to it time out or get connection-refused, with no obvious error pointing at the label mismatch (`kubectl get endpoints <service>` showing empty is the diagnostic). Another frequent issue: not setting resource `requests`/`limits` on Pods — without `requests`, the scheduler can't make good placement decisions and Pods may be evicted under node pressure; without `limits`, a runaway process (e.g., a memory leak in a model-serving container) can consume an entire node's resources and affect other Pods.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.real_example: A model-serving Deployment with `replicas: 3` and Pod template labeled `app: sentiment-api` is exposed via a Service with `selector: {app: sentiment-api}` and `port: 80 -> targetPort: 8000`. An Ingress rule routes `api.example.com/sentiment/*` to this Service. When a developer accidentally relabels the Deployment's Pods to `app: sentiment-api-v2` without updating the Service selector, `kubectl get endpoints sentiment-api` shows `<none>` — the Service exists and the Ingress routes to it, but it has no Pods to send traffic to, and all requests return 503.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_it_is: ConfigMaps and Secrets are Kubernetes objects for injecting configuration data into Pods without baking it into container images. A ConfigMap holds non-sensitive key-value data (feature flags, config file contents, environment-specific settings); a Secret holds sensitive data (API keys, database passwords, TLS certificates) — structurally similar to ConfigMaps but with additional handling intended to reduce accidental exposure (base64 encoding, restricted access via RBAC, and integration with external secret managers).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.why_it_exists: Hardcoding configuration (especially environment-specific values like database URLs, or secrets like API keys) into container images violates the principle of building one image and deploying it identically across environments — and committing secrets into images or source control is a severe security risk. ConfigMaps/Secrets decouple configuration from the image: the same image is deployed everywhere, with environment-specific config and secrets supplied separately at deploy time.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.how_it_works: A ConfigMap/Secret is created from literals, files, or YAML manifests (`kubectl create configmap app-config --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info` or `kubectl create secret generic db-creds --from-literal=password=...`). Pods consume them either as environment variables (`envFrom: configMapRef:` / `secretKeyRef:`) or as mounted files (a volume where each key becomes a file containing its value) — the file-mount approach is preferred for Secrets because environment variables can leak via process listings, crash dumps, or child-process inheritance, whereas mounted files have more controlled access. Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded (NOT encrypted) by default in `etcd` unless encryption-at-rest is explicitly configured — base64 is encoding for transport, not security.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.use_when: Use ConfigMaps for non-sensitive configuration that varies by environment (feature flags, log levels, model version to load, endpoint URLs). Use Secrets (or better, an external secret manager integration like AWS Secrets Manager / HashiCorp Vault via a CSI driver or operator) for credentials, API keys, and certificates — and prefer mounting as files over environment variables for sensitive values.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.avoid_when: Don't rely on raw Kubernetes Secrets as your only protection for highly sensitive credentials in regulated environments — without encryption-at-rest enabled for `etcd` and tight RBAC, anyone with `get secrets` permission (or `etcd` access) can trivially decode them. For such cases, use an external secrets manager with Kubernetes integration (e.g., External Secrets Operator syncing from AWS Secrets Manager/Vault), which provides rotation, auditing, and stronger encryption guarantees.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_goes_wrong: A very common mistake is treating base64 encoding as encryption — `kubectl get secret my-secret -o yaml` shows base64 strings that anyone with read access (or a `kubectl get secret -o jsonpath` one-liner) can trivially decode, so RBAC on Secrets must be tight. Another issue: ConfigMap/Secret changes don't automatically restart Pods that consume them as environment variables — a Pod keeps running with the old values until it's manually restarted (mounted-file volumes *do* update live via `kubelet`'s periodic sync, but env vars are set only at container start), leading to confusing 'I updated the config but nothing changed' situations.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.real_example: A model-serving Deployment mounts a Secret containing a database password as a file at `/etc/secrets/db-password` (read by the app at startup) and a ConfigMap as environment variables for `MODEL_VERSION` and `LOG_LEVEL`. When the team rotates the database password by updating the Secret, the mounted file updates within ~1 minute (kubelet sync interval) without a restart — but when they update `MODEL_VERSION` in the ConfigMap expecting the running Pods to pick up the new model, nothing changes until they run `kubectl rollout restart deployment/model-api`, because env-var-sourced config is only read at container startup.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_it_is: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) is a Kubernetes controller that automatically adjusts the number of Pod replicas in a Deployment (or StatefulSet/ReplicaSet) based on observed metrics — most commonly CPU or memory utilization, but also custom metrics (e.g., requests-per-second, queue depth, GPU utilization) via the custom/external metrics APIs.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.why_it_exists: Traffic to ML serving APIs is rarely constant — it varies by time of day, business events, or batch job schedules. Statically provisioning for peak load wastes resources (and money) during off-peak times; provisioning for average load causes degraded performance/dropped requests during peaks. HPA automates the trade-off: scale up when load increases (maintaining latency/throughput targets), scale down when load decreases (saving cost), within configured min/max bounds.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.how_it_works: HPA periodically (default every 15s) queries the Kubernetes Metrics API (or custom metrics adapters, e.g., Prometheus Adapter) for the current value of the target metric across the Deployment's Pods, compares it to the configured target (e.g., `targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 70`), and computes a desired replica count proportionally: `desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetricValue / targetMetricValue)`, bounded by `minReplicas`/`maxReplicas`. It then updates the Deployment's `replicas` field, and the Deployment controller handles actually creating/terminating Pods. For ML workloads, custom metrics (e.g., requests-in-flight, GPU utilization from DCGM exporter, or queue length from a message broker) are often more meaningful than CPU, since GPU-bound inference may show low CPU usage even when the GPU (and thus the actual capacity) is saturated.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.use_when: Use HPA for stateless serving Deployments where load varies meaningfully over time and where adding replicas genuinely increases capacity (i.e., each replica can independently serve requests). For GPU workloads, configure HPA on a GPU-relevant custom metric (GPU utilization, requests-in-flight, queue depth) rather than CPU, since CPU usage often doesn't reflect GPU saturation.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.avoid_when: Don't use HPA for workloads where scaling out doesn't help — e.g., a single stateful process that can't be horizontally replicated, or a workload bottlenecked on a shared downstream resource (a database connection pool, a single-instance model) where adding more Pods just adds more contention without adding throughput. Also be cautious combining HPA with very large/slow-to-start Pods (e.g., Pods that take minutes to load a large model) — reactive scaling may be too slow to handle sudden spikes, and you may need proactive/scheduled scaling instead.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_goes_wrong: A frequent issue is 'thrashing' — replicas scaling up and down rapidly because the metric oscillates around the target threshold; this is mitigated with stabilization windows (`behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds`) that prevent scaling down too quickly after a scale-up. Another common pitfall: HPA scaling based on CPU for a GPU-bound inference service — CPU usage stays low (most work happens on the GPU), so HPA never scales up even as GPU utilization (and request latency) climbs to saturation, because the metric being watched doesn't reflect the actual bottleneck.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.real_example: An inference Deployment has `minReplicas: 2, maxReplicas: 10`, scaling on a custom Prometheus metric `http_requests_in_flight` with `targetAverageValue: 20`. During a traffic spike, in-flight requests per Pod rise to 40, so HPA scales from 2 to 4 replicas (`ceil(2 × 40/20)`); a `scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300` ensures that once traffic drops, replicas don't immediately shrink back, avoiding flapping during a brief lull followed by another spike.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_it_is: Running ML workloads on Kubernetes requires scheduling Pods onto nodes that have GPUs, which Kubernetes handles via GPU resource requests (`nvidia.com/gpu: 1` in the Pod spec, exposed by the NVIDIA device plugin), combined with node selectors/affinity/taints-tolerations to ensure GPU Pods land on GPU nodes and non-GPU Pods don't waste expensive GPU node capacity.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.why_it_exists: Kubernetes clusters for ML workloads are typically heterogeneous — a mix of cheap CPU-only nodes (for APIs, preprocessing, general services) and expensive GPU nodes (for training/inference). Without explicit scheduling constraints, the scheduler could place a CPU-only Pod on a GPU node (wasting expensive capacity) or fail to place a GPU Pod correctly (since the scheduler doesn't know about GPUs without the device plugin). Node selectors, affinity, and taints/tolerations give cluster operators fine-grained control over this placement.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.how_it_works: The NVIDIA device plugin (a DaemonSet running on GPU nodes) advertises each GPU node's GPU count to the Kubernetes scheduler as an 'extended resource' (`nvidia.com/gpu`). A Pod requesting `resources: limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 1` can only be scheduled on a node with at least one available GPU — the scheduler treats this like any other resource request (CPU/memory) for bin-packing. To *prevent* non-GPU Pods from landing on GPU nodes (and to actively *attract* GPU Pods to GPU nodes), operators typically: (1) apply a taint to GPU nodes (`nvidia.com/gpu=true:NoSchedule`) so only Pods with a matching toleration can be scheduled there, and (2) use `nodeSelector` or `nodeAffinity` on GPU Pods to require GPU-node labels. This combination ensures GPU nodes are reserved for GPU workloads and GPU Pods land only on appropriate hardware.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.use_when: Use this pattern for any Kubernetes cluster with mixed CPU/GPU node pools — virtually all production ML clusters. Combine with cluster autoscaler node groups per instance type (e.g., a `g5.xlarge` node group for inference, a `p4d.24xlarge` node group for training) so GPU capacity scales independently and by GPU type.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.avoid_when: If a cluster is entirely GPU nodes (rare and expensive) or entirely CPU (no ML training/inference on K8s), these constraints add unnecessary configuration. For very small setups, a single node pool with manual scheduling decisions might be simpler than building out taints/affinity rules.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is Pods stuck in `Pending` indefinitely because they request `nvidia.com/gpu` but no node in the cluster has that extended resource registered (NVIDIA device plugin not installed/running on those nodes) — `kubectl describe pod` shows 'Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu' but it's easy to misdiagnose as a quota issue rather than a missing device plugin. Another pitfall: forgetting tolerations on GPU Pods when GPU nodes are tainted — the Pod is correctly requesting a GPU but can't schedule onto the tainted GPU node because it lacks the matching toleration, again resulting in `Pending`.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.real_example:
```yaml
spec:
  tolerations:
    - key: "nvidia.com/gpu"
      operator: "Exists"
      effect: "NoSchedule"
  nodeSelector:
    cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator: nvidia-tesla-t4
  containers:
    - name: inference
      resources:
        limits:
          nvidia.com/gpu: 1
```
This Pod spec tolerates the GPU-node taint, requires scheduling onto a node labeled with T4 GPUs, and requests one GPU — the scheduler places it only on a tainted, T4-equipped node with an available GPU, while a CPU-only API Pod (no toleration, no GPU request) is never scheduled there.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_it_is: Helm is the de facto package manager for Kubernetes. A 'chart' is a templated bundle of Kubernetes YAML manifests (Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Ingress, HPA, etc.) parameterized with values (`values.yaml`), allowing one chart to be deployed multiple times with different configurations (e.g., dev/staging/prod, or different models) via `helm install`/`helm upgrade`.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.why_it_exists: A single ML service deployment might require 5-10 separate YAML manifests (Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret, HPA, ServiceAccount...) — managing these as raw YAML across multiple environments means either duplicating files with small differences (drift-prone) or complex `sed`/templating scripts. Helm templatizes all of this: write the manifests once with `{{ .Values.X }}` placeholders, define environment-specific values in separate `values-{env}.yaml` files, and `helm install/upgrade` renders and applies the final manifests — also tracking deployment history for easy rollback (`helm rollback`).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.how_it_works: A chart's directory structure includes `Chart.yaml` (metadata), `values.yaml` (default configuration values), and `templates/` (Kubernetes manifest templates using Go template syntax referencing `.Values.*`, `.Release.*`, `.Chart.*`). `helm install my-model ./chart -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=v2.3.1` renders all templates with the merged values (defaults + file overrides + `--set` overrides) and applies the resulting manifests to the cluster, recording this as a 'release.' `helm upgrade` re-renders with new values/chart version and applies the diff; `helm rollback my-model 1` reverts to a previous release revision's rendered manifests.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.use_when: Use Helm when deploying the same application across multiple environments/instances with configuration differences (replica counts, resource limits, image tags, feature flags per environment), or when packaging a reusable deployment template for multiple models that share the same serving pattern (e.g., a generic 'model-server' chart instantiated once per model with different `values.yaml`).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.avoid_when: For a single, simple deployment with no meaningful environment variation, plain YAML manifests (possibly with `kustomize` for light overlay-based customization) may be simpler than Helm's templating language, which can become hard to read/debug when heavily nested with conditionals and loops. Avoid excessive templating abstraction that obscures what's actually being deployed — sometimes explicit YAML is more debuggable than a deeply parameterized template.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_goes_wrong: Helm's Go templating syntax (`{{ if }}`, `{{ range }}`, whitespace control with `{{- ... -}}`) has a notoriously sharp learning curve — subtle whitespace/indentation errors produce invalid YAML that's hard to debug (`helm template` to render locally without applying is the standard debugging step). Another common issue: `helm upgrade` failures mid-way can leave a release in a `failed` or `pending-upgrade` state that blocks subsequent upgrades until manually resolved (`helm rollback` or `helm upgrade --force`); teams often wrap Helm operations in CI with explicit timeout and rollback-on-failure logic to avoid stuck releases.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.real_example: A 'model-server' Helm chart templatizes Deployment, Service, HPA, and Ingress, with `values.yaml` exposing `image.repository`, `image.tag`, `resources.limits.nvidia\.com/gpu`, `replicaCount`, and `ingress.host`. The same chart is used for three different models: `helm install fraud-model ./model-server -f values-fraud.yaml`, `helm install nlp-model ./model-server -f values-nlp.yaml`, each `values-*.yaml` overriding the image, GPU count, and hostname — avoiding three separate copies of near-identical YAML.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_it_is: GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in CI/CD platform, where workflows (YAML files in `.github/workflows/`) define jobs triggered by repository events (push, pull request, tag). A standard ML service pipeline runs: **test** (unit/integration tests, linting), **build** (build the Docker image), **push** (push the image to a container registry like ECR/GCR/Docker Hub), and **deploy** (update the Kubernetes deployment, e.g., via `kubectl set image` or `helm upgrade`, to use the new image).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.why_it_exists: Manually building images and applying Kubernetes manifests for every change is slow, error-prone (forgetting a step, deploying an untested image, deploying the wrong tag), and doesn't scale to a team. Automating this pipeline ensures every deployed image has passed tests, is built reproducibly from a known commit, is traceable (image tags often include the git SHA), and deployments happen consistently — turning 'deploy' from a manual ritual into a reliable, auditable process triggered by a merge.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.how_it_works: A workflow triggers on `push` to `main` (or on tag creation for releases). The `test` job checks out code, sets up the runtime (Python via `actions/setup-python`), installs dependencies, and runs `pytest`/linters — if this fails, the pipeline stops and no image is built. The `build` job (depending on `test` passing) builds the Docker image, often tagging it with the git SHA (`docker build -t myregistry/my-api:${{ github.sha }} .`) for traceability. The `push` job authenticates to the container registry (using secrets stored in GitHub's encrypted secrets store) and pushes the tagged image. The `deploy` job then updates the Kubernetes deployment to use the new image tag — either directly (`kubectl set image deployment/my-api my-api=myregistry/my-api:${{ github.sha }}`) or by updating a Helm `values.yaml`/GitOps repo that a tool like ArgoCD then syncs.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.use_when: Use this pattern for any ML service with a production Kubernetes deployment — it's the standard 'path to production' for code changes. Gate the `deploy` job on environment protection rules (e.g., manual approval for production deploys, automatic for staging) and ensure the `test` job includes anything that should block a bad deploy (unit tests, model sanity checks, contract tests against the API schema).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.avoid_when: For research/training code that doesn't get 'deployed' as a service (e.g., notebooks, one-off experiment scripts), a full build→push→deploy pipeline is unnecessary — CI there might just run linting/tests. Also avoid auto-deploying directly to production on every merge to `main` without any gate (manual approval, canary, or automated smoke tests) for high-stakes services — at minimum a staging deploy + smoke test before production promotion is safer.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.what_goes_wrong: A common security mistake is hardcoding registry credentials or kubeconfig data directly in workflow YAML instead of using GitHub Encrypted Secrets — secrets in plain workflow files are visible to anyone with read access to the repo (and to forks in some configurations). Another frequent issue: tagging images as `latest` instead of an immutable identifier (git SHA or semantic version) — `latest` makes rollbacks ambiguous (which `latest` was actually running?) and can cause cache/pull inconsistencies across nodes (some nodes may have cached an older `latest`).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Docker & Kubernete.real_example:
```yaml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt && pytest
  build-and-push:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with: { registry: ${{ secrets.ECR_REGISTRY }}, username: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}, password: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }} }
      - run: |
          docker build -t $ECR_REGISTRY/my-api:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker push $ECR_REGISTRY/my-api:${{ github.sha }}
  deploy:
    needs: build-and-push
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - run: kubectl set image deployment/my-api my-api=$ECR_REGISTRY/my-api:${{ github.sha }} -n prod
```
The `environment: production` key enables GitHub's required-reviewer approval gate before the `deploy` job runs, even though `test` and `build-and-push` run automatically.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_it_is: MLflow Tracking is the core component of MLflow for recording the inputs and outputs of ML experiments: `mlflow.log_param()` records hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size), `mlflow.log_metric()` records evaluation results (accuracy, loss — optionally as a time series across training steps), `mlflow.log_artifact()` saves arbitrary files (plots, datasets, checkpoints), and `mlflow.log_model()`/`mlflow.<flavor>.log_model()` saves a trained model in MLflow's standardized format alongside its metadata.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.why_it_exists: Without systematic tracking, ML experimentation devolves into spreadsheets, filenames like `model_v2_final_FINAL.pt`, and lost context about which hyperparameters produced which results — making it impossible to reproduce a good result or compare runs rigorously. MLflow Tracking provides a structured, queryable record of every experiment run: what configuration was used, what the results were, and what artifacts (including the model itself) were produced — all linked together and stored centrally.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.how_it_works: Each call to `mlflow.start_run()` (often as a context manager: `with mlflow.start_run():`) creates a 'run' — a unique ID under which subsequent `log_param`/`log_metric`/`log_artifact`/`log_model` calls are recorded. These are written to a tracking server's backend store (a database for params/metrics/metadata) and artifact store (typically S3/GCS/Azure Blob/local filesystem for files and model binaries). `log_metric` accepts an optional `step` argument, allowing metrics to be logged as a time series across training epochs/steps, which the MLflow UI then plots. `log_model` serializes the model using a framework-specific 'flavor' (e.g., `mlflow.sklearn.log_model`, `mlflow.pytorch.log_model`) plus a generic format (`MLmodel` file, `conda.yaml`/`requirements.txt`) that records exactly how to load and serve it later, independent of the original training code.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.use_when: Use MLflow Tracking for every non-trivial training run — logging params/metrics costs almost nothing and pays off the first time you need to answer 'what configuration produced our best model from three weeks ago?' Use `log_model` specifically when a run produces a model you might want to register, serve, or compare against other runs' models.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.avoid_when: For extremely short exploratory scripts (e.g., a 10-second sanity check on a tiny dataset) where you have no intention of comparing or reproducing the result, the overhead of setting up logging may not be worth it — though even here, a habit of always logging tends to pay off when an 'exploratory' run turns out to matter later.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is logging metrics without a `step` parameter when they're actually a time series (e.g., per-epoch loss) — MLflow then overwrites the same metric value repeatedly instead of building a curve, and the UI shows only the last value instead of a useful plot. Another pitfall: logging huge artifacts (e.g., full datasets or many large checkpoints) to a tracking server backed by local disk or a small object store without monitoring storage growth — tracking servers can silently accumulate terabytes of artifacts over time, becoming an operational/cost surprise.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.real_example:
```python
with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.log_param("learning_rate", 0.001)
    mlflow.log_param("batch_size", 32)
    for epoch in range(10):
        train_loss = train_one_epoch(...)
        mlflow.log_metric("train_loss", train_loss, step=epoch)
    mlflow.log_artifact("confusion_matrix.png")
    mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, "model")
```
Later, `mlflow.search_runs(filter_string="metrics.train_loss < 0.1 AND params.batch_size = '32'")` finds exactly the runs matching those criteria, with one-click access to the logged model and confusion matrix plot.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_it_is: MLflow Autologging (`mlflow.autolog()`, or framework-specific variants like `mlflow.sklearn.autolog()`, `mlflow.xgboost.autolog()`, `mlflow.tensorflow.autolog()`) automatically instruments supported ML libraries to log parameters, metrics, and the trained model itself — without requiring any explicit `log_param`/`log_metric`/`log_model` calls in your training code.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.why_it_exists: Manually logging every relevant hyperparameter and metric is repetitive and easy to forget — especially with libraries that have dozens of constructor parameters (e.g., `RandomForestClassifier`) or that compute many useful metrics internally (e.g., XGBoost's per-iteration evaluation metrics). Autologging captures this 'for free' by hooking into the library's own APIs, ensuring consistent, comprehensive logging without per-script boilerplate.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.how_it_works: Calling `mlflow.sklearn.autolog()` (or the generic `mlflow.autolog()`, which enables autologging for all detected supported libraries) patches the relevant library's training functions/classes — e.g., for scikit-learn, it wraps `estimator.fit()` so that when you call `model.fit(X, y)`, MLflow automatically starts a run (if none is active), logs all of the estimator's `get_params()` as MLflow params, logs training metrics (and, for classifiers, common evaluation metrics if a test set is provided), and logs the fitted estimator as an MLflow model — all triggered by your normal `.fit()` call with zero extra lines.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.use_when: Use autologging as the default for any supported framework (scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, TensorFlow/Keras, PyTorch Lightning, Spark MLlib) — it's nearly free and captures a comprehensive baseline of params/metrics/model that you can supplement with custom `log_metric`/`log_param` calls for anything autolog doesn't capture (e.g., custom business metrics).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.avoid_when: For training code using libraries/patterns autolog doesn't support (custom training loops in raw PyTorch without Lightning, custom model classes), autolog won't capture anything meaningful and you need manual logging. Also, in highly customized pipelines where autolog's automatic run-management (starting/ending runs implicitly) conflicts with your own explicit `mlflow.start_run()` structure, the interaction can cause confusing nested-run behavior — read the framework-specific autolog docs for run-lifecycle interactions.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_goes_wrong: Autolog can log an overwhelming number of parameters (every constructor argument of an estimator, including ones you never touched and that took default values), cluttering the UI and making it harder to spot the parameters that actually varied across runs — filtering/searching by the params you care about mitigates this. Another issue: autolog's automatic model logging captures the model as the framework saved it at `.fit()` time — if you do further post-processing (calibration, threshold tuning) after `.fit()`, the autologged model won't reflect those changes unless you explicitly log the final model separately.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.real_example:
```python
import mlflow
mlflow.sklearn.autolog()

with mlflow.start_run():
    model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=10)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    # autolog already recorded n_estimators, max_depth, all other RF params,
    # training accuracy/F1 if eval set inferred, and the fitted model
    preds = model.predict(X_test)
    mlflow.log_metric("test_accuracy", accuracy_score(y_test, preds))  # custom metric added on top
```
The run page shows ~15 auto-captured RandomForest hyperparameters and metrics plus the one custom metric, with the model artifact ready to register — without writing any `log_param` calls.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_it_is: The MLflow Model Registry is a centralized store for managing the lifecycle of trained models as named, versioned entities. A logged model from a run can be 'registered' under a model name (e.g., `fraud-classifier`), creating Version 1; subsequent registrations of new models under the same name create Version 2, 3, etc. Each version can be assigned a 'stage' — `None`, `Staging`, `Production`, or `Archived` — representing its position in the deployment lifecycle.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.why_it_exists: An MLflow run produces an artifact tied to a specific experiment/run ID — useful for tracking, but not a stable reference for 'the model currently serving production traffic.' Downstream systems (serving infrastructure, CI/CD) need a stable name and a way to ask 'what's the current production model for `fraud-classifier`?' that doesn't change when a new run happens, but DOES change when a team deliberately promotes a new version. The Registry provides this stable indirection layer plus an audit trail of stage transitions.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.how_it_works: `mlflow.register_model(model_uri="runs:/<run_id>/model", name="fraud-classifier")` creates (or adds a new version to) a registered model. Each version has metadata (source run, creation time, description) and a 'stage.' Transitioning a version's stage (`client.transition_model_version_stage(name="fraud-classifier", version=3, stage="Production")`) is a deliberate, often manually-reviewed action — and by default, transitioning a new version to `Production` does NOT automatically archive the previous production version (you can configure `archive_existing_versions=True` to do so). Serving systems reference models by stage (`models:/fraud-classifier/Production`) rather than by version number, so promoting a new version to Production automatically redirects consumers without their configuration changing.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.use_when: Use the Registry whenever multiple model versions exist for the same logical model and you need a controlled, auditable promotion process (Staging for validation, Production for live serving, Archived for retired versions) — essentially any team with more than one person training models for the same production system.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.avoid_when: For a single-developer research project with no deployment, the Registry's stage/versioning ceremony adds overhead with no consumer benefit — plain run tracking suffices until there's an actual 'production' to promote to.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_goes_wrong: A common process gap is treating stage transitions as purely a labeling exercise without an actual validation gate — promoting to `Production` should imply the model passed some evaluation (offline metrics threshold, A/B test, fairness checks), but if that's not enforced (e.g., via CI checks before allowing the transition), the Registry's stages become just labels that don't guarantee quality. Another issue: stage names (`Staging`/`Production`/`Archived`) are global conventions that don't map perfectly onto every team's actual environments (e.g., teams with `dev`/`qa`/`staging`/`prod`) — MLflow's newer 'Model Registry with aliases and tags' (in MLflow 2.x) addresses this with more flexible labeling than the fixed four stages.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.real_example: A fraud model's run produces `runs:/abc123/model`, registered as `fraud-classifier` version 5. After offline evaluation confirms it beats the current production model on a holdout set, an engineer transitions version 5 to `Staging`, where it's shadow-deployed alongside the current production model (version 4) for a week. After shadow metrics look good, version 5 is transitioned to `Production` (with `archive_existing_versions=True`, automatically moving version 4 to `Archived`), and the serving system — which loads `models:/fraud-classifier/Production` — picks up version 5 on its next restart/reload without any config change.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_it_is: MLflow Projects is a convention for packaging ML code in a reusable, reproducible way — a directory (or Git repo) containing an `MLproject` file that defines the project's entry points (commands to run), their parameters, and the environment (conda environment, Docker image, or virtualenv requirements) needed to run them. `mlflow run <project_uri> -P param=value` then executes an entry point in a fresh, correctly-configured environment.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.why_it_exists: Sharing ML code as 'here's my script, here's roughly what packages I had installed' leads to 'works on my machine' problems — different package versions, missing system dependencies, or undocumented assumptions about the environment cause the same code to produce different (or no) results elsewhere. MLflow Projects formalizes the environment specification alongside the code and entry points, so anyone (or any automated system, like a CI pipeline or orchestrator) can run `mlflow run` and get the same environment and the same documented parameters.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.how_it_works: An `MLproject` YAML file declares `name`, an environment spec (`conda_env: conda.yaml`, `docker_env: {image: ...}`, or a `python_env.yaml`), and `entry_points` — each with a `command` template (e.g., `python train.py --lr {lr} --epochs {epochs}`) and declared `parameters` with types/defaults. `mlflow run https://github.com/org/project -e train -P lr=0.01` clones the repo, builds/activates the specified environment, and runs the `train` entry point's command with `lr=0.01` substituted — MLflow handles environment creation so the runner doesn't need to manually replicate the conda/Docker setup.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.use_when: Use MLflow Projects when you need to share training code across teams/environments with guaranteed reproducibility — e.g., a research team hands off a training pipeline to an MLOps team to run on different infrastructure, or a CI pipeline runs `mlflow run` as a step in a larger DAG (Airflow/Kubeflow can invoke MLflow Projects as tasks).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.avoid_when: If your team already has a standardized containerized training pipeline (e.g., every training job is a Docker image run via Kubernetes Jobs with its own environment management), MLflow Projects' environment abstraction may be redundant — you'd be specifying environment twice (once in your Dockerfile, once in `MLproject`). In that case just use the container directly and use MLflow Tracking (not Projects) for logging.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_goes_wrong: A common pitfall is letting the `MLproject`'s environment spec (conda.yaml) drift out of sync with what's actually needed — e.g., a new dependency is `pip install`'d manually during development but never added to `conda.yaml`, so `mlflow run` from a clean environment fails with an import error that doesn't reproduce on the developer's machine (where the package happens to already be installed). Another issue: Docker-based MLflow Projects require the runner to have Docker available and the image pre-built/pushed — if the image build step isn't part of the reproducibility story, 'reproducible' breaks down if the image is later deleted or becomes unavailable.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.real_example:
```yaml
# MLproject
name: fraud-training
conda_env: conda.yaml
entry_points:
  train:
    parameters:
      lr: {type: float, default: 0.01}
      epochs: {type: int, default: 10}
    command: "python train.py --lr {lr} --epochs {epochs}"
```
`mlflow run . -e train -P lr=0.005 -P epochs=20` creates the conda environment from `conda.yaml` (if not already cached), then runs `python train.py --lr 0.005 --epochs 20` inside it — a teammate running the same command on a different machine gets an identical environment, eliminating 'it worked on my machine' as a variable.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_it_is: MLflow Serving (`mlflow models serve`) spins up a local REST API server that loads a logged/registered MLflow model and exposes a `/invocations` endpoint accepting JSON (or CSV) input and returning predictions — without writing any serving code, because the model's `MLmodel` metadata already describes how to load and run it.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.why_it_exists: Once a model is logged with `mlflow.<flavor>.log_model()`, MLflow already knows the model's framework, dependencies (`conda.yaml`/`requirements.txt`), and input/output signature. MLflow Serving leverages this to provide an instant, generic 'turn this logged model into an API' command — useful for quick local testing, demos, or low-stakes internal serving without building a custom FastAPI/Flask wrapper.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.how_it_works: `mlflow models serve -m models:/fraud-classifier/Production -p 5000` loads the specified model version (from the Registry or a run URI), reconstructs its environment (optionally in a fresh conda env via `--env-manager conda`, ensuring the exact dependency versions used at training time), and starts a Flask-based (or, with `--enable-mlserver`, MLServer-based for higher performance) HTTP server. POSTing JSON to `/invocations` (in the `dataframe_split`, `dataframe_records`, or `inputs`/tensor format matching the model's signature) returns predictions as JSON.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.use_when: Use MLflow Serving for quickly validating a registered model end-to-end (does it load? does it produce sensible outputs given real-looking input?), for local development/demos, or for low-traffic internal tools where standing up a custom serving stack isn't justified.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.avoid_when: Avoid MLflow's built-in Flask-based server for production traffic at any meaningful scale — it's single-threaded by default and not designed for high concurrency or low-latency SLAs. For production, either export the model and serve it via a dedicated framework (FastAPI wrapping the model, BentoML, TorchServe, Triton) or use `--enable-mlserver` (MLServer is more production-capable, supporting batching and multi-model serving) — but even then, evaluate against purpose-built serving infrastructure for high-scale needs.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is environment mismatch — if `mlflow models serve` is run without recreating the exact training environment (`--env-manager local` reuses whatever's currently installed), subtle library version differences between training and serving can cause different predictions for the same input (e.g., a different scikit-learn version changing default behavior of a transformer). Another pitfall: the default input format expectations (`dataframe_split` vs `dataframe_records` vs raw tensor `inputs`) are easy to get wrong when constructing request payloads, producing confusing 400 errors about schema mismatches that don't clearly state which format is expected.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.real_example:
```bash
mlflow models serve -m "models:/fraud-classifier/Production" -p 5001 --env-manager conda
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5001/invocations \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"dataframe_split": {"columns": ["amount","merchant_risk"], "data": [[120.5, 0.8]]}}'
```
This recreates the conda environment the model was trained in (ensuring matching library versions) and returns `{"predictions": [0]}` — useful for a quick sanity check before wiring the model into a real serving pipeline.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_it_is: The MLflow Tracking UI (`mlflow ui`, or the hosted UI on a tracking server) is a web interface for browsing experiments and runs — viewing/sorting/filtering runs by their logged parameters and metrics, plotting metric curves over training steps, comparing multiple runs side-by-side (including parallel coordinates plots and scatter plots of metric-vs-parameter relationships), and browsing/downloading logged artifacts and models.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.why_it_exists: Logged data (via `log_param`/`log_metric`/`log_artifact`) is only useful if it can be explored and compared — raw database rows aren't actionable. The UI turns the tracking database into an interactive workspace for the core experimentation workflow: 'I ran 20 variants overnight — which one is best, and what made it different from the others?'
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.how_it_works: The UI reads from the same backend store that `log_*` calls write to. The runs table shows one row per run with columns for any logged param/metric (configurable), sortable/filterable with a search syntax similar to SQL (`metrics.accuracy > 0.9 AND params.model_type = 'xgboost'`). Selecting multiple runs and clicking 'Compare' shows a parallel-coordinates plot (each axis a parameter/metric, each line a run — useful for spotting which hyperparameter ranges correlate with better metrics) and overlaid metric-vs-step line charts (e.g., comparing training loss curves across runs to spot overfitting differences). Each run's detail page lists all params/metrics/tags and provides a file browser for artifacts, including a 'register model' button if a model artifact is present.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.use_when: Use the UI as the primary interface for reviewing hyperparameter sweep results, debugging why a particular run underperformed (comparing its params/metric curves against a successful run), and for the human-in-the-loop step of deciding which run's model to register/promote.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.avoid_when: For programmatic/automated comparison (e.g., a script that automatically picks the best run from a sweep by some criterion and registers it), use the `mlflow.search_runs()` Python API directly rather than the UI — the UI is for human exploration, not automation.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_goes_wrong: With a large number of runs (hundreds/thousands from extensive hyperparameter sweeps), the default runs table can become slow to load and hard to navigate without using search filters and column customization — teams that don't adopt a tagging/naming convention (e.g., tagging runs with a sweep ID) find it hard to isolate 'the 50 runs from yesterday's sweep' from everything else in the experiment. Another issue: metric plots default to step-based x-axes, which can be misleading when comparing runs with different total step counts or different logging frequencies — wall-clock-time x-axis is sometimes more meaningful for comparing training efficiency.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.real_example: After a 30-run learning-rate/batch-size sweep, an engineer filters the runs table to `metrics.val_accuracy > 0.85`, narrowing 30 runs to 4 candidates, then selects those 4 and opens the Compare view — the parallel-coordinates plot immediately shows that all 4 top runs used `batch_size=64` while runs with `batch_size=128` consistently scored lower, informing the next sweep's search space.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_it_is: Databricks provides a managed, integrated version of MLflow as part of its platform — the Tracking Server, Model Registry, and (in newer versions) Unity Catalog-integrated model governance are hosted and operated by Databricks, tightly integrated with Databricks notebooks, jobs, clusters, and Delta Lake tables, removing the need to self-host an MLflow tracking server and its backend database/artifact store.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.why_it_exists: Self-hosting MLflow requires operating a tracking server, a backend database (Postgres/MySQL for run metadata), and an artifact store (S3/Azure Blob/GCS), plus managing access control, scaling, and backups. For organizations already using Databricks for data engineering and ML, a managed MLflow integrated into the same workspace (with shared authentication, access controls via Unity Catalog, and notebooks that automatically log to the right experiment) removes this operational burden and provides tighter integration (e.g., model lineage linking back to the Delta tables used for training).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.how_it_works: In a Databricks notebook, `mlflow.start_run()` and `log_*` calls automatically target the workspace's managed tracking server with no configuration — experiments are organized in the workspace's folder structure, and runs are visible in the Databricks UI's 'Experiments' section. The Model Registry is similarly managed; with Unity Catalog integration, registered models become Unity Catalog objects (`catalog.schema.model_name`) with the same governance (access control, lineage, audit logs) as tables, and model versions can be directly deployed to Databricks Model Serving (a managed serving endpoint) with a few clicks/API calls.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.use_when: Use managed MLflow on Databricks when your training/data pipelines already run on Databricks — you get tracking, registry, and serving without standing up separate infrastructure, plus governance integration (who can register/promote/serve which models) consistent with your data access controls.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.avoid_when: If your ML infrastructure is not on Databricks (e.g., training on Kubernetes/SageMaker, with models served via your own Kubernetes cluster), self-hosted or cloud-native MLflow (e.g., AWS-managed MLflow on SageMaker) avoids paying for and depending on a platform you're not otherwise using. Also, registries tied to Unity Catalog create a dependency on Databricks for model governance — migrating away later means migrating that governance metadata too.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_goes_wrong: A common gotcha is assuming managed MLflow on Databricks behaves identically to open-source self-hosted MLflow in all respects — there are Databricks-specific differences (e.g., experiment organization tied to workspace folders, certain APIs requiring Databricks-specific authentication tokens when accessed from outside Databricks). Another issue: teams that adopt Unity Catalog-based model registries get strong governance, but migrating existing 'workspace' registry models to Unity Catalog models is a deliberate migration step, not automatic — organizations on older Databricks MLflow setups may have two registry systems to reconcile.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.real_example: A data science team trains models in Databricks notebooks reading from Delta Lake tables; `mlflow.autolog()` automatically logs to the workspace experiment tied to that notebook. After review in the Databricks Experiments UI, the best run's model is registered to Unity Catalog as `ml_prod.fraud.fraud_classifier`, where access is governed by the same Unity Catalog permissions as the underlying Delta tables — and the model is deployed to a Databricks Model Serving endpoint directly from the registry UI, with autoscaling and request logging managed by Databricks.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_it_is: This is the same MLflow Model Registry covered in the earlier note ('register, stage, archive'), revisited from the operational/automation angle: how version numbers and stages are used programmatically — via the MLflow client API rather than the UI — to drive CI/CD-based promotion pipelines, automated rollback, and consumer-side model resolution (`models:/<name>/<stage_or_version>`).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.why_it_exists: The earlier note covers the *what* — a name has versions, versions have stages. This note covers the *how teams operationalize it*: in mature MLOps setups, stage transitions aren't manual UI clicks but are triggered by CI/CD pipelines after automated validation (a 'promote to Staging' step runs after a model passes offline eval thresholds; 'promote to Production' runs after a shadow-deployment period passes), and consumer services resolve `models:/fraud-classifier/Production` at load time so that a promotion automatically takes effect for all consumers without redeploying them.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.how_it_works: The `MlflowClient` Python API exposes `get_latest_versions(name, stages=[...])`, `transition_model_version_stage(name, version, stage, archive_existing_versions=...)`, and `search_model_versions(filter_string=...)` for programmatic version/stage management. A CI pipeline might: train a candidate model, register it (creating a new version, initially with no stage), run an evaluation job comparing it against the current `Production` version's metrics on a held-out set, and — if it's better by some margin — call `transition_model_version_stage(..., stage="Production", archive_existing_versions=True)`. Serving code that does `mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/fraud-classifier/Production")` at startup (or on a periodic reload) automatically picks up whichever version currently holds that stage, without needing to know the specific version number.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.use_when: Use version-based, automated promotion when you want model updates to be a *data/pipeline* event rather than a *code deployment* event — e.g., a nightly retraining job that, if the new model passes automated checks, becomes production automatically (with alerting/rollback if it underperforms post-deployment). This decouples 'ship new code' from 'ship a new model,' which is valuable when models retrain far more often than code changes.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.avoid_when: For models where every production change requires human sign-off (regulatory requirements, high-stakes decisions), fully automated stage transitions remove a deliberate human checkpoint — in those cases, automate everything up to 'ready for review' (e.g., transition to `Staging` automatically, but require a human action to reach `Production`).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_goes_wrong: A subtle issue with `models:/<name>/Production`-style resolution combined with in-memory model caching in serving code: if a service loads the model once at startup and never reloads, a stage transition to a new version has NO effect until the service restarts — teams sometimes assume promotion is instantaneous when it's actually gated by the consumer's reload behavior. Another pitfall: automated promotion based solely on a single aggregate metric (e.g., overall accuracy) can promote a model that's better on average but worse for a critical subgroup — automated gates should check segment-level metrics, not just aggregates, before auto-promoting.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.real_example: A nightly Airflow DAG retrains `fraud-classifier`, registers the new version, runs an evaluation task comparing it against `models:/fraud-classifier/Production` on yesterday's labeled transactions, and — only if the new version's recall at the target false-positive rate improves AND doesn't regress on a 'high-value transaction' subgroup — calls `transition_model_version_stage(stage="Production", archive_existing_versions=True)`. The serving fleet polls the registry every 10 minutes and hot-reloads when the `Production` version changes, so a successful nightly retrain is live within ~10 minutes with zero human action — and if the new model regresses post-deployment, an on-call engineer can run `transition_model_version_stage(stage="Production")` on the previous version number to instantly roll back.

7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_it_is: Weights & Biases (W&B) is a hosted (and self-hostable) experiment tracking platform offering rich, real-time visualization of training metrics, system resource usage (GPU utilization, memory), model/data versioning ('Artifacts'), hyperparameter sweep automation ('Sweeps'), and team collaboration features (shared dashboards, reports, comments) — generally considered to have a more polished UI/visualization experience than MLflow's, at the cost of being a SaaS product (with a free tier and paid team/enterprise tiers) rather than a fully self-hosted open-source default.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.why_it_exists: While MLflow focuses on lifecycle management (tracking → registry → serving) with a relatively basic UI, W&B focuses on the experimentation and collaboration experience — making it easy to watch live training curves update in real-time from remote GPU clusters, compare dozens of runs visually, share interactive reports with non-technical stakeholders, and automate hyperparameter search — areas where teams doing heavy iterative research particularly value W&B's polish.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.how_it_works: `wandb.init(project="fraud-detection")` starts a run; `wandb.log({"loss": loss, "accuracy": acc}, step=epoch)` streams metrics to W&B's servers in real-time (visible in a live-updating dashboard while training is still running, unlike tools where you only see results after a run completes or on manual refresh). W&B automatically captures system metrics (GPU/CPU/memory utilization over time) alongside your logged metrics, useful for diagnosing whether a slow run is data-loading-bound or compute-bound. 'Artifacts' version datasets/models with lineage tracking (this model artifact was produced by this run, which consumed this dataset artifact). Reports combine plots, markdown, and embedded run comparisons into shareable documents.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.use_when: Use W&B for research-heavy teams doing many iterative experiments where real-time visibility into training (especially for long-running jobs on remote clusters) and rich comparison/visualization tooling significantly speeds up iteration, and where the team is comfortable with a SaaS dependency (or self-hosts the enterprise on-prem version).
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.avoid_when: For organizations with strict data residency/security requirements that preclude SaaS tools (and without budget/ops capacity for self-hosted W&B), or for teams primarily needing the lifecycle/registry/serving aspects (where MLflow's registry integration is more mature and open-source-native), MLflow may be the better fit — many teams use both: W&B for experimentation/visualization, MLflow for registry/serving.
7|🔴 T1 Infrastructure|Experiment Trackin.what_goes_wrong: Logging very high-frequency metrics (e.g., per-step rather than per-epoch for long training runs) can generate large volumes of logged data, impacting both network overhead during training (each `wandb.log` call sends data) and dashboard responsiveness when viewing runs with millions of logged points — downsampling or logging at coarser granularity is often needed. Another issue: real-time streaming to an external service means training jobs have a network dependency — in air-gapped or unreliable-network training environments, W&B's offline mode (`wandb.init(mode="offline")`, syncing later) is needed, and forgetting to configure this can cause training scripts to hang or error on connectivity issues.
