7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.why_it_exists: While general orchestrators (Airflow, Kubeflow, etc., covered in Orchestration & Streaming) can certainly orchestrate SageMaker API calls, SageMaker Pipelines provides an AWS-native alternative that requires no separate orchestration infrastructure (no Airflow scheduler/metadata DB to run) — pipeline definitions are submitted to SageMaker, which manages execution, retries, caching, and lineage tracking entirely as a managed service, with tight integration to other SageMaker components (e.g., a 'Register Model' step that writes directly to the SageMaker Model Registry, or conditional steps that branch based on evaluation metrics).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.how_it_works: A pipeline is defined as a sequence of `Step` objects (`ProcessingStep`, `TrainingStep`, `TransformStep`, `ConditionStep`, `RegisterModel`, etc.) in the SageMaker Python SDK, each wrapping an underlying SageMaker job type, with data dependencies expressed via `step.properties` referencing outputs of earlier steps. The pipeline is compiled to a JSON definition and submitted to the SageMaker Pipelines service, which executes steps in dependency order (parallelizing independent steps), with each step's execution being a standard SageMaker job (Processing/Training/etc.) — meaning step-level caching (skip re-running a step if its inputs/code haven't changed, similar to other pipeline frameworks), parameterization (pipeline parameters that can be overridden per execution), and a visual DAG view in SageMaker Studio for monitoring runs.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.use_when: Use SageMaker Pipelines when your training/deployment workflow is built primarily on other SageMaker components (Training Jobs, Processing Jobs, Model Registry) and you want orchestration that's natively integrated with those — avoiding the need to run/maintain a separate orchestrator (Airflow/Kubeflow) just to sequence SageMaker API calls.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.avoid_when: If your organization's broader data/ML pipelines span beyond SageMaker (e.g., a single orchestrated pipeline that includes non-ML ETL jobs, multi-cloud steps, or steps on Kubernetes), a general-purpose orchestrator (Airflow, Dagster, etc.) that can coordinate across all these systems — including calling SageMaker as one part of a larger DAG — is more appropriate than SageMaker Pipelines, which is scoped to SageMaker-native step types.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.what_goes_wrong: A common limitation teams hit is that **SageMaker Pipelines' step types are somewhat constrained** to SageMaker-native job types — incorporating arbitrary custom logic (e.g., 'call this internal microservice API') requires wrapping it as a Processing Step (running a custom container), which is more roundabout than a general orchestrator's flexibility to run arbitrary code/tasks. Another pitfall: **pipeline parameter typing and caching behavior** has a learning curve — pipeline parameters (`ParameterString`, `ParameterInteger`, etc.) and step caching keys need careful configuration, and teams new to the SDK sometimes get unexpected cache hits (a step is skipped using stale cached results when they expected it to re-run) due to caching configuration that doesn't account for all relevant changed inputs.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.real_example: A SageMaker Pipeline: `ProcessingStep` (feature engineering, output to S3) → `TrainingStep` (train on engineered features) → `ProcessingStep` (evaluate on holdout set, output a metrics JSON) → `ConditionStep` (if accuracy in the metrics JSON > 0.85) → `RegisterModel` (register to SageMaker Model Registry with status 'PendingManualApproval'). The pipeline is parameterized by `TrainingInstanceType` and `InputDataUri`, allowing the same pipeline definition to be re-run with different inputs/instance sizes — visible as a DAG in SageMaker Studio showing each execution's step statuses and the evaluation metrics that determined whether the conditional registration step ran.

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.what_it_is: SageMaker Endpoints provide AWS's managed real-time model serving — deploying a trained model (or multiple models) behind a persistent, auto-scaling HTTPS endpoint that handles incoming inference requests, with AWS managing the underlying compute, load balancing, and (optionally) auto-scaling based on traffic.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.why_it_exists: Self-hosting a model server (the Flask/FastAPI/TorchServe/Triton patterns covered earlier) requires provisioning compute, configuring auto-scaling, setting up load balancing, monitoring, and handling deployments/rollbacks yourself. SageMaker Endpoints externalize all of this — deploy a model artifact + container, and AWS provides a managed, scalable, monitored HTTPS endpoint, with features like multi-model endpoints (hosting many models on shared infrastructure for cost efficiency), serverless inference (no provisioned instances at all, pay-per-invocation), and built-in A/B testing via 'production variants'.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.how_it_works: A SageMaker model (a reference to model artifacts in S3 + a container image specifying how to serve it) is deployed to an endpoint by creating an 'endpoint configuration' (specifying instance type/count, or serverless configuration) and then the endpoint itself — SageMaker provisions the specified instances, deploys the container (which must implement SageMaker's serving contract — a `/ping` health check and `/invocations` prediction endpoint, satisfied automatically by SageMaker's pre-built framework containers, or implementable in custom containers), and routes traffic to it via a managed HTTPS URL. 'Production variants' allow splitting traffic across multiple model versions (for A/B testing/canary deployment) within one endpoint, and auto-scaling policies (based on `InvocationsPerInstance` or other CloudWatch metrics) adjust instance count within configured min/max bounds.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.use_when: Use SageMaker Endpoints when you want managed real-time serving infrastructure within AWS without operating your own serving cluster — particularly the **serverless inference** option for workloads with intermittent/unpredictable traffic (pay only per invocation, with cold-start latency tradeoffs), or **multi-model endpoints** when hosting many models with low individual traffic (sharing instance capacity rather than provisioning per-model infrastructure).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.avoid_when: For ultra-low-latency requirements (sub-10ms), the additional network hop and SageMaker's invocation overhead may not meet requirements as well as co-located/specialized serving (e.g., Triton on dedicated infrastructure within your own VPC's lowest-latency path). Also, for organizations using Kubernetes for serving across multi-cloud or on-prem environments, SageMaker Endpoints introduce an AWS-specific serving mechanism alongside (rather than unified with) Kubernetes-based serving (KServe/Triton-on-K8s) used elsewhere — consider consistency needs.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.what_goes_wrong: A common cost issue is **leaving endpoints running** — unlike Training Jobs (ephemeral by design), Endpoints run continuously (provisioned instances billed 24/7) until explicitly deleted, and forgotten test/experiment endpoints are a frequent source of unexpected AWS bills. Another frequent issue is **cold-start latency with serverless inference** — serverless endpoints scale to zero when idle, and the first request after idle incurs a cold-start delay (loading the model into a fresh container) that can be seconds, problematic for latency-sensitive applications with sporadic traffic patterns; provisioned concurrency (keeping some instances warm) mitigates this at additional cost.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.real_example: A model is deployed to a SageMaker real-time endpoint with `instance_type='ml.m5.xlarge'`, `initial_instance_count=2`, and an auto-scaling policy targeting `InvocationsPerInstance=1000` with min=2/max=10 instances. A second 'production variant' running a candidate model version receives 10% of traffic for canary evaluation, configured via `production_variants` weights — CloudWatch metrics for both variants (latency, error rate, invocation count) are compared before shifting the candidate to 100% by updating the variant weights, all without redeploying the endpoint.

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.what_it_is: SageMaker Batch Transform is AWS's managed service for running offline/batch inference — given a trained model and a dataset in S3, it provisions ephemeral compute, runs inference on the entire dataset, writes predictions back to S3, and tears down the infrastructure, with no persistent endpoint required.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.why_it_exists: Not every inference workload needs a real-time endpoint — many use cases (scoring a database of customers monthly, generating predictions for an entire catalog overnight) are inherently batch: process a large dataset once, get results, done. Running a persistent SageMaker Endpoint for this would mean paying for always-on infrastructure that's idle most of the time. Batch Transform mirrors Training Jobs' ephemeral-compute model (provision → run → save results → terminate) but for inference, directly addressing the 'batch vs. real-time' distinction covered in the Model Serving subtopic, specifically for the AWS/SageMaker ecosystem.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.how_it_works: A Batch Transform job is configured with a SageMaker model (the same model artifact + container used for Endpoints), an input S3 location (data to score, in a supported format — CSV, JSON Lines, etc.), instance type/count, and an output S3 location. SageMaker provisions the specified instances, downloads input data, runs it through the model container's `/invocations` interface in batches (with configurable `MaxPayloadInMB` and `BatchStrategy` for how records are grouped per inference call), writes predictions to the output S3 location (one output file per input file by default), and terminates instances on completion — supporting multi-instance parallelism for large datasets (input files are automatically sharded across instances).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.use_when: Use Batch Transform for periodic/scheduled bulk scoring where results aren't needed instantly — e.g., monthly churn scores for the entire customer base, nightly product recommendations refresh, or one-off scoring of a historical dataset — leveraging the same trained model artifact used for real-time endpoints without needing to stand up endpoint infrastructure.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.avoid_when: For low-latency, per-request inference (a user waiting for a response), Batch Transform's job-based model (minutes of provisioning + processing time) is entirely unsuitable — use SageMaker Endpoints. Also, for very small/frequent batch jobs, the per-job provisioning overhead may make a persistent (possibly auto-scaling-to-zero) endpoint, or a different batch-processing approach (e.g., AWS Lambda for small batches), more cost/time-efficient than spinning up Batch Transform infrastructure repeatedly.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is **input data sharding mismatches** — if the input format/sharding doesn't align with how `BatchStrategy` and `MaxPayloadInMB` are configured, individual transform requests to the model container can be too large (causing payload-size errors) or too small (causing excessive per-request overhead); tuning these for the specific model container's expectations requires some experimentation. Another pitfall: **output file correlation** — Batch Transform produces one output file per input file (with a `.out` suffix by default), and if downstream processes expect predictions joined back to specific input records (e.g., by an ID column), the job needs `join_source='Input'` configured so output includes the original input alongside predictions — without this, correlating predictions back to source records requires careful ordering assumptions that can silently break if SageMaker's internal batching reorders records.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.real_example: A retail company runs a monthly SageMaker Batch Transform job: input is a CSV in S3 with one row per customer (3 million rows, sharded across 50 files), the SageMaker model is a churn-prediction XGBoost model, and the job runs on 5 `ml.m5.xlarge` instances (each processing 10 input files in parallel) with `join_source='Input'` so each output row contains the original customer ID alongside the predicted churn probability — the job completes in ~20 minutes, writing results to S3 where a downstream Athena query joins the scores into the marketing team's customer segmentation dashboard.

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.what_it_is: This is SageMaker's specific managed feature store implementation — a dual online (low-latency DynamoDB-backed) and offline (S3 + Glue/Athena-queryable, partitioned by time) store for ML features, with a 'Feature Group' as the core abstraction (a versioned schema of features for an entity, e.g., 'customer features' with columns and a record identifier + event-time field).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.why_it_exists: The earlier foundational note (in Data & Feature Management) introduced feature stores generally — Feast, Tecton, and SageMaker Feature Store as a category — covering *why* feature stores exist (online/offline consistency, point-in-time correctness, avoiding feature-computation duplication) and *what* the core abstractions are. This note goes deeper into SageMaker Feature Store *specifically* as an AWS-native implementation of that pattern — relevant when the choice has already been made to build on AWS, and the question becomes 'how do I use SageMaker's specific feature store, and how does it integrate with the rest of SageMaker (Training Jobs, Pipelines, Endpoints)?'
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.how_it_works: A 'Feature Group' is created with a schema (feature names/types), a `RecordIdentifierFeatureName` (the entity key, e.g., `customer_id`) and an `EventTimeFeatureName` (timestamp for point-in-time queries). Writing a record via `PutRecord` (or batch ingestion from a Processing Job) stores it in the **online store** (DynamoDB-backed, for `GetRecord` low-latency lookups at inference time) and asynchronously replicates to the **offline store** (S3, in Parquet, partitioned by ingestion time, queryable via Athena/Glue for training-data generation with point-in-time-correct joins via Athena SQL). SageMaker Feature Store integrates with Pipelines (a Processing Step can write computed features directly to a Feature Group) and with Endpoints (inference code can call `GetRecord` to fetch precomputed features for a given entity ID at serving time).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.use_when: Use SageMaker Feature Store when you've chosen AWS as your ML platform and want a feature store that integrates natively with SageMaker Training/Pipelines/Endpoints without operating separate infrastructure (vs. self-hosting Feast, or using a third-party managed feature store like Tecton) — particularly convenient when feature computation is already happening within SageMaker Processing Jobs/Pipelines.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.avoid_when: If your ML infrastructure is multi-cloud or Kubernetes-centric (not SageMaker-centric), an open-source/portable feature store (Feast) avoids coupling feature infrastructure to AWS-specific services (DynamoDB, Glue). Also, SageMaker Feature Store's offline store query performance (via Athena) may not match purpose-built feature-store query engines for very large-scale point-in-time joins — teams with extremely demanding offline-feature-generation workloads sometimes find specialized feature stores (Tecton) or data-warehouse-native approaches more performant.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.what_goes_wrong: A common cost/latency issue is the **online-offline replication lag** — writes to the online store are immediately available via `GetRecord`, but offline-store replication (for training data) is asynchronous and can lag by minutes, so a training pipeline that queries the offline store immediately after a feature-computation job may miss the most recent records; pipelines need to account for this lag (e.g., wait/poll before querying offline data). Another pitfall: **DynamoDB costs for the online store** — high-cardinality entities with frequent feature updates (e.g., per-second feature updates for millions of entities) can generate substantial DynamoDB read/write costs if not provisioned/capacity-planned appropriately (on-demand vs. provisioned capacity mode tradeoffs).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.real_example: A SageMaker Pipeline's `ProcessingStep` computes daily aggregated customer features (e.g., `avg_order_value_30d`) and writes them to a `customer-features` Feature Group via batch `PutRecord` calls. A real-time recommendation Endpoint, on receiving a request for `customer_id=12345`, calls `GetRecord` against the online store (sub-10ms DynamoDB lookup) to retrieve `avg_order_value_30d` as a model input feature — while the model-training pipeline separately queries the offline store via Athena, joining the Feature Group's historical Parquet data with point-in-time correctness against training labels.

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.what_it_is: SageMaker Model Registry is AWS's native model versioning and lifecycle-management service — models are grouped into 'Model Package Groups' (representing a logical model, e.g., 'fraud-detector'), with each registered version ('Model Package') carrying metadata (training job lineage, evaluation metrics, approval status: PendingManualApproval/Approved/Rejected) and serving as the deployable unit referenced by SageMaker Endpoints.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.why_it_exists: This is a second occurrence of 'model registry' within Phase 7 — the earlier MLflow Model Registry notes (in Experiment Tracking) covered the general concept (register/stage/archive lifecycle, and automation/CI-CD versioning workflows) using MLflow as the example implementation. SageMaker Model Registry exists because organizations building on AWS/SageMaker want that same registry pattern — versioned models with approval gates before deployment — implemented as a native AWS service that integrates directly with SageMaker Pipelines (a `RegisterModel` step) and Endpoints (deploy directly from a registered Model Package), without needing to run/integrate MLflow's tracking server.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.how_it_works: A 'Model Package Group' is a named collection representing one logical model over time (e.g., 'fraud-detector'); each training run that produces a candidate can be registered as a new 'Model Package' (version) within that group, capturing the model artifact location, inference container, and (via `ModelMetrics`) evaluation results. Each Model Package has an `ApprovalStatus` (defaults to `PendingManualApproval`) — a human (or an automated Lambda triggered by EventBridge on registration) reviews the metrics and sets status to `Approved` or `Rejected`. Deployment (creating/updating a SageMaker Endpoint) references a specific Model Package, and approval-status changes can trigger EventBridge events that invoke deployment pipelines (e.g., a Lambda that creates/updates an endpoint when a model is Approved) — implementing the automated promotion pattern from a fully AWS-native toolchain.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.use_when: Use SageMaker Model Registry when your training (SageMaker Pipelines) and serving (SageMaker Endpoints) are both AWS-native — the registry then provides the connective tissue (versioning + approval gating + deployment triggers) without introducing a separate experiment-tracking system's registry. It's the natural choice for an all-SageMaker MLOps toolchain.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.avoid_when: If experiment tracking is done in MLflow/W&B (common even for teams that deploy via SageMaker), maintaining model versions in *both* that tool's registry and SageMaker Model Registry creates duplicate bookkeeping — teams need to decide on a single source of truth for 'which model version is in production' (often SageMaker Model Registry, if SageMaker Endpoints are the deployment target, with MLflow used purely for experiment tracking/comparison rather than as the registry of record).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.what_goes_wrong: A frequent organizational issue is **registry fragmentation** — if some teams register models in MLflow's registry and others in SageMaker's (or both, inconsistently), there's no single answer to 'what's running in production for model X', making audits and incident response harder; establishing one registry as authoritative (and treating the other, if used, as supplementary) avoids this. Another pitfall: **approval status doesn't enforce deployment** — setting a Model Package to `Approved` doesn't automatically deploy it (unless an automation pipeline is wired to react to that event); teams sometimes assume 'Approved' means 'live in production' when it actually just means 'cleared for deployment', and a manual or separately-triggered deployment step is still needed.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.real_example: A SageMaker Pipeline ends with a `RegisterModel` step that creates a new Model Package in the `fraud-detector` Model Package Group with `ApprovalStatus='PendingManualApproval'` and attached evaluation metrics (precision/recall on a holdout set). An ML engineer reviews the metrics in SageMaker Studio's Model Registry view and changes the status to `Approved`. An EventBridge rule watching for this status change triggers a Lambda function that updates the production SageMaker Endpoint's 'production variant' to point at the newly-approved Model Package's artifact, completing an automated (but human-gated) deployment from registration to production.

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.what_it_is: SageMaker JumpStart is AWS's hub of pre-trained, pre-packaged foundation models and traditional ML models — accessible from within SageMaker Studio (or via SDK), allowing one-click deployment of models (LLMs, vision models, etc. from providers like Hugging Face, Meta, Stability AI, and AWS's own) to SageMaker Endpoints, or one-click fine-tuning on your own data, without manually sourcing/packaging model artifacts and containers.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.why_it_exists: Setting up a model for SageMaker deployment from scratch — finding the right model artifact, building/sourcing a compatible inference container, configuring the serving contract — is significant setup work, especially for popular open-source/foundation models that many teams want to use as-is or fine-tune. JumpStart pre-packages hundreds of such models with ready-to-deploy containers and configurations, reducing 'I want to try this open-source LLM on SageMaker' from days of container/integration work to a few clicks or lines of SDK code.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.how_it_works: JumpStart provides a catalog of models, each with pre-built artifacts and SageMaker-compatible inference containers maintained by AWS/partners. From Studio's JumpStart UI (or `sagemaker.jumpstart` SDK), selecting a model and clicking 'Deploy' creates a SageMaker Endpoint running that model with sensible default instance types pre-selected based on the model's requirements. For fine-tuning, JumpStart provides pre-configured training scripts/containers for supported models — point at your training data in S3, and JumpStart launches a SageMaker Training Job using a fine-tuning recipe appropriate for that model architecture (e.g., LoRA fine-tuning for an LLM), producing a fine-tuned model artifact deployable the same way as the base model.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.use_when: Use JumpStart for rapid prototyping/evaluation of open-source or foundation models on SageMaker infrastructure — quickly standing up an endpoint for an open-source LLM to test against your use case, or fine-tuning a pre-trained model on your data without building custom training/serving containers from scratch.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.avoid_when: For production deployments with specific customization needs (custom preprocessing, specific container optimizations, non-standard serving logic), JumpStart's pre-packaged containers may be a starting point but often need to be customized beyond what the one-click deployment provides — teams typically graduate from JumpStart prototypes to custom-built SageMaker models/containers for production. Also, JumpStart's model catalog, while large, doesn't include every model — for very new or niche models not yet in the catalog, you're back to manual container/artifact packaging regardless.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.what_goes_wrong: A common cost issue is the same as with other SageMaker Endpoints — JumpStart-deployed endpoints run on provisioned (billed) instances continuously until deleted, and the 'one-click deploy' convenience means it's easy to spin up (and forget about) endpoints during exploration, especially for large models requiring expensive GPU instances. Another pitfall: **default instance recommendations may not be cost-optimal** — JumpStart suggests instance types that will *work* for a given model, but these defaults aren't always the most cost-effective choice for your actual traffic/latency requirements; teams should benchmark and potentially right-size instances rather than accepting defaults for production use.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|SageMaker.real_example: A team evaluating whether an open-source LLM (available via JumpStart) meets their summarization use case deploys it to a SageMaker Endpoint with one click from Studio's JumpStart catalog (selecting a `ml.g5.2xlarge` instance as suggested), tests it via the SageMaker SDK's `predict()` against sample documents, and — finding it promising but needing domain adaptation — uses JumpStart's fine-tuning workflow to LoRA-fine-tune the model on their internal document corpus (a SageMaker Training Job using JumpStart's pre-configured fine-tuning script), then deploys the fine-tuned artifact to a new endpoint for further evaluation, all without writing a custom Dockerfile.

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|AWS Bedroc.what_it_is: AWS Bedrock is a fully-managed service providing API access to a range of foundation models (Anthropic's Claude, Meta's Llama, Amazon's Titan/Nova, Cohere, Mistral, and others) through a unified API — no infrastructure to provision, with pay-per-token pricing, plus features like fine-tuning, knowledge bases (managed RAG), guardrails (content filtering), and agents (tool-use orchestration).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|AWS Bedroc.why_it_exists: Teams wanting to use foundation models face a choice: call a model provider's API directly (e.g., Anthropic's API), or self-host an open-source model (via SageMaker JumpStart, vLLM, etc.). Bedrock offers a third path for AWS-centric organizations: access multiple providers' models through one AWS-native API, with billing consolidated into AWS accounts, data staying within the customer's AWS environment/VPC (important for compliance — model providers don't see/retain customer data by default), and integration with other AWS services (IAM for access control, CloudWatch for monitoring, Bedrock Guardrails for safety filtering) — addressing enterprise procurement/compliance/integration needs that calling external APIs directly doesn't satisfy as cleanly.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|AWS Bedroc.how_it_works: Bedrock exposes a unified `InvokeModel`/`Converse` API — specify a model ID (e.g., `anthropic.claude-3-5-sonnet`, `meta.llama3-70b`) and a request payload, and Bedrock routes to the appropriate underlying model, returning a response in a normalized format (the `Converse` API provides a consistent interface across providers, reducing per-provider code differences). 'Knowledge Bases for Bedrock' provides managed RAG — point it at documents in S3, and Bedrock handles chunking, embedding (via a chosen embedding model), vector storage (in OpenSearch Serverless, Aurora, or other supported vector stores), and retrieval-augmented generation in a single API call. 'Bedrock Agents' orchestrate multi-step tool-use workflows (the model decides which APIs/Lambda functions to call to fulfill a request). Fine-tuning ('Custom Models') allows fine-tuning select base models on your data, with the resulting custom model also served via Bedrock's managed infrastructure.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|AWS Bedroc.use_when: Use Bedrock when you want managed access to multiple foundation model providers within an AWS-native, IAM-governed environment — particularly attractive for enterprises with AWS-centric compliance/procurement requirements, or teams wanting to easily compare/switch between models from different providers without separate API integrations and contracts for each.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|AWS Bedroc.avoid_when: If you need the absolute latest model versions/features from a specific provider immediately upon release, there's sometimes a lag between a provider's direct API release and availability on Bedrock. Also, for self-hosted open-source models where you need full control over serving infrastructure (custom batching, specific quantization, on-prem/air-gapped deployment), Bedrock's managed-API model doesn't apply — use SageMaker JumpStart + vLLM/TGI or similar self-hosted serving instead.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|AWS Bedroc.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is **model-specific prompt/parameter differences leaking through the 'unified' API** — while `Converse` normalizes the basic request/response shape, different underlying models have different context limits, system-prompt handling, and tool-use formats, so code that works well with one Bedrock model may need adjustment when switching to another, despite the unified-API promise. Another pitfall with **Knowledge Bases (managed RAG)** is limited control over the chunking/retrieval strategy compared to a custom RAG pipeline — for use cases needing fine-tuned retrieval (custom chunking logic, hybrid search, reranking strategies beyond what's configurable), teams often outgrow the managed Knowledge Base and build a custom retrieval pipeline using Bedrock just for the generation step.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|AWS Bedroc.real_example: An enterprise customer-support application uses Bedrock's `Converse` API to call Claude for generating responses, with a Bedrock Knowledge Base (backed by the company's product documentation in S3, indexed into an OpenSearch Serverless vector store) providing RAG context — IAM policies restrict which internal applications/roles can invoke which models, CloudWatch logs every invocation for audit purposes, and Bedrock Guardrails filter responses for PII before they're returned to support agents, all without the company's data leaving their AWS account/VPC boundary, satisfying their compliance team's requirements for handling customer data with third-party AI models.

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|S3, ECR, I.what_it_is: S3 (Simple Storage Service), ECR (Elastic Container Registry), and IAM (Identity and Access Management) are foundational AWS services that underpin virtually every ML workflow on AWS: S3 stores data/model artifacts/training outputs as objects; ECR stores the Docker container images used for training/serving; IAM controls *who* (users, roles, services) can access *what* (S3 buckets, SageMaker resources, ECR repositories) — the plumbing that every SageMaker (and most non-SageMaker AWS ML) workflow depends on.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|S3, ECR, I.why_it_exists: Every ML workflow needs to store large amounts of data and artifacts durably and cost-effectively (S3's role), package and version the code/environment that runs training and serving (ECR's role for container images), and enforce least-privilege access so that, e.g., a training job's compute role can read training data but not arbitrary production databases (IAM's role). These three services are the substrate that SageMaker (and Bedrock, and most AWS ML services) build on — understanding them is essential for understanding *why* an AWS ML pipeline is structured the way it is (data in S3, containers in ECR, permissions via IAM roles attached to jobs/endpoints).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|S3, ECR, I.how_it_works: **S3**: data is stored as objects in buckets, organized by key prefixes (acting like folder paths) — training jobs read input data from S3 URIs and write model artifacts/checkpoints back to S3; lifecycle policies can auto-archive/delete old objects to control storage costs. **ECR**: a private Docker registry — custom training/serving container images are built locally or in CI, tagged, and pushed to an ECR repository; SageMaker Training Jobs/Endpoints reference an ECR image URI to know what container to run. **IAM**: 'roles' (not users) are the typical mechanism for service-to-service permissions — a SageMaker Training Job runs with an attached 'execution role' that grants it permission to read specific S3 buckets, pull from specific ECR repositories, and write logs to CloudWatch; IAM policies are JSON documents specifying allowed actions on specific resource ARNs, following the principle of least privilege (a training job's role should only have access to the buckets/repos it actually needs, not blanket S3/ECR access).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|S3, ECR, I.use_when: These three are not optional/situational — they're the baseline for any AWS-based ML workflow. The relevant 'use when' question is about *how carefully* to configure them: production ML systems should have tightly-scoped IAM roles per workload (a training role, a separate inference role, separate from data-engineering roles), versioned/immutable ECR images (avoid `:latest` tags for reproducibility — pin to specific image digests/tags), and S3 bucket organization/lifecycle policies that reflect data governance requirements (e.g., separating raw data, processed features, and model artifacts into different prefixes/buckets with appropriate retention).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|S3, ECR, I.avoid_when: N/A in the sense that these are foundational — but common anti-patterns to avoid: using overly broad IAM policies (`s3:*` on `*` resources) for convenience during development and never tightening them for production (a major security/compliance gap); using mutable `:latest` ECR tags for production training/serving (breaks reproducibility — you can't be sure which exact image version produced a given model); and treating S3 as a flat dump without naming/versioning conventions, making it hard to trace which S3 objects correspond to which training run/model version months later.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|S3, ECR, I.what_goes_wrong: The most common IAM issue is **overly permissive execution roles** discovered during security audits — a SageMaker execution role created early in a project with broad `AmazonS3FullAccess` (for convenience) remains in place in production, meaning a compromised training job (e.g., via a malicious dependency in a training script) could access *any* S3 bucket the role can reach, not just the intended training data — least-privilege IAM policies, scoped to specific bucket ARNs/prefixes, are essential but often retrofitted late (and painfully) rather than designed in from the start. A common ECR issue is **image bloat and pull latency** — large custom training/serving images (many GB, due to unnecessary dependencies/layers) slow down job startup (image pull time) and increase ECR storage costs; multi-stage Docker builds (covered in Docker & Kubernetes) help keep images lean. An S3 issue: **inconsistent key/prefix conventions** across teams make it hard to apply lifecycle policies or locate artifacts — e.g., model artifacts from different training runs scattered without a `model_name/version/timestamp/` convention become difficult to clean up or audit.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|S3, ECR, I.real_example: A SageMaker Training Job's execution role (`arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/ml-training-role`) has a policy granting `s3:GetObject`/`s3:ListBucket` scoped to `arn:aws:s3:::company-ml-data/training-data/*` and `s3:PutObject` scoped to `arn:aws:s3:::company-ml-artifacts/models/*` — it cannot read other buckets or write outside the artifacts prefix. The training container image is built in CI, tagged with the git commit SHA (`123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/training:a1b2c3d`), and pushed to ECR — the SageMaker job references this exact tag, so the model artifact produced can always be traced back to the exact code+dependency versions that produced it via the image tag, satisfying the team's reproducibility requirements.

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|EC2 GPU in.what_it_is: p3, p4, g4, and g5 are AWS EC2 instance families providing GPU-accelerated compute, differing in GPU generation/count and the balance of compute-vs-cost — p3 (NVIDIA V100, training-focused), p4 (NVIDIA A100, large-scale training), g4 (NVIDIA T4, cost-effective inference/light training), and g5 (NVIDIA A10G, a newer balance of inference and moderate training) — the underlying compute that SageMaker Training Jobs/Endpoints (and any self-managed EC2-based ML workload) run on.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|EC2 GPU in.why_it_exists: Different ML workloads have very different GPU requirements — large-scale distributed training of big models benefits from the highest-end GPUs with fast interconnects (p4, with A100s and NVLink/EFA networking for multi-node training), while serving a moderately-sized model for inference doesn't need (and shouldn't pay for) that level of hardware (g4/g5 with T4/A10G GPUs offer much lower cost per hour while still providing meaningful GPU acceleration for inference and smaller training jobs). Understanding these families lets you match instance choice to workload, directly controlling cost — the difference between p4 and g4 instance-hours can be an order of magnitude in price.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|EC2 GPU in.how_it_works: Each family offers multiple sizes (e.g., `p3.2xlarge` with 1 V100, up to `p3.16xlarge` with 8 V100s; `p4d.24xlarge` with 8 A100s and high-bandwidth EFA networking for multi-node scaling; `g4dn.xlarge` with 1 T4 up to `g4dn.12xlarge` with 4 T4s; `g5.xlarge` with 1 A10G up to `g5.48xlarge` with 8 A10Gs). When used with SageMaker, you specify the instance type as a string (e.g., `instance_type='ml.p4d.24xlarge'`) for Training Jobs or Endpoints, and SageMaker provisions that underlying EC2 instance type. For self-managed workloads, you launch EC2 instances of these types directly (with appropriate AMIs containing GPU drivers/CUDA, or use the Deep Learning AMIs which come pre-configured) — multi-instance distributed training on p4d instances leverages EFA (Elastic Fabric Adapter) networking for the low-latency inter-node communication that frameworks like PyTorch DDP/Horovod require at scale.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|EC2 GPU in.use_when: Use **p4** (A100) for large-scale model training, especially multi-node distributed training where EFA networking matters — the highest performance but highest cost. Use **p3** (V100) for training workloads where A100-level performance isn't needed and cost is a concern relative to p4 (V100 is an older generation, often cheaper, including more spot availability). Use **g5** (A10G) for a balance of inference serving and moderate fine-tuning/training workloads — A10G offers good price/performance for many production inference use cases. Use **g4** (T4) for cost-sensitive inference serving of smaller models, or light development/testing work where the cheapest GPU access is the priority.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|EC2 GPU in.avoid_when: Avoid defaulting to the largest/most expensive instance type 'to be safe' — many inference workloads run fine on g4/g5, and using p4 for inference is usually wasteful (high idle-capacity cost). Conversely, avoid under-provisioning for training — attempting to train a large model on g4 (T4, with limited VRAM — typically 16GB) when it requires more memory leads to out-of-memory errors and forces workarounds (smaller batch sizes, gradient checkpointing) that may be more costly in wall-clock time/engineer-effort than simply using an instance with more GPU memory.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|EC2 GPU in.what_goes_wrong: A frequent cost issue is **GPU instance availability and spot pricing volatility** — the most popular GPU instance types (especially p4d) can have limited on-demand availability in certain regions/AZs, and spot prices/interruption rates fluctuate significantly with demand, sometimes making 'cheaper' spot instances impractical for time-sensitive training if interruptions are frequent (tying back to the spot-instance checkpointing considerations covered in the SageMaker Training Jobs note). Another common mistake is **VRAM mismatches** — choosing an instance based on its 'GPU count' without checking per-GPU memory (a `g4dn.xlarge`'s single T4 has 16GB VRAM, while a `g5.xlarge`'s A10G has 24GB, and a `p4d.24xlarge`'s A100 has 40GB or 80GB depending on variant) — a model/batch-size combination that fits on one GPU type may OOM on another with less VRAM despite both being 'GPU instances'.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|AWS|EC2 GPU in.real_example: A team fine-tunes a 7B-parameter LLM using LoRA: they initially try `g5.2xlarge` (1× A10G, 24GB VRAM) but hit out-of-memory errors with their desired batch size; switching to `g5.12xlarge` (4× A10G, 96GB total VRAM, enabling model+data parallelism) resolves it at moderate additional cost. For their final full-parameter fine-tuning run (requiring far more memory and benefiting from fast multi-GPU interconnect), they use a `p4d.24xlarge` (8× A100 80GB with NVLink) for a few hours — paying a high hourly rate but for a short, well-defined job, while their always-on inference endpoint for the fine-tuned model runs on a cheaper `g5.xlarge`, optimizing cost across the very different training vs. serving workload profiles.

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_it_is: Data parallelism is a distributed training strategy where the *same* model is replicated on each of N GPUs, and each replica processes a different shard (mini-batch) of the training data in parallel — gradients computed by each replica are then synchronized (typically averaged) across all GPUs before the model weights are updated, keeping all replicas identical after each step.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.why_it_exists: The most common bottleneck in training is simply 'too much data, takes too long on one GPU' — data parallelism is the most straightforward way to use multiple GPUs to speed up training when the model itself fits comfortably on a single GPU's memory: N GPUs can process N times as much data per step (or the same amount N times faster), with each GPU doing the same computation on different data, requiring relatively simple changes to a single-GPU training script.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.how_it_works: Each of N GPUs holds a full copy of the model. A global batch is split into N micro-batches, one per GPU. Each GPU performs a forward and backward pass on its micro-batch, producing local gradients. An **all-reduce** operation (a collective communication primitive) sums/averages gradients across all GPUs, so every GPU ends up with the same averaged gradient — each GPU then applies the optimizer step using this averaged gradient, keeping all model replicas in sync. The effective batch size is `micro_batch_size × N`, and learning rate often needs scaling (e.g., linear scaling rule) to account for the larger effective batch size.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.use_when: Use data parallelism whenever the model fits in a single GPU's memory and you want to speed up training (or train on more data per step) by adding more GPUs — it's the default/simplest distributed training strategy and should be the first thing tried before reaching for model/tensor/pipeline parallelism, which are needed only when the model itself is too large for one GPU.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.avoid_when: Data parallelism alone doesn't help when the model itself doesn't fit on a single GPU (e.g., a large LLM whose parameters+optimizer-states+activations exceed one GPU's memory) — in that case, model/tensor/pipeline parallelism (or memory-efficient data parallelism like ZeRO/FSDP, covered later) is needed regardless of how many GPUs you have. Also, at very large GPU counts, all-reduce communication overhead can become a bottleneck relative to compute — beyond some point, adding more data-parallel replicas yields diminishing returns due to communication cost dominating.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_goes_wrong: A common pitfall is **forgetting to scale the learning rate** with the effective batch size — training with 8 GPUs (8x the effective batch size) using the same learning rate tuned for single-GPU training often converges to a worse solution or trains less efficiently; the linear scaling rule (multiply LR by N, often with a warmup period) is the standard mitigation but requires deliberate configuration. Another issue is **batch normalization statistics across replicas** — standard BatchNorm computes statistics per-GPU (per micro-batch), which with small micro-batches can give noisy statistics different from what a single large batch would produce; SyncBatchNorm (synchronizing statistics across all GPUs) addresses this but adds communication overhead.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.real_example: A team training an image classification model on a single GPU takes 10 hours for 50,000 images/epoch with batch size 64. Moving to 8 GPUs with data parallelism, each GPU processes a micro-batch of 64 (effective batch size 512), with gradients all-reduced after each step — training time drops to roughly 1.5 hours/epoch (not exactly 8x due to communication overhead), and the team scales the learning rate from 0.001 to 0.008 (8x) with a 5-epoch warmup to maintain convergence quality comparable to the single-GPU baseline.

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_it_is: DistributedDataParallel (DDP) is PyTorch's built-in implementation of data parallelism — wrapping a model in `torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel` automatically handles gradient all-reduce across processes (typically one process per GPU), overlapping communication with backward-pass computation for efficiency, and is the recommended (over the older, less efficient `DataParallel`) way to do multi-GPU/multi-node training in PyTorch.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.why_it_exists: PyTorch's original `DataParallel` (single-process, multi-thread, with a 'main' GPU gathering/scattering data) had significant inefficiencies (Python GIL contention, imbalanced GPU memory usage, single-process bottleneck) and didn't scale to multi-node setups. DDP was built as the modern replacement: each GPU runs in its own process (avoiding GIL issues), gradient synchronization uses efficient NCCL all-reduce, and the architecture scales naturally from single-node multi-GPU to multi-node multi-GPU — becoming the standard for PyTorch distributed training, and the foundation that higher-level tools (Lightning, Hugging Face Accelerate, DeepSpeed's data-parallel mode) build on.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.how_it_works: Training is launched with one process per GPU (via `torchrun` or `torch.multiprocessing.spawn`), each process initializing a 'process group' (via `torch.distributed.init_process_group`, typically with the NCCL backend for GPU communication) and wrapping its local model copy in `DDP(model)`. During the backward pass, DDP registers hooks on each parameter's gradient computation — as soon as a parameter's gradient is ready, DDP begins an asynchronous all-reduce for that gradient (bucketed with nearby parameters for efficiency) *while* the backward pass continues computing other gradients, overlapping communication with computation to hide latency. After backward completes, all processes have synchronized (averaged) gradients and each independently calls `optimizer.step()` — since all started with identical weights and apply identical (averaged) gradients, all replicas remain identical.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.use_when: Use DDP as the default for any PyTorch multi-GPU training where the model fits on a single GPU — it's well-optimized, well-documented, and integrates with `torchrun` for easy multi-node launches (e.g., on SageMaker's multi-instance training, which sets up the necessary environment variables for `torchrun`).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.avoid_when: DDP alone doesn't solve memory constraints — if the model (plus optimizer states/gradients/activations) doesn't fit on a single GPU even with a tiny batch size, DDP's full-model-replica-per-GPU approach is infeasible; FSDP or DeepSpeed ZeRO (covered later, which shard the model/optimizer state across GPUs rather than replicating) are needed instead.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_goes_wrong: A very common error is **forgetting `DistributedSampler`** — without it, every GPU's DataLoader iterates over the *full* dataset (not a unique shard), meaning each epoch processes the same data N times redundantly (wasting compute) rather than each GPU seeing 1/N of the data; `DistributedSampler` must be used (and `.set_epoch()` called each epoch for correct shuffling) for DDP training to actually parallelize data processing as intended. Another frequent issue is **unused parameters causing hangs** — if some parameters don't receive gradients in a particular forward pass (e.g., conditional branches in the model), DDP's all-reduce can hang waiting for gradients that never come, requiring `find_unused_parameters=True` (with a performance cost) or restructuring the model to always use all parameters.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.real_example:
```python
import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP
from torch.utils.data import DistributedSampler

dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl")
model = DDP(model.to(local_rank), device_ids=[local_rank])
sampler = DistributedSampler(dataset)
for epoch in range(epochs):
    sampler.set_epoch(epoch)
    for batch in DataLoader(dataset, sampler=sampler, batch_size=32):
        loss = model(batch).loss
        loss.backward()  # DDP overlaps all-reduce with this
        optimizer.step()
```
Launched via `torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 train.py` for 8-GPU single-node training — `torchrun` sets `RANK`, `LOCAL_RANK`, `WORLD_SIZE` environment variables that `init_process_group` and `DistributedSampler` use to correctly partition data and coordinate gradient synchronization across all 8 processes.

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_it_is: Horovod is an open-source distributed training framework (originally from Uber) that adds data-parallel distributed training to TensorFlow, PyTorch, and other frameworks via a relatively small code change — using efficient all-reduce communication (via NCCL/MPI) and a unified API that works similarly regardless of the underlying ML framework.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.why_it_exists: Before frameworks had mature built-in distributed training (PyTorch's DDP, TF's `tf.distribute`), distributed training required significant framework-specific boilerplate, and teams using multiple frameworks (some models in TensorFlow, some in PyTorch) had to learn different distributed APIs for each. Horovod provided a consistent, relatively simple API (`hvd.DistributedOptimizer` wrapping any framework's optimizer) that worked across frameworks, with efficient ring-all-reduce communication, becoming popular for multi-framework organizations and for its straightforward `horovodrun` launcher for multi-node training.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.how_it_works: Horovod initializes with `hvd.init()`, which establishes the process's rank/size within the distributed job (via MPI or Gloo). The optimizer is wrapped: `optimizer = hvd.DistributedOptimizer(optimizer)` — this wrapped optimizer automatically performs all-reduce on gradients before applying updates, using ring-allreduce (each GPU communicates only with its neighbors in a ring topology, achieving bandwidth-optimal communication for gradient synchronization). Training is launched via `horovodrun -np N -H host1:4,host2:4 python train.py`, which starts N processes across the specified hosts, each running the (mostly-unmodified) training script with Horovod's initialization/optimizer-wrapping added.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.use_when: Use Horovod for organizations needing a consistent distributed-training approach across multiple ML frameworks (TensorFlow and PyTorch both in use), or for teams already invested in Horovod's tooling/expertise from earlier adoption (before native framework solutions matured).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.avoid_when: For pure-PyTorch shops, native DDP (and FSDP/DeepSpeed for memory-constrained large models) is now generally preferred — it's more tightly integrated with PyTorch's ecosystem (autograd hooks, newer features), has more active development focus, and avoids an additional dependency (Horovod requires MPI/NCCL setup that can be its own operational overhead). Similarly, TensorFlow's native `tf.distribute.Strategy` APIs have matured significantly, reducing the relative advantage Horovod once had for TF users.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_goes_wrong: A common operational pain point is **Horovod's MPI dependency** — setting up MPI correctly across multi-node clusters (SSH configuration, host files, network configuration for MPI communication) is its own source of friction, especially in containerized/Kubernetes environments where MPI's process-launching model doesn't map naturally onto container orchestration (requiring MPI Operator for Kubernetes or similar). Another issue: as the framework-native distributed APIs (DDP, FSDP) have matured and gained more features (e.g., FSDP's memory sharding has no direct Horovod equivalent), teams using Horovod for memory-constrained large-model training hit a ceiling that requires migrating to DeepSpeed/FSDP anyway — Horovod remains primarily a pure-data-parallelism tool.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.real_example: A research lab with both a computer-vision team (TensorFlow) and an NLP team (PyTorch) standardizes on Horovod for distributed training infrastructure — both teams' training scripts add `hvd.init()` and wrap their optimizer with `hvd.DistributedOptimizer`, and both are launched via the same `horovodrun` command on the lab's shared GPU cluster, letting the infrastructure team support one distributed-training launch mechanism instead of maintaining separate DDP and `tf.distribute` cluster configurations.

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_it_is: Model parallelism is a distributed training strategy where *different parts of a single model* are placed on different GPUs (rather than replicating the whole model on each GPU, as in data parallelism) — used when a model is too large to fit on a single GPU's memory, regardless of batch size.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.why_it_exists: Data parallelism (replicating the full model on each GPU) hits a hard wall when the model itself — its parameters, gradients, optimizer states, and activations — exceeds a single GPU's memory (e.g., a model with tens of billions of parameters won't fit on an 80GB A100 even with batch size 1). Model parallelism solves the *memory* problem (not the speed problem) by distributing the model's components across multiple GPUs, so collectively the GPUs have enough memory for the whole model even though no single GPU holds all of it — this is the prerequisite that makes training very large models (LLMs) possible at all.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.how_it_works: In its simplest form ('naive' model parallelism), different layers (or groups of layers) of the model are assigned to different GPUs — e.g., layers 1-10 on GPU 0, layers 11-20 on GPU 1. During the forward pass, GPU 0 computes layers 1-10's output and sends it (the activations) to GPU 1, which computes layers 11-20, and so on; backward pass reverses this, sending gradients back. The two more sophisticated and commonly-used forms of model parallelism — **tensor parallelism** (splitting individual operations/layers across GPUs) and **pipeline parallelism** (splitting the model into sequential stages processed in a pipelined fashion) — are covered as separate items in this subtopic, since 'naive' model parallelism (as described here) suffers from severe GPU idle time (only one GPU computes at a time while others wait).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.use_when: Use (some form of) model parallelism when the model's parameters alone (let alone activations/optimizer states) exceed a single GPU's memory — this is mandatory, not optional, for training models beyond a certain size (roughly, models with tens of billions+ parameters on current-generation GPUs), and is combined with data parallelism (each model-parallel 'group' is replicated data-parallel-style across additional GPUs) for large-scale training.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.avoid_when: If the model fits on a single GPU, model parallelism adds communication overhead (activations/gradients passed between GPUs holding different model parts) and complexity without benefit — data parallelism alone is simpler and typically faster for models that fit. Naive (layer-split) model parallelism specifically should be avoided in favor of pipeline parallelism (which pipelines multiple micro-batches to keep GPUs busier) or tensor parallelism, since naive model parallelism's severe GPU-idle-time problem makes it rarely used in practice as described.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_goes_wrong: The defining failure mode of naive model parallelism is **GPU idle time / poor utilization** — if GPU 0 holds layers 1-10 and GPU 1 holds layers 11-20, during the forward pass GPU 1 sits idle while GPU 0 computes, then GPU 0 sits idle while GPU 1 computes — at any instant, only one GPU is doing useful work, so adding more GPUs this way doesn't proportionally speed up training (it only enables fitting bigger models, at a throughput cost). This is precisely the problem pipeline parallelism's micro-batch pipelining addresses (covered in the dedicated Pipeline Parallelism note).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.real_example: A 70B-parameter model's weights alone require ~140GB in fp16 — far exceeding a single 80GB A100's memory even before accounting for activations and optimizer states. A naive model-parallel split puts the first 40 transformer layers on GPU 0 and the remaining 40 on GPU 1 (each GPU holding ~70GB of weights) — this makes training *possible* (the model fits across 2 GPUs), but a profiler would show GPU 1 idle during most of the forward pass on GPU 0's layers, and vice versa during backward — motivating the team to adopt pipeline parallelism (processing multiple micro-batches in a pipelined fashion across the same GPU split) to improve utilization, as covered in the Pipeline Parallelism note.

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_it_is: Tensor parallelism splits individual matrix operations (the large matrix multiplications inside transformer layers — attention and feed-forward weight matrices) across multiple GPUs, so that a single layer's computation is performed cooperatively by several GPUs simultaneously, each handling a slice of the matrices involved.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.why_it_exists: Naive/pipeline model parallelism splits the model *between* layers (some layers on GPU 0, others on GPU 1) — but for extremely large individual layers (e.g., a feed-forward matrix with tens of billions of parameters in a single weight matrix), even one layer might be too large for one GPU, or splitting between layers alone doesn't provide enough parallelism for the largest models. Tensor parallelism splits *within* a layer — e.g., a weight matrix is split column-wise across GPUs, each GPU computes a partial result using its slice, and partial results are combined (via all-reduce) — enabling models where even individual layers exceed single-GPU memory, and is a core technique (alongside pipeline and data parallelism) for training the largest LLMs.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.how_it_works: For a linear layer `Y = XW`, the weight matrix `W` can be split column-wise into `[W1, W2]` across 2 GPUs — each GPU computes `Y1 = XW1` and `Y2 = XW2` independently (each GPU needs the full input `X`, but only its slice of `W`), and the results are concatenated (`Y = [Y1, Y2]`) — for the next layer's matrix multiplication, an all-reduce or all-gather combines these partial results as needed. In transformer architectures, Megatron-LM's tensor parallelism scheme splits attention heads across GPUs (each GPU computes a subset of attention heads) and splits the feed-forward layer's hidden dimension, requiring two all-reduce operations per transformer layer (one after attention, one after the feed-forward block) — this communication happens on every forward AND backward pass, requiring very high-bandwidth interconnects (NVLink within a node) to be efficient, which is why tensor parallelism is typically used *within* a single node (across GPUs connected by NVLink) rather than across nodes.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.use_when: Use tensor parallelism for very large models where individual layers (specifically, the largest weight matrices) are too large for one GPU, and when you have high-bandwidth intra-node GPU interconnects (NVLink) — tensor parallelism's frequent communication makes it primarily suitable within a single multi-GPU node, combined with pipeline parallelism across nodes for the largest training setups (a '3D parallelism' combining data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.avoid_when: Tensor parallelism's per-layer communication overhead makes it inefficient across slower interconnects (e.g., across nodes connected by Ethernet rather than NVLink/InfiniBand) — for cross-node splitting, pipeline parallelism (which communicates only between pipeline stages, much less frequently) is preferred. Also, for models that fit within a single GPU (or that fit with FSDP/ZeRO-style sharding without tensor parallelism's added complexity), the implementation complexity of tensor parallelism (requiring model-architecture-aware splitting of specific operations) isn't worth it — it's reserved for the largest-scale training.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_goes_wrong: The most direct failure mode is using tensor parallelism across **low-bandwidth interconnects** — because tensor parallelism requires communication on every layer's forward and backward pass (multiple all-reduces per transformer block), running it across nodes connected by standard Ethernet (rather than NVLink/InfiniBand) makes communication the dominant cost, often making training *slower* than not parallelizing at all; tensor-parallel degree should generally not exceed the number of GPUs with fast interconnect within a node (e.g., 8 for an 8-GPU node). Another issue: implementing tensor parallelism correctly requires understanding the specific model architecture's operations (which matrices to split, where all-reduces are needed) — frameworks like Megatron-LM provide this for transformer architectures, but adapting it to novel architectures requires careful, error-prone manual work.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.real_example: Training a 175B-parameter GPT-style model on a cluster of 8-GPU nodes (each node's 8 A100s connected via NVLink): the model uses tensor-parallel degree 8 (splitting each transformer layer's attention heads and feed-forward matrices across all 8 GPUs in a node, leveraging NVLink's high bandwidth for the frequent all-reduces), combined with pipeline-parallel degree across nodes (different layers on different nodes, with less-frequent inter-node communication) and data parallelism across pipeline-parallel groups — this '3D parallelism' (Megatron-LM + DeepSpeed style) is how the largest models are trained, with each parallelism dimension matched to the interconnect bandwidth available at that level (NVLink for tensor-parallel, slower inter-node links for pipeline-parallel).

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_it_is: Pipeline parallelism splits a model into sequential stages (groups of consecutive layers), with each stage placed on a different GPU — unlike naive model parallelism's severe idle-time problem, pipeline parallelism processes multiple micro-batches in a pipelined fashion (like an assembly line), so that while GPU 2 processes micro-batch 1's stage, GPU 1 can already start processing micro-batch 2's stage, keeping more GPUs busy simultaneously.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.why_it_exists: Naive model parallelism (splitting layers across GPUs) leaves most GPUs idle most of the time because only one GPU computes at once. Pipeline parallelism addresses this directly: by splitting the training batch into smaller micro-batches and pipelining them through the stage-split model (similar to CPU instruction pipelining), multiple GPUs can be active simultaneously on different micro-batches at different stages — substantially improving GPU utilization while retaining the memory benefit of splitting the model across GPUs (necessary for models too large for one GPU).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.how_it_works: The model's layers are partitioned into K sequential stages, each on a different GPU (GPU 0 has layers 1-N/K, GPU 1 has layers N/K+1-2N/K, etc.). A training batch is split into M micro-batches. In the forward pass, GPU 0 processes micro-batch 1, then passes its output to GPU 1 while GPU 0 immediately starts on micro-batch 2 — this creates a pipeline where, after a 'fill' period, all K GPUs are simultaneously processing different micro-batches at different stages. The backward pass similarly pipelines in reverse. The unavoidable idle time at the start (filling the pipeline) and end (draining it) is called the 'pipeline bubble' — its relative cost decreases as the number of micro-batches M increases relative to the number of stages K (more micro-batches amortize the bubble overhead). Schedules like GPipe (simple fill-then-drain) and PipeDream/interleaved schedules (more sophisticated overlapping of forward/backward across stages) trade off bubble size, memory usage, and implementation complexity.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.use_when: Use pipeline parallelism (typically combined with tensor and data parallelism for the largest models) when the model doesn't fit on a single GPU/node and you need to split across nodes with lower-bandwidth interconnects than tensor parallelism tolerates — pipeline parallelism's stage-boundary communication (activations passed between stages) is much less frequent/smaller than tensor parallelism's per-layer all-reduces, making it more tolerant of inter-node network latency.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.avoid_when: For models that fit on a single GPU (or single node with tensor parallelism), pipeline parallelism's added complexity (pipeline bubble overhead, more complex scheduling, harder debugging of which stage/micro-batch an error occurred in) isn't worth it. Also, with too few micro-batches relative to pipeline stages, the bubble overhead dominates — pipeline parallelism needs enough micro-batches (and correspondingly, the activation-memory cost of holding many in-flight micro-batches' activations) to be efficient, which interacts with memory constraints in ways that need careful tuning.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_goes_wrong: The defining tuning challenge is the **bubble-vs-memory tradeoff** — more micro-batches reduce the relative bubble overhead (better GPU utilization) but require storing more in-flight activations simultaneously (more memory), and the optimal balance depends on the specific model/hardware; getting this wrong means either poor utilization (too few micro-batches, large bubble) or out-of-memory errors (too many micro-batches, activation memory explosion). Another common issue is **load imbalance across stages** — if layers aren't evenly distributed (e.g., the embedding layer + first transformer block on GPU 0 is much heavier than other stages), the slowest stage becomes the bottleneck for the whole pipeline, and naive equal-layer-count splitting doesn't always produce equal compute-time splits.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.real_example: A 4-GPU pipeline-parallel setup splits a 48-layer transformer into 4 stages of 12 layers each (GPU 0: layers 1-12, GPU 1: 13-24, etc.). A training batch is split into 8 micro-batches using GPipe-style scheduling — after the pipeline fills (GPU 0 processes micro-batch 1, then 2, ..., while GPU 1 starts on micro-batch 1 once GPU 0 finishes it, etc.), at steady state all 4 GPUs are simultaneously processing different micro-batches at different stages. With 8 micro-batches and 4 stages, the bubble overhead is roughly (4-1)/8 ≈ 37% — the team experiments with 16 micro-batches (reducing bubble to ~19%) but must also reduce per-micro-batch size to keep activation memory within bounds, illustrating the bubble-vs-memory tradeoff in practice.

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_it_is: ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer), developed by Microsoft as part of DeepSpeed, is a memory-optimization technique for data-parallel training that eliminates the redundancy of each GPU storing a full copy of optimizer states, gradients, and (in stage 3) model parameters — instead, these are *sharded* (partitioned) across data-parallel GPUs, with each GPU holding only its shard, dramatically reducing per-GPU memory usage while preserving data parallelism's simplicity (no model-architecture-specific splitting like tensor/pipeline parallelism).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.why_it_exists: In standard data parallelism (DDP), every GPU holds a *full* copy of the model parameters, gradients, AND optimizer states (for Adam, optimizer states are 2x the parameter count in fp32 — momentum and variance) — for large models, this redundancy (the same data replicated on every GPU) wastes enormous amounts of memory that could instead be used for larger models/batches. ZeRO's insight: since data-parallel GPUs only need their *own* shard of optimizer states/gradients/parameters at the moment they're used (with communication to gather what's needed when needed), storing full redundant copies is unnecessary — ZeRO progressively eliminates this redundancy across three stages, each trading a bit more communication for substantial memory savings.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.how_it_works: **ZeRO Stage 1** shards optimizer states across data-parallel GPUs — each GPU computes its full gradient as usual, but only updates (and stores optimizer state for) its shard of parameters, then broadcasts updated parameters to all GPUs (reducing memory ~4x for Adam). **ZeRO Stage 2** additionally shards gradients — during backward pass, each GPU only retains gradients for its parameter shard (reduce-scatter instead of all-reduce), further reducing memory (~8x total). **ZeRO Stage 3** additionally shards the model parameters themselves — each GPU holds only 1/N of the parameters at rest, and gathers the full parameters for a layer just-in-time during forward/backward pass (via all-gather), then discards them after use — enabling the largest memory savings (memory scales down roughly linearly with GPU count) at the cost of additional communication for parameter gathering.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.use_when: Use ZeRO (via DeepSpeed) when training large models with data parallelism and memory is the binding constraint — ZeRO Stage 1/2 are nearly 'free' (minimal extra communication, large memory savings) and should be used by default for large-model data-parallel training; Stage 3 is used when even Stage 2's memory savings aren't enough (the model itself, not just optimizer states, doesn't fit), accepting more communication overhead for the ability to train much larger models than would otherwise fit.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.avoid_when: For small models where memory isn't a constraint, ZeRO's sharding/communication overhead provides no benefit over standard DDP — use DDP for simplicity. ZeRO Stage 3's parameter-gathering communication can become a significant overhead at very large scale or with slow interconnects — in those regimes, combining ZeRO (typically stage 1/2) with model/tensor/pipeline parallelism (3D parallelism) rather than relying on ZeRO stage 3 alone may be more efficient.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_goes_wrong: A common issue with **ZeRO Stage 3** is that its just-in-time parameter gathering means a layer's full parameters only exist transiently during that layer's forward/backward computation — code that assumes it can access `model.layer.weight` directly at arbitrary times (e.g., for custom logging/inspection, or certain weight-tying schemes) may find the parameter is a sharded placeholder rather than the full tensor unless accessed within the correct context manager, causing confusing bugs for code written assuming standard PyTorch parameter access. Another pitfall: ZeRO's memory savings interact with **checkpoint saving/loading** — sharded optimizer states/parameters need to be correctly gathered (or saved in sharded format and correctly reloaded with matching GPU count) for checkpointing, and mismatched checkpoint formats (saved with one ZeRO stage/GPU count, loaded with another) are a common source of errors when resuming training.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.real_example: A team training a 13B-parameter model on 8x A100 (40GB each) finds that standard DDP with Adam doesn't fit (model + gradients + Adam states for 13B params in fp16/fp32 mixed precision exceeds 40GB per GPU even with the model alone needing ~26GB, leaving little room for optimizer states/activations). Enabling DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 2 shards optimizer states and gradients across the 8 GPUs (each GPU storing ~1/8 of these), reducing per-GPU memory enough to fit comfortably with room for a reasonable batch size — achieved by adding a DeepSpeed config (`"zero_optimization": {"stage": 2}`) with no changes to the model architecture itself.

7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_it_is: FSDP (Fully Sharded Data Parallel) is PyTorch's native implementation of ZeRO-Stage-3-style full sharding — model parameters, gradients, and optimizer states are all sharded across data-parallel workers, with each worker gathering the full parameters for a given layer just-in-time during forward/backward computation and then re-sharding (discarding the gathered copy) afterward, integrated directly into PyTorch (`torch.distributed.fsdp`) rather than requiring DeepSpeed as an external dependency.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.why_it_exists: ZeRO Stage 3 (via DeepSpeed) demonstrated the value of fully-sharded training for fitting very large models, but required adopting DeepSpeed's training loop/configuration conventions (a separate framework layered on PyTorch). FSDP brings this capability natively into PyTorch — for teams whose training code is structured around PyTorch's native APIs (and especially those already using DDP), FSDP offers a more drop-in path to full-sharding memory savings (`model = FSDP(model)` is conceptually similar to `model = DDP(model)`) without adopting DeepSpeed's broader framework, and has become the standard choice for large-model training in PyTorch-native codebases (e.g., used for training many open-source LLMs).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.how_it_works: FSDP wraps the model (often layer-by-layer, with 'FSDP units' typically corresponding to transformer blocks) — each FSDP unit's parameters are sharded across all data-parallel workers at rest. During forward pass, when a given unit is about to be computed, FSDP performs an all-gather to reconstruct that unit's full parameters on every worker, computes the forward pass for that unit, then immediately re-shards (frees the gathered copy) before moving to the next unit — so at any instant, only one (or a few, with prefetching) units' full parameters exist in memory per worker, not the whole model. Backward pass mirrors this (gather, compute gradients, reduce-scatter gradients back to sharded form, re-shard). 'Mixed precision' and 'CPU offloading' options further reduce memory at the cost of speed.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.use_when: Use FSDP for large-model training in PyTorch-native codebases where ZeRO-Stage-3-level memory savings are needed (the model doesn't fit with standard DDP, even with ZeRO Stage 1/2-equivalent optimizations) — it's become a standard choice for fine-tuning/training large language models without leaving the PyTorch ecosystem, and integrates with Hugging Face's `accelerate`/`transformers` libraries for relatively easy adoption with existing model code.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.avoid_when: For models that fit comfortably with standard DDP, FSDP's all-gather/re-shard overhead per unit adds communication cost without memory benefit — use DDP. Also, FSDP's per-unit gather/compute/reshard pattern can complicate certain use cases (e.g., models with complex parameter-sharing/tying across distant layers may need careful FSDP-unit boundary configuration to avoid incorrect sharding of shared parameters).
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.what_goes_wrong: A common configuration issue is **FSDP unit boundaries (the `auto_wrap_policy`)** — if units are too small (e.g., wrapping every individual `nn.Linear`), the all-gather/re-shard overhead per unit dominates (too much communication, too granular); if too large (e.g., wrapping the whole model as one unit), memory savings are minimal (back to needing the whole model's parameters gathered at once); choosing unit boundaries that align with the model's natural structure (e.g., one FSDP unit per transformer block) is the typical sweet spot but requires understanding `auto_wrap_policy` configuration. Another frequent issue is **checkpoint format complexity** — FSDP checkpoints are sharded by default (each worker saves its shard), and converting to/from a 'full' (unsharded) checkpoint for inference or sharing requires explicit gather operations (`FSDP.state_dict_type` configuration) — getting this wrong leads to checkpoints that can't be loaded with a different GPU count or outside FSDP.
7|🔴 T1 Cloud ML Platforms|Distributed Tr.real_example:
```python
from torch.distributed.fsdp import FullyShardedDataParallel as FSDP
from torch.distributed.fsdp.wrap import transformer_auto_wrap_policy

model = FSDP(
    model,
    auto_wrap_policy=functools.partial(
        transformer_auto_wrap_policy, transformer_layer_cls={TransformerBlock}
    ),
    mixed_precision=mp_policy,
)
```
