7|🔴 T1 🔬 LLMOps Specifics|LLMOps Specifi.what_goes_wrong: Beyond the dataset-staleness and judge-flakiness issues noted in earlier tool-specific notes (LangSmith, DeepEval), a broader process issue is **eval thresholds becoming stale relative to the application's evolving quality bar** — a threshold set when the application was new and rough might be too lenient once the application has matured and users expect higher quality, but thresholds are rarely revisited unless something prompts it; periodically reviewing whether current thresholds still reflect the desired quality bar (not just whether the pipeline is green) keeps eval-driven CI meaningful over time. Another issue: **gating on aggregate scores hiding regressions in specific slices** — an aggregate metric across a diverse evaluation dataset can stay flat (or even improve) while quality regresses significantly for a specific subset of inputs (a particular topic, language, or user segment) that happens to be a small fraction of the dataset — slicing evaluation results by relevant dimensions (not just looking at the aggregate) catches regressions that aggregate-only gating would miss.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 LLMOps Specifics|LLMOps Specifi.real_example: A team maintains an evaluation dataset of 150 examples for their RAG-based support assistant, including 20 examples specifically drawn from past incidents (each representing a previously-identified failure mode that was fixed and added to the dataset as a regression test). When a developer proposes a change to the retrieval-ranking logic intended to improve overall relevance, CI runs the full evaluation suite — the aggregate RAGAS faithfulness score improves slightly as expected, but the slice of 20 incident-derived examples shows 2 of them now fail (the ranking change, while improving average relevance, regressed two specific previously-fixed edge cases). This slice-level visibility (not just the aggregate, which looked like an improvement) flags the regression for the developer to investigate before merging, who finds the ranking change needs an additional tie-breaking rule to avoid reintroducing those specific past failures.

7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.what_it_is: This note covers the Characteristic Stability Index (CSI) alongside PSI, in the specific context of credit-risk/regulatory model monitoring (common in banking): PSI is typically applied to a model's overall output (the credit score or predicted probability distribution) to monitor whether the *population* being scored has shifted, while CSI applies the identical PSI formula to each individual input *characteristic* (feature) — e.g., separately computing a stability index for 'applicant age distribution,' 'income distribution,' etc. — to pinpoint which specific input variables are driving any overall population shift.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.why_it_exists: This is a second occurrence — the earlier PSI note (Monitoring & Drift) covered the PSI formula and its conventional thresholds (>0.1 noticeable shift, >0.25 significant shift) as a general drift-monitoring metric. This note covers PSI's specific role within **regulatory model-validation frameworks** common in banking/credit risk (e.g., under frameworks like SR 11-7 in the US), where monitoring isn't just 'is there drift' in general but specifically requires: (a) PSI on the overall score distribution as a population-stability check, and (b) CSI computed per-characteristic to satisfy the regulatory expectation that model validators can identify *which specific input variables* changed when overall population stability degrades — a feature-level diagnostic granularity that the general PSI framing doesn't emphasize.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.how_it_works: PSI and CSI use the identical formula (Σ (current_% − reference_%) × ln(current_% / reference_%) summed over bins) — the distinction is purely in *what's being binned and compared*. For PSI, the bins are typically deciles of the model's score/probability output, comparing the reference (e.g., model-development sample) population's score distribution against the current population's. For CSI, the same calculation is performed independently for each input characteristic used by the model — binning each characteristic's values (e.g., income into bands) and comparing reference vs. current proportions per band — producing one CSI value per characteristic. A monitoring report for a credit model typically presents an overall PSI alongside a table of CSI values for every input characteristic, sorted by magnitude, so that if PSI indicates overall instability, the CSI table immediately shows which characteristics contribute most.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.use_when: Use PSI+CSI together in regulated lending/credit-risk contexts (or any context with similar model-validation/governance requirements) where monitoring reports need to both flag overall population instability (PSI) and attribute it to specific input variables (CSI) for model risk management documentation and regulatory review — the per-characteristic breakdown is often a documented requirement, not just a debugging convenience.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.avoid_when: For ML monitoring outside regulated contexts (where there's no requirement for per-characteristic stability reporting in a specific format), computing CSI for every input feature of a model with hundreds of features produces a large table that may be more naturally explored via other feature-attribution-style drift tools (e.g., the domain-classifier approach covered next, which directly ranks features by their contribution to detected drift) rather than a fixed PSI/CSI table format inherited from credit-risk conventions.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is **binning choices affecting CSI comparability across characteristics** — since CSI depends on how each characteristic is binned (e.g., income might be binned into deciles while a categorical variable like 'employment type' has its natural categories as bins), CSI values across different characteristics aren't directly comparable in an absolute sense the way one might assume from seeing them in the same table — a CSI of 0.15 for one variable and 0.08 for another doesn't necessarily mean the first variable shifted 'twice as much' in any deeper sense, just that its particular binning produced a larger index value; CSI is most useful for tracking a *given* characteristic's stability *over time* (consistent binning) rather than for cross-characteristic ranking in an absolute sense.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.real_example: A bank's credit-scoring model monitoring report shows overall PSI of 0.18 (above the 0.1 'noticeable shift' threshold but below 0.25). The accompanying CSI table shows most input characteristics have CSI below 0.05, but 'applicant income' has a CSI of 0.21 — immediately localizing the population shift to a change in the income distribution of applicants (perhaps reflecting a shift in the bank's marketing/acquisition channels toward a different income segment) rather than a broad shift across all characteristics. This directs the model-risk team's investigation specifically toward understanding the income-distribution change and assessing whether the model's income-related behavior remains appropriate for the new population, rather than a broader (and more costly) full model revalidation.

7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.what_it_is: This note covers the Cramer-von Mises (CvM) test alongside the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test as complementary distributional-comparison tests: where KS's statistic is the *single maximum* distance between two empirical CDFs, CvM's statistic is an *integral* (sum) of squared differences between the two CDFs across their entire range — making CvM more sensitive to distributional differences that are spread out (or concentrated in the tails) rather than concentrated at one point, which is where KS's single-max-distance statistic is most sensitive.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.why_it_exists: This is a second occurrence — the earlier KS test note (Monitoring & Drift) covered KS's max-CDF-distance statistic D = max|F_ref(x) − F_cur(x)| as a general distribution-comparison test for drift monitoring. This note covers **why a single test isn't always sufficient**: KS is most sensitive to differences near the *median* of a distribution (where CDFs tend to be steepest, so a shift there produces the largest CDF gap) and can be relatively insensitive to differences concentrated in the *tails* (where CDFs are flatter, so even a meaningful tail shift produces a small CDF gap) — CvM's integral-based statistic, by summing squared differences across the whole range, weights tail differences more than KS does, making the *combination* of both tests more robust than either alone for catching different drift patterns.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.how_it_works: The CvM statistic is computed as an integral (in practice, a sum over the empirical sample) of the squared difference between the two samples' empirical CDFs: ω² = ∫ (F_reference(x) − F_current(x))² dH(x), where H is a weighting function based on the combined sample. Unlike KS's single max-difference, every point along the distribution contributes to CvM's statistic, with squaring ensuring all contributions are positive (no cancellation between regions where one CDF is above vs. below the other). In practice, drift-monitoring tools often compute both KS and CvM (along with other tests) for each feature and flag drift if *either* exceeds its respective significance threshold — since a feature whose distribution has shifted primarily in its tails might show a non-significant KS statistic but a significant CvM statistic, and vice versa for a feature with a clear median shift but minimal tail change.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.use_when: Use CvM alongside KS (rather than relying on KS alone) when tail behavior of a feature's distribution matters for the application — e.g., for a feature where rare-but-extreme values are particularly important to the model's behavior (fraud amounts, for instance, where the tail of the transaction-amount distribution is often where fraud signal concentrates), a shift confined to the tail could be operationally significant while producing only a modest KS statistic.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.avoid_when: For features where only central-tendency shifts matter (and tail behavior is not operationally significant for the model), adding CvM alongside KS provides limited additional value while increasing the number of statistical tests being run (and therefore the number of significance thresholds/multiple-comparison considerations to manage) — for a monitoring system already tracking many features, adding a second test per feature roughly doubles the alerting surface, which should be weighed against the marginal detection benefit for features where it doesn't matter.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.what_goes_wrong: A common issue with running multiple statistical tests (KS and CvM) per feature, each with its own significance threshold, is **increased false-positive alert rate from multiple comparisons** — if a feature is flagged as 'drifted' whenever *either* test is significant, and both tests have, say, a 5% false-positive rate under no real drift, the combined false-positive rate for that feature is higher than either test alone (since either triggering counts as a flag) — for a monitoring system tracking many features with both tests, this compounds into a meaningfully higher overall false-alarm rate than a single-test approach, which may need correction (e.g., adjusting individual test thresholds, or requiring both tests to agree) to keep the overall alert volume manageable.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.real_example: A drift-monitoring system flags a transaction-amount feature: the KS test shows D=0.04 (not significant — the bulk of the distribution, around typical transaction amounts, hasn't shifted much), but the CvM test is significant — driven by a shift in the extreme tail (a small but non-trivial increase in very-large transactions in the current period). Because the monitoring system runs both tests and flags on either, this tail shift is caught despite KS alone missing it — and given the domain (transaction amounts, where large-value outliers are disproportionately relevant to fraud models), the team investigates and finds a new merchant category with characteristically larger transaction sizes was recently onboarded, which is relevant context for interpreting the fraud model's behavior on this new segment.

7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.what_it_is: Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) is a kernel-based statistical test for comparing two distributions — unlike KS, CvM, and PSI (which operate on a single variable's distribution at a time), MMD operates on *multivariate* data (including high-dimensional embeddings), computing a distance between two samples' distributions in a kernel-induced feature space, making it well-suited to detecting drift in high-dimensional representations like the embeddings used in deep learning and LLM applications.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.why_it_exists: PSI, KS, and CvM (covered above) are univariate tests — applied per-feature, one variable at a time. But many modern ML systems' most informative 'features' are high-dimensional embeddings (image embeddings, text embeddings) where drift might manifest as a shift in the overall *distribution of embedding vectors* in a way that no single dimension's univariate distribution clearly shows — a shift could be in the *joint* relationship among dimensions (a rotation or shift in the embedding space) rather than any individual coordinate's marginal distribution. MMD addresses this by operating directly on multivariate samples (e.g., comparing a reference set of embedding vectors against a current set), connecting to the embedding-drift visualization approaches covered for Arize AI and Arize Phoenix earlier in this phase — MMD provides a *statistical test* (a number with a significance threshold) for the kind of shift those tools visualize.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.how_it_works: MMD computes the distance between two distributions' mean embeddings in a 'kernel feature space' — using a kernel function (commonly a Gaussian/RBF kernel) that implicitly maps data into a (typically infinite-dimensional) feature space where the distance between the two samples' mean representations captures differences in the full distributions (not just their means in the original space), including differences in variance, skew, and higher-order structure. In practice, MMD is computed as an average of kernel evaluations between pairs of points within and across the two samples (an unbiased estimator involves comparing within-reference pairwise kernel values, within-current pairwise kernel values, and cross reference-current pairwise kernel values) — yielding a single number where larger values indicate the two samples' distributions are more different; a permutation test (repeatedly shuffling which points belong to 'reference' vs. 'current' and recomputing MMD) establishes whether the observed MMD is statistically significant given the sample sizes.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.use_when: Use MMD for drift detection on multivariate or high-dimensional data — embedding vectors from a vision or language model, or any feature set where the *joint* distribution (not just per-feature marginals) is what matters — particularly relevant for monitoring whether the inputs to a deep-learning model's later layers (or an LLM's embedding space, connecting to Arize Phoenix's embedding-visualization approach) have shifted in ways that per-feature univariate tests would miss.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.avoid_when: For low-dimensional tabular features where per-feature univariate tests (PSI, KS, CvM) already provide interpretable, per-feature drift signals (which directly suggest *which feature* to investigate), MMD's single aggregate multivariate statistic is less directly actionable — MMD tells you 'the joint distribution has shifted' but not *which dimensions* drove that, requiring additional analysis (or a complementary per-feature test) to localize the cause, whereas univariate tests are inherently localized to begin with.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is **kernel bandwidth (a hyperparameter of the kernel function) significantly affecting MMD's sensitivity** — a kernel with too large a bandwidth treats most points as 'similar' regardless of real differences (reducing MMD's sensitivity to genuine drift), while too small a bandwidth makes MMD overly sensitive to any sampling noise (flagging drift even from natural sample-to-sample variation) — choosing an appropriate bandwidth (often via heuristics based on the data's pairwise distances) matters for getting a meaningful significance threshold, and a poorly-chosen bandwidth can make MMD either useless (never significant) or noisy (always significant). Computational cost is another issue: MMD's pairwise-kernel-evaluation computation scales quadratically with sample size, which can become expensive for large reference/current samples without subsampling.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.real_example: A team monitoring an LLM-based document-classification system computes MMD between the embeddings of a reference set of documents (from when the model was validated) and the embeddings of a recent week's incoming documents. MMD is significant, indicating the joint embedding distribution has shifted — but since MMD itself doesn't say *why*, the team follows up with Arize Phoenix's embedding visualization (covered in LLM Observability & Evaluation), which shows the recent documents' embeddings cluster in a region distinct from the reference documents — on inspection, this corresponds to a new document type (a different language) that wasn't present in the reference set, giving the team both a statistical signal (MMD) that something changed and a visual/qualitative understanding (via the embedding visualization) of *what* changed.

7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.what_it_is: The domain classifier approach detects drift by training a binary classifier whose job is to distinguish 'reference' samples from 'current' samples — label every reference-period example as class 0 and every current-period example as class 1, train a classifier on this labeling task, and evaluate its AUC (or accuracy) on held-out data: if the classifier can't do better than chance (AUC ≈ 0.5), the two distributions are indistinguishable (no drift); if the classifier achieves high AUC (approaching 1.0), the two periods are easily separable (strong drift).
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.why_it_exists: MMD (covered above) gives a single statistical distance for multivariate drift but doesn't directly explain *which features* are responsible. The domain classifier approach addresses this gap elegantly by reusing standard supervised-learning tooling: any classifier that supports feature importances (e.g., a gradient-boosted tree) can be trained for the reference-vs-current discrimination task, and its feature-importance ranking directly identifies *which input features* the classifier relies on to distinguish the two periods — those are the features driving the detected drift. This turns drift detection into a familiar binary-classification problem, with all the associated tooling (cross-validation, feature importance, SHAP) immediately applicable.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.how_it_works: Concretely: take a window of reference data and a window of current data, concatenate them, add a binary label column ('is_current'), and train a classifier (often a simple model like logistic regression or gradient-boosted trees) to predict this label from the original features. Evaluate the classifier's AUC on a held-out split of this combined dataset. An AUC near 0.5 means the classifier's predictions are no better than random — the reference and current distributions look the same from the model's perspective (no detectable drift). An AUC significantly above 0.5 (e.g., 0.75+) means the classifier can reliably tell which period a sample came from — the distributions have diverged. For multivariate or high-dimensional data (including embeddings), this same approach works directly — the classifier operates on whatever feature representation is available, making it a flexible complement to MMD. Feature importances or SHAP values from the trained classifier then rank which original features contribute most to the separability, giving a feature-level breakdown analogous to CSI's per-characteristic breakdown but derived automatically rather than via per-feature statistical tests.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.use_when: Use the domain classifier approach when you want both a single aggregate drift signal (the AUC) AND an automatic feature-level breakdown of what's driving it, without manually running and interpreting separate per-feature tests (PSI/KS/CvM) for every feature — particularly convenient for high-dimensional feature sets or embeddings where running dozens/hundreds of individual univariate tests would be unwieldy, and where a single AUC number is an intuitive 'how much has changed' summary that's easy to communicate (an AUC of 0.5 = 'nothing changed', 0.9 = 'these look like completely different populations').
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.avoid_when: For small datasets (where training a reliable classifier on the reference-vs-current task may overfit and produce an artificially high AUC even without real drift) or for situations requiring a formal statistical significance threshold with known false-positive rates (where PSI/KS/CvM's established conventions and significance tests are more standard and easier to defend in a report), the domain classifier's AUC lacks the same well-established interpretive conventions — 'AUC of 0.6, is that drift or not?' is a less standardized question than 'PSI > 0.25, is that drift or not?'.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.what_goes_wrong: A common pitfall is **using a feature that trivially separates the two periods for reasons unrelated to meaningful drift** — e.g., if a timestamp or an auto-incrementing ID column is accidentally included as a feature, the classifier will achieve near-perfect AUC by simply learning 'higher IDs/later timestamps = current period,' which is trivially true by construction and doesn't reflect any meaningful distributional shift in the *actual model features* — such leakage features must be excluded before training the domain classifier, or the AUC will be uninformatively high (≈1.0) regardless of whether real feature drift occurred.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.real_example: An ML platform team builds an automated drift-monitoring pipeline that, for each model, trains a lightweight gradient-boosted classifier weekly to distinguish 'last month's serving inputs' from 'this week's serving inputs.' Most weeks, AUC hovers around 0.52-0.55 (essentially no drift). One week, AUC jumps to 0.81, and the top feature by importance is 'user_country' — investigation reveals the product launched in three new countries that week, shifting the geographic distribution of users. This single automated check (one classifier, one AUC, one feature-importance ranking) replaces what would otherwise require running and interpreting dozens of separate per-feature PSI/KS computations, while also directly pointing at the responsible feature.

7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.what_it_is: This note presents a diagnostic decision framework for triaging a production model performance drop by systematically distinguishing between three categories: **data drift** — the distribution of inputs P(X) has changed (e.g., feature distributions shift, but the relationship between features and target is unchanged); **label drift** — the distribution of the target/outcome P(y) has changed (e.g., the overall rate of the positive class shifts, independent of input changes); and **concept drift** — the relationship P(y|X) between inputs and target has changed (the same input now maps to a different 'correct' output than before).
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.why_it_exists: This is at least a third occurrence of drift-taxonomy content — earlier notes (Monitoring & Drift: 'Data drift,' 'Concept drift,' 'Prediction drift'; Monitoring & Observability: second-occurrence deep-dives on data drift detection and concept drift) each covered these categories largely as *definitions*, explaining what each type of drift conceptually means. This note's distinct framing is **diagnostic**: given an observed drop in a production model's performance metric, how do you work through these three categories as hypotheses to systematically narrow down the cause — including introducing **label drift** explicitly as its own category (P(y) shift) which the earlier notes didn't isolate as a separate diagnostic branch from concept drift, even though both involve the target variable.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.how_it_works: A practical diagnostic sequence: (1) Check data drift first — run PSI/KS/CvM/domain-classifier checks (all covered above) on input features; if inputs haven't shifted, data drift is ruled out as the primary cause. (2) Check label drift — if ground-truth labels are available (even with delay), compare the distribution of P(y) between reference and current periods; if the positive-class rate has shifted substantially (e.g., fraud rate genuinely increased due to a new fraud campaign) while input feature distributions look stable, this points to label drift — the *world* changed (more fraud is happening) even if the *inputs the model sees* look statistically similar. (3) Check concept drift — if both inputs and the marginal label distribution look stable, but the model's predictions are increasingly miscalibrated or inaccurate for *given* input patterns, the input-output relationship itself has changed — e.g., a particular combination of features that used to indicate low fraud risk now indicates high fraud risk because fraudsters have adapted their patterns to look like that combination. The three checks are not mutually exclusive — multiple can co-occur — but working through them in this order (input-only checks first, since they don't require waiting for labels; then label-distribution checks; then full P(y|X) checks, which require both recent inputs and recent labels) prioritizes the checks that can be done fastest.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.use_when: Use this diagnostic framework whenever a production model's monitored performance metric (accuracy, AUC, calibration) degrades and the root cause isn't immediately obvious — it provides a structured triage path that avoids jumping straight to 'the model needs retraining' (the right response to concept drift) when the actual issue might be a label-distribution shift (which might call for threshold recalibration rather than full retraining) or even just a data-quality issue masquerading as data drift.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.avoid_when: When ground-truth labels are never available (a pure label-delay or no-label setting), the label-drift and concept-drift legs of this framework can't be directly checked via label-distribution comparison — in that case, NannyML-style label-free performance estimation (covered next) becomes the primary tool, since it estimates whether *performance itself* (which reflects concept/label drift jointly) has changed without requiring the labels that this diagnostic framework's later steps would otherwise need.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.what_goes_wrong: A common mistake is **treating 'no data drift detected' as proof that 'nothing is wrong' and stopping the investigation there** — since data drift checks (step 1) are the easiest and fastest to run (no labels needed), teams often run only these and conclude the model is fine if input distributions look stable, missing label drift or concept drift that wouldn't show up in input-distribution checks at all — a model's performance can degrade significantly due to concept drift (the relationship between inputs and outputs changing) while every individual input feature's distribution remains statistically indistinguishable from the reference period.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.real_example: A churn-prediction model's precision drops noticeably over a quarter. Step 1 (input PSI/domain-classifier checks) shows no significant data drift — customer feature distributions (tenure, usage, plan type) look stable. Step 2 (label distribution) shows the overall churn rate has increased from 5% to 8% — this is label drift: more customers are churning overall, independent of any change in their feature profiles. Step 3 (concept-level analysis on the subset where labels are available) further reveals that customers with a specific usage pattern (previously low-churn) are now churning at elevated rates — a new competitor's pricing promotion changed what that usage pattern *means* for churn risk, i.e., concept drift layered on top of the label drift. The combined diagnosis (label drift from a market-wide trend, plus concept drift in a specific segment) leads to a targeted retraining focused on that segment's features rather than a full model rebuild.

7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.what_it_is: This note deep-dives into NannyML's core algorithms — Confidence-Based Performance Estimation (CBPE) and Direct Loss Estimation (DLE) — both designed to estimate a production model's performance metrics (accuracy, AUC, F1, MAE, etc.) *without access to ground-truth labels*, addressing the label-delay problem where outcomes (e.g., whether a loan defaulted, whether a transaction was actually fraud) aren't known for days, weeks, or months after the prediction is made.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.why_it_exists: This is a second occurrence — the earlier note ('Whylogs, Arize, Fiddler, NannyML — alternatives,' Monitoring & Drift) mentioned NannyML briefly as one of several monitoring-tool alternatives without explaining its distinguishing technique. This note covers NannyML's actual core contribution: while PSI/KS/CvM/MMD/domain-classifier (all covered above) detect *input* drift, and the concept/label/data drift taxonomy (covered above) explains *why* performance might change, none of those directly answer 'what is my model's accuracy *right now*, today, for predictions made this week' when labels for this week's predictions won't be available for months — CBPE and DLE directly estimate that current performance number, closing the loop the taxonomy note explicitly flagged as needing a label-free solution.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.how_it_works: **CBPE** works for probabilistic classifiers: rather than waiting for true labels, it uses the model's own predicted probabilities (confidence scores) for current data, combined with the *known relationship* between confidence and correctness observed on a labeled reference/validation set (i.e., a calibration curve — 'when the model says 80% confident, how often is it actually right, based on validation data?'). For each current prediction, CBPE estimates the probability it's correct based on its confidence score and the reference calibration curve, then aggregates these per-prediction estimates into an estimated overall accuracy/AUC/F1 for the current period — effectively answering 'if the model's confidence-to-correctness relationship from validation still holds, what would today's accuracy be, given today's confidence scores?' **DLE** is more general (works for regression and cases where CBPE's calibration assumption is less suitable): it trains a *secondary model* whose job is to predict the primary model's error/loss for each prediction, using the same features as the primary model plus the primary model's prediction as inputs, trained on a labeled reference set; this secondary model is then applied to current (unlabeled) data to estimate the loss for each current prediction, which aggregates into an estimated performance metric.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.use_when: Use NannyML's CBPE/DLE when ground-truth labels are delayed (the common case for credit risk, fraud, churn, and many other business outcomes) and you need a *current* performance estimate for alerting/dashboards — rather than waiting weeks for labels to arrive before knowing whether the model's performance has degraded, CBPE/DLE provide a 'best estimate, available today' that can trigger investigation well before the lagged ground-truth confirmation arrives, directly addressing the diagnostic framework's (covered above) limitation when labels aren't yet available.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.avoid_when: CBPE's accuracy depends on the assumption that the confidence-to-correctness *calibration relationship* from the reference period still holds for current data — if the model's underlying behavior has changed dramatically (severe concept drift), this calibration assumption itself may break down, making CBPE's estimates unreliable exactly when they'd be most needed; in such cases, CBPE estimates should be treated as directional early-warning signals to be confirmed once real labels arrive, not as a permanent substitute for ground-truth-based evaluation.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is **CBPE estimates drifting away from reality without an obvious signal that something is wrong** — because CBPE's estimate is itself a model-based estimate (relying on the reference calibration curve), if that calibration relationship silently breaks down (e.g., due to concept drift changing what confidence scores 'mean'), CBPE will confidently report an estimated performance number that looks reasonable but is systematically wrong, and there's no automatic alarm for 'the calibration assumption underlying this estimate may no longer hold' — teams using CBPE/DLE need periodic 'reality checks' against actual labels (once available, even if delayed) to validate that the estimates have been tracking true performance, rather than treating the label-free estimates as infallible.
7|🟡 T2 🔬 Drift Detection (Deep)|Drift De.real_example: A credit-risk team's loan-default model has a 12-month label delay (you only know for certain whether a loan defaulted after up to a year). Using NannyML's CBPE, the team gets a daily *estimated* AUC for the model's recent predictions, based on the confidence-score calibration established during validation. Three months after a model update, the estimated AUC shows a gradual decline from 0.81 to 0.76 — well before any actual default outcomes for loans issued post-update are even available. This early estimated-performance signal prompts an investigation (which, combined with the drift-taxonomy framework above, traces the decline to a data-drift issue in a key income-verification feature caused by an upstream data-pipeline change) and a fix, months before the ground-truth-based evaluation would have surfaced the same degradation through the normal labeled-performance reporting cycle.

7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.what_it_is: This note presents a deployment-strategy **selection framework** covering four patterns side by side — canary (gradual traffic ramp to a new version with automated rollback gates), blue/green (instant full-traffic cutover between two complete parallel environments, with the old environment kept warm for instant rollback), shadow (new version receives mirrored traffic but its outputs are never user-facing), and A/B (a fixed traffic split between versions for statistical comparison) — organized around the question 'given this model change and this risk tolerance, which pattern fits?'
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.why_it_exists: This is at least a third occurrence of this strategy set — the earlier 'A/B testing, shadow deployment, canary releases' note (Monitoring & Drift) introduced the *concepts* of three of these strategies, and the Testing & Reliability notes on 'Shadow deployment' and 'Gradual rollout — canary deployment' each deep-dived into the *automation mechanics* of running shadow tests and canary pipelines as CD stages. This note adds **blue/green** (not previously covered) and reframes all four as a **decision framework** — given specific constraints (need for instant rollback? need for statistical confidence vs. business metrics? infrastructure cost tolerance? can the new version's outputs be silently discarded?), which pattern(s) apply — a selection-criteria framing distinct from both the prior conceptual-definitions framing and the prior automation-mechanics framing.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.how_it_works: The decision framework runs through key axes: **Rollback speed** — blue/green offers the fastest rollback (instant traffic-switch back to the still-running 'blue' environment, no need to re-deploy), while canary's rollback is also fast (route traffic back to 100% old version) but the canary's already-served requests already happened; shadow has zero user-facing rollback risk since it never serves users. **Infrastructure cost** — blue/green requires running two full-capacity environments simultaneously (2x infrastructure during the cutover window), while canary and shadow can run the new version at a much smaller scale (just enough to handle the canary traffic percentage, or to process mirrored shadow traffic). **Statistical rigor** — A/B testing is the only one of the four designed for formal statistical comparison (with pre-registered sample sizes and significance tests), whereas canary's traffic ramp is typically driven by health-check thresholds (error rates, latency) rather than a designed experiment. **Risk to real outputs** — shadow is the only pattern where the new version's predictions never affect a real user, making it the safest first step for high-risk changes, often used as a precursor stage before canary/A-B.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.use_when: Use this framework when planning a deployment pipeline for a new model version and multiple stages are warranted: e.g., shadow first (validate the new model can run in production and compare its predictions against the live model with zero user risk) → canary (gradually expose real users with automated rollback gates) → A/B test (once the canary has proven stable at, say, 10-20% traffic, run a longer, statistically-designed comparison to confirm the business-metric impact before full rollout) — combining patterns in sequence rather than choosing just one, with blue/green reserved for changes where instant full-cutover/rollback is specifically valuable (e.g., infrastructure or serving-stack changes where a gradual ramp doesn't make sense).
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.avoid_when: Don't default to the most elaborate multi-stage pipeline (shadow → canary → A/B → full rollout) for every change — for low-risk changes (e.g., a minor prompt-template tweak with strong offline eval coverage), a simple canary with tight automated gates may be sufficient, and running a full sequence for every change slows down iteration speed without proportional risk reduction; match the pipeline's elaborateness to the change's actual risk profile.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.what_goes_wrong: A common mistake is **treating these patterns as mutually exclusive choices rather than complementary stages**, leading teams to either over-invest (running a full A/B test for every trivial change, burning weeks of calendar time waiting for statistical significance on changes that don't need it) or under-invest (skipping straight to canary/full-rollout for changes that would have benefited from a shadow-deployment validation step first, especially for changes where the new model's *raw outputs* — not just aggregate metrics — need scrutiny before any user sees them).
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.real_example: A team rolling out a new fraud-detection model uses all four patterns in sequence over two weeks: shadow deployment for 3 days (comparing the new model's flagging decisions against the current model's on live transactions, with zero impact on users, surfacing a class of transactions where the new model disagreed significantly); canary at 5% → 25% → 50% over the next 4 days (with automated gates on false-positive rate and latency, catching and auto-rolling-back once at the 25% stage due to a latency regression that was then fixed); a 1-week A/B test at 50/50 to get statistically significant business-metric comparisons (fraud caught vs. false declines) before committing; and finally a blue/green cutover for the production database schema change that accompanied the new model (where instant rollback capability was valued because a schema issue would be harder to gradually unwind than a model-output issue).

7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.what_it_is: Champion/challenger is a deployment pattern where the current production model (the 'champion') continues serving the primary traffic while one or more candidate models (the 'challengers') run continuously alongside it — receiving either a small slice of live traffic or shadow traffic — with their performance tracked over an extended period; a challenger that consistently outperforms the champion on the metrics that matter is promoted to become the new champion, and the old champion may itself become a challenger (or be retired).
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.why_it_exists: A/B testing (covered in the previous note) is typically a *time-boxed experiment* — run for a defined period to reach statistical significance on a specific question, then concluded. Champion/challenger is instead an **ongoing operational pattern** — common in domains with periodic model refreshes (credit scoring, recommendation systems, ad ranking) where new candidate models are continuously trained (e.g., weekly retraining) and need a standing process for deciding 'should this week's new model replace the current production model?' rather than a one-off experiment design — it exists to make 'is the new model better?' a routine, repeatable operational question rather than a bespoke experiment each time.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.how_it_works: The champion model serves the bulk (or all) of production traffic and is the system of record. One or more challenger models are deployed alongside it — either receiving a small percentage of live traffic (similar to a low-traffic canary, but intended to run *indefinitely* rather than ramp up) or receiving shadow traffic. Performance metrics for champion and each challenger are tracked continuously on a rolling window (e.g., trailing 30 days) using the same evaluation criteria. A promotion decision process — which can be manual (a model-risk committee reviews challenger performance periodically) or automated (a challenger that beats the champion by a defined margin for a sustained period is auto-promoted) — determines whether/when a challenger becomes the new champion. The previous champion is often retained as a challenger or fallback for some period, providing a built-in comparison baseline for the new champion's early performance.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.use_when: Use champion/challenger in settings with frequent model retraining where you need an ongoing, low-overhead way to validate that each new model candidate is actually an improvement before it becomes the default — particularly valuable in regulated domains (credit risk) where a documented, repeatable comparison process (rather than ad-hoc one-off A/B tests for each model update) supports model-governance and audit requirements.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.avoid_when: For one-off model changes (not part of a recurring retraining cadence) or for changes where a quick, time-boxed A/B test can answer the question adequately, setting up an ongoing champion/challenger comparison infrastructure is more operational overhead than needed — champion/challenger's value comes from amortizing the comparison infrastructure across *many* recurring model updates, which doesn't pay off for a single isolated change.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is **challenger models accumulating without clear retirement criteria** — if multiple challengers are continuously evaluated alongside the champion but the promotion bar is rarely met (or promotion decisions are slow/political), teams end up running and monitoring many stale challenger models indefinitely, consuming serving infrastructure and monitoring attention without ever being promoted or retired — a defined challenger lifecycle (e.g., 'a challenger that hasn't beaten the champion within 90 days is retired') prevents this accumulation.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.real_example: A recommendation-system team retrains candidate ranking models weekly. Each new candidate becomes a challenger, receiving 2% of traffic alongside the reigning champion (which serves 98%). Click-through-rate and downstream conversion are tracked on a trailing 14-day window for both. Most weeks, the new challenger's metrics are within noise of the champion's and it's retired without promotion; roughly once a month, a challenger shows a sustained, statistically meaningful CTR improvement and is promoted to champion, with the previous champion demoted to challenger status (where it continues to serve as a sanity-check baseline for a few weeks before being fully retired).

7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.what_it_is: Multi-armed bandit (MAB) deployment optimization uses bandit algorithms (epsilon-greedy, Upper Confidence Bound/UCB, or Thompson sampling) to *dynamically* allocate production traffic among multiple model variants based on their observed performance so far, continuously shifting more traffic toward better-performing variants — in contrast to A/B testing's fixed traffic split that doesn't change until the experiment concludes.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.why_it_exists: A/B testing's fixed split (e.g., 50/50) means that for the entire duration of the experiment, a meaningful fraction of users are served by whichever variant turns out to be worse — this is the cost of 'exploration' in service of statistical confidence. Multi-armed bandits exist to reduce this cost: by continuously adapting the traffic split toward the variant that's performing better *so far*, bandits minimize 'regret' (the cumulative loss from serving suboptimal variants during the comparison period) — valuable when the cost of serving a worse variant is high (e.g., directly impacts revenue per request) and a fixed-split experiment's exploration cost is undesirable.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.how_it_works: **Epsilon-greedy**: with probability (1-ε), route traffic to the currently-best-performing variant; with probability ε, route to a random variant (to keep exploring in case the 'best' variant's lead is due to noise or conditions change). **UCB (Upper Confidence Bound)**: for each variant, compute an upper-confidence-bound estimate of its true performance (combining its observed average performance with an 'uncertainty bonus' that's larger for variants with less data) and route traffic to the variant with the highest UCB — this naturally balances exploiting known-good variants with exploring under-sampled ones, since under-sampled variants get a larger uncertainty bonus. **Thompson sampling**: maintain a probability distribution (e.g., Bayesian posterior) over each variant's true performance based on observed data, and for each incoming request, sample from each variant's distribution and route to whichever variant's sample is highest — variants with more favorable and/or more certain posteriors get more traffic, automatically. All three approaches continuously update their traffic allocation as new performance data arrives, rather than fixing a split upfront.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.use_when: Use multi-armed bandits when comparing multiple model variants (more than two is common) where the cost of serving a worse variant is directly tied to a measurable per-request outcome (click, conversion, revenue) that's observable quickly — e.g., ad/content ranking, pricing, or recommendation variants — and where minimizing cumulative exploration cost matters more than obtaining a clean, fixed-sample-size statistical comparison.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.avoid_when: When the goal is to make a *confident, defensible decision* about which variant is better (e.g., for a launch decision that will be reviewed by stakeholders, or where a specific statistical-significance threshold is a documented requirement), A/B testing's fixed design and well-understood significance-testing framework is more appropriate — bandit algorithms optimize for *minimizing regret during* the comparison, not for producing the cleanest possible *evidence* of which variant is better, and their traffic allocations can be harder to translate into a simple 'variant B was X% better with Y% confidence' statement.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is **bandits converging prematurely on a variant due to early noise** — if one variant happens to get lucky outcomes early on (small-sample variance), epsilon-greedy or UCB algorithms with poorly-tuned exploration parameters can shift traffic heavily toward that variant before enough data has accumulated to know whether the early lead is real, and because the disadvantaged variant then receives less traffic, it takes even longer to accumulate enough data to potentially overturn that early (possibly incorrect) lead — a 'rich get richer' dynamic that can lock in a suboptimal variant; sufficient initial exploration (or algorithms like Thompson sampling that naturally account for uncertainty) mitigates this but doesn't eliminate it.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.real_example: An e-commerce site tests five different product-ranking model variants for a category page using Thompson sampling on click-through rate. Initially, traffic is split roughly evenly across all five (high uncertainty for each). Within a few days, two variants pull ahead and receive an increasing share of traffic, while the other three (which performed clearly worse early on) receive diminishing but non-zero traffic (Thompson sampling never fully zeroes out a variant, preserving some ongoing exploration in case conditions change). After two weeks, one variant has emerged as the clear winner and receives the large majority of traffic — achieving this without ever fixing a 20%-per-variant split for the full two weeks, reducing the cumulative CTR loss compared to what a fixed 5-way A/B test would have cost during the same period.

7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.what_it_is: This note deep-dives into the specific products — LaunchDarkly, Unleash, and Flagsmith — as feature-flag platforms applied to ML deployment patterns: each provides a dashboard/SDK combination for defining flags (boolean toggles, multivariate flags for model-version selection, or percentage-rollout flags), targeting rules (which users/segments see which variant), and instant remote updates (SDKs poll or stream flag-state changes without requiring a redeploy).
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.why_it_exists: This is a second occurrence — the earlier 'Feature flag management' note (Additional Production Tools) introduced feature flags conceptually as a 'kill switch' and runtime-control mechanism, listing these three tools at a high level. This note covers them as **concrete building blocks for the deployment patterns in this subtopic**: a percentage-rollout flag in LaunchDarkly/Unleash/Flagsmith can implement the traffic-ramping of a canary deployment (covered above) at the application layer rather than the infrastructure layer; a targeting-rule flag can implement an A/B test's traffic split with fine-grained segment control (e.g., 'only users in this country see the new model'); and the instant-toggle capability is what makes a feature flag a faster rollback mechanism than even blue/green's environment-switch — the focus here is on *how these specific products' features map onto the deployment patterns* already discussed, not on the general kill-switch concept.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.how_it_works: **LaunchDarkly**: enterprise SaaS platform; flags can be boolean, multivariate (e.g., a flag returning 'model-v1' / 'model-v2' / 'model-v3' strings used to select which model endpoint to call), or percentage-based; targeting rules combine user attributes (segment, region, account tier) with percentage rollouts within segments; includes built-in experimentation features that tie flag exposure to metric tracking, effectively providing A/B-test infrastructure on top of the flag system. **Unleash**: open-source (with a paid enterprise/cloud option), self-hostable, with a similar flag-types/targeting-rules model; its self-hosted nature is often chosen for data-residency or cost reasons at scale (avoiding per-seat/per-MAU SaaS pricing). **Flagsmith**: also open-source and self-hostable, organizes flags within an organization → project → environment hierarchy (e.g., separate flag states for dev/staging/production environments of the same project), with SDKs for evaluating flags client-side or server-side. Across all three, the application code calls the SDK at the decision point ('which model should I call for this request?'), and the SDK returns a value based on the current flag configuration — changes to that configuration (made via the platform's dashboard or API) propagate to running application instances within seconds, without a deployment.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.use_when: Use a feature-flag platform as the traffic-routing layer for deployment patterns when the routing decision needs to be made *within application code* (e.g., 'which model endpoint should this request call') rather than at the infrastructure/networking layer (e.g., Kubernetes service mesh traffic splitting) — flag-based routing is often faster to change (instant, no infra changes) and easier for non-infrastructure teams (product managers, data scientists) to control via a dashboard, making it well-suited for business-logic-level rollout decisions (which model variant a user sees) as opposed to infrastructure-level rollout decisions (which pod version receives traffic).
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.avoid_when: For purely infrastructure-level rollout decisions (shifting traffic between Kubernetes deployments of the same service, independent of application-level business logic), infrastructure-native progressive-delivery tools (Argo Rollouts, Flagger — covered next) operate at the right layer without requiring application code to call a flag-evaluation SDK on every request — using a feature-flag platform for what is fundamentally an infrastructure traffic-split adds an unnecessary application-level dependency and another system to keep in sync with the actual deployed infrastructure state.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is **flag sprawl and stale flags** — once a model rollout is complete and a flag has served its purpose (e.g., 'use-new-recommendation-model', now at 100% for months), if the flag and its associated conditional code branches aren't cleaned up, the codebase accumulates dead flag-check branches and the flag-management dashboard accumulates flags whose current state no one remembers the reason for — over time this makes it harder to reason about what's actually running in production ('is this flag at 100% because we finished the rollout, or because someone set it to 100% temporarily during an incident and forgot to revert?'), requiring periodic flag-cleanup processes.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.real_example: A team uses LaunchDarkly to roll out a new LLM-based summarization model: a multivariate flag 'summarization-model-version' returns 'gpt-4-baseline' or 'claude-challenger' based on a percentage rollout (starting at 5%, the team manually increases it via the LaunchDarkly dashboard as monitoring confirms healthy latency/cost/quality metrics — implementing the canary pattern's traffic ramp without any infrastructure changes). When a quality regression is noticed at 25% traffic, an on-call engineer flips the flag back to 0% for the challenger via the dashboard — taking effect within seconds across all running application instances, faster than even a blue/green infrastructure cutover would have been, because no infrastructure state changed at all, only the application-level routing decision.

7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.what_it_is: This note deep-dives into Argo Rollouts and Flagger — the two leading Kubernetes-native progressive-delivery controllers — as the specific tools that implement the automated canary-rollout mechanics described in the earlier 'Gradual rollout — canary deployment' note: both replace a standard Kubernetes Deployment's all-at-once rolling update with a controller-managed, staged traffic shift, automatically querying metrics and deciding whether to proceed, pause, or roll back at each stage.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.why_it_exists: This is a second occurrence — the earlier 'Gradual rollout — canary deployment' note (Testing & Reliability) covered the *general pattern* of automated, gated traffic-ramping (1% → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% with health-check gates) without naming specific implementing tools. This note covers the two dominant **tool-specific implementations**: Argo Rollouts (a CRD-based controller, part of the Argo project alongside Argo CD/Argo Workflows — connecting to GitOps/CD pipeline concepts) and Flagger (a Flux-ecosystem operator) — covering how each integrates with Kubernetes traffic-management mechanisms (service meshes, ingress controllers, load balancers) and metrics providers to actually execute the staged rollout described conceptually in the earlier note.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.how_it_works: **Argo Rollouts** introduces a `Rollout` custom resource that replaces a standard `Deployment` — it defines the canary steps (traffic percentages and pause durations) and `AnalysisTemplate` resources that specify metrics queries (against Prometheus, Datadog, or other providers) and success/failure thresholds for each step; traffic shifting is delegated to a traffic-management plugin — Argo Rollouts integrates with Istio, Linkerd, SMI, NGINX Ingress, or cloud load balancers (ALB) to actually split traffic at the specified percentages. As each step completes, Argo Rollouts runs the associated `AnalysisRun`, querying the configured metrics, and automatically promotes to the next step, pauses for manual approval, or aborts and rolls back based on the analysis result. **Flagger** operates similarly but as part of the Flux GitOps ecosystem — it watches a target Deployment, and on a new version's rollout, creates a temporary canary Deployment, gradually shifts traffic (via a service mesh like Istio/Linkerd or via Gateway API) while querying Prometheus metrics, and automatically promotes (copies the new version to the primary Deployment) or rolls back based on metric thresholds — Flagger's design emphasizes integration with GitOps (a Git commit triggers the new version, Flagger handles the progressive rollout automatically without further manual steps).
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.use_when: Use Argo Rollouts if the team is already invested in the Argo ecosystem (Argo CD for GitOps deployments, Argo Workflows for pipelines — both covered elsewhere in this phase) for consistency, or if fine-grained manual control over promotion (pause-for-approval steps) is important. Use Flagger if the team uses Flux for GitOps and wants progressive delivery to be a largely hands-off extension of the existing GitOps flow (commit → automatic progressive rollout → automatic promotion/rollback, with minimal manual intervention).
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.avoid_when: For teams not running Kubernetes (e.g., serverless model endpoints, managed platforms like SageMaker or Vertex AI that have their own built-in canary/traffic-splitting features), Argo Rollouts and Flagger don't apply — those platforms' native deployment-traffic-splitting features (covered in the AWS group of this phase, for example) serve the same progressive-delivery goal without needing a Kubernetes-native controller; introducing Argo Rollouts/Flagger only makes sense when the serving infrastructure is already Kubernetes-based.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.what_goes_wrong: A common issue is **metrics-provider misconfiguration causing analysis steps to silently pass or fail incorrectly** — both Argo Rollouts' `AnalysisTemplate` and Flagger's metric checks depend on correctly-configured queries against the metrics backend (e.g., a Prometheus query for error rate scoped to the canary pods specifically); if the query is misconfigured (e.g., it accidentally queries metrics for *all* pods including the stable version, diluting any canary-specific signal), the analysis step can report 'healthy' even when the canary itself is failing, defeating the purpose of the automated gate — validating that analysis queries are correctly scoped to the canary's specific pods/version label is essential and easy to get wrong.
7|🔴 T1 🔬 Deployment Patterns|Deployment.real_example: A team deploying a new model-serving container uses Argo Rollouts with an `AnalysisTemplate` that queries Prometheus for the canary pods' p99 latency and error rate every 2 minutes during each traffic-percentage step (10% → 30% → 60% → 100%, each held for 10 minutes). During a rollout, the analysis at the 30% step detects the canary's error rate exceeding the threshold (a memory-leak-induced OOM under the increased traffic share) and Argo Rollouts automatically aborts the rollout, scales the canary back to 0%, and routes all traffic back to the stable version — all without any human intervention, surfacing only an alert that the rollout was automatically aborted along with the analysis results that triggered it, for the team to investigate the memory leak before retrying.
